content.text: Based on the CLARB Exam Blueprint (Effective December 2023)
90 Scored Items | Computer-Based | Multiple Choice + Graphic AITs
3-Hour Time Limit
Note: Update the Table of Contents after opening in Word by right-clicking and selecting 'Update Field.'

LARE Section 1, Inventory, Analysis, and Project Management, tests your ability to gather, analyze, and synthesize site information and manage the pre-design phase of landscape architecture projects. It is one of four sections of the Landscape Architect Registration Examination (L.A.R.E.) administered by the Council of Landscape Architectural Registration Boards (CLARB).
Format: Computer-based, consisting of multiple-choice questions and graphic Advanced Item Types (AITs)
The exam is organized into five content domains. Understanding the weight of each domain should directly inform how you allocate your study time.
EXAM TIP: Physical Analysis alone accounts for nearly 40% of the exam. Dedicate proportional study time to soils, hydrology, topography, vegetation, and climate analysis.
•  Allocate study time proportionally to domain weights. Physical Analysis deserves the most time.
•  Practice reading maps, soil surveys, FIRM maps, and aerial photographs. The exam includes graphic AIT questions requiring interpretation of visual data.
•  Know your data sources: match the right agency/tool to the right data type (USGS for topography, NRCS for soils, FEMA for flood data, Census Bureau for demographics).
•  Create flashcards for regulatory terms and acronyms (NEPA, NHPA, Section 404, PROWAG, IAP2).
•  Take practice exams under timed conditions 2 weeks before the exam. Use the free CLARB demo exam to familiarize yourself with the testing platform.
•  Use the flag-and-return strategy: on the computer-based exam, flag difficult questions and return to them after completing easier ones.
•  Read questions carefully. Many wrong answers are partially correct. Look for the MOST correct or PRIMARY answer.

This is the highest-weighted domain on the exam. It tests your ability to analyze natural and physical site conditions including soils, topography, hydrology, vegetation, climate, ecology, and utilities.

Soil is a dynamic, natural body composed of mineral particles, organic matter, water, and air. Understanding soil is fundamental to virtually every aspect of landscape architecture, from grading and drainage to plant selection and structural design.
O Horizon: Organic layer of decomposing plant and animal matter on the surface
A Horizon (Topsoil): Dark, mineral-rich layer with organic matter; most biological activity occurs here; critical for plant growth
B Horizon (Subsoil): Accumulation of clay, iron oxides, and minerals leached from above; often denser and less fertile
C Horizon: Weathered parent material; partially broken-down bedrock with little biological activity
R Horizon (Bedrock): Unweathered solid rock underlying all soil layers
•  Climate (temperature, precipitation)
•  Living organisms (vegetation, microorganisms, fauna)
•  Relief/Topography (slope, aspect, elevation)
•  Parent material (bedrock, glacial deposits, alluvium)
•  Time (duration of soil development)
Soil texture refers to the relative proportions of sand, silt, and clay in a soil sample. The USDA Soil Texture Triangle classifies soil into 12 texture classes based on these proportions.

rows: Gritty feel; large pore spaces; drains quickly; low nutrient-holding capacity
Smooth, flour-like feel; moderate drainage; moderate fertility; erosion-prone when wet
Sticky when wet, hard when dry; very small pore spaces; slow drainage; high nutrient-holding capacity; shrink-swell potential

content.text: Loam: The ideal soil for most landscape applications, loam is a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay (roughly 40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay). It combines good drainage with adequate moisture and nutrient retention.

EXAM TIP: Exam questions often ask you to identify soil behavior from texture descriptions. Remember: Sand = fast drainage, low nutrients. Clay = slow drainage, high nutrients, shrink-swell risk. Loam = balanced, ideal for planting.

The NRCS (Natural Resources Conservation Service) classifies soils into four Hydrologic Soil Groups based on their runoff potential and infiltration rates. These groups are essential for stormwater calculations.

rows: Moderately deep, well-drained; silt loam, loam
Soils with a layer that impedes drainage; sandy clay loam
Clay soils, high water table, shallow to bedrock

content.text: EXAM TIP: HSGs move from A (best infiltration, least runoff) to D (worst infiltration, most runoff). For stormwater infiltration BMPs like rain gardens, Group A and B soils are most suitable. Group D soils are problematic and may require underdrains.
The NRCS Web Soil Survey (websoilsurvey.nrcs.usda.gov) is the primary free tool for accessing detailed soil data for any location in the United States. It provides:
•  Soil map units and their geographic extent
•  Soil properties: texture, depth, drainage class, permeability, pH, shrink-swell potential
•  Suitability ratings for various land uses (building, agriculture, recreation)
•  Hydrologic Soil Group classification
•  Hydric soil identification (a key wetland indicator)
•  Erosion hazard ratings (K-factor)

Hydric Soils: Soils that formed under conditions of saturation, flooding, or ponding long enough during the growing season to develop anaerobic conditions. Hydric soils are one of three indicators used to delineate jurisdictional wetlands (along with hydrophytic vegetation and wetland hydrology).
Bearing Capacity: The ability of soil to support structural loads without excessive settlement. Sandy and gravelly soils generally have higher bearing capacity than clay soils.

Shrink-Swell Potential: The tendency of clay soils to expand when wet and shrink when dry. High shrink-swell soils can damage foundations, pavements, and utilities. Common in soils with montmorillonite clay.
Frost Susceptibility: Silty soils are most susceptible to frost heave because their pore sizes draw water upward through capillary action, which then freezes and expands.
Erosion Potential (K-Factor): A measure of a soil's susceptibility to erosion by water. Silty soils have the highest K-factors (most erodible). Sandy and clay soils are generally more resistant.
Percolation Rate: The speed at which water moves through saturated soil, measured in inches per hour. Critical for septic system design and stormwater infiltration feasibility.
Topographic maps use contour lines to represent three-dimensional terrain on a two-dimensional surface. Mastering contour interpretation is essential for the exam.
•  Contour lines connect points of equal elevation.
•  Closely spaced contours indicate steep slopes; widely spaced contours indicate gentle slopes.
•  Contour lines forming a V pointing uphill indicate a valley, swale, or drainage channel.
•  Contour lines forming a V pointing downhill indicate a ridge or spur.
•  Contour lines never cross (except in rare overhanging cliff situations).
•  Concentric closed contours indicate a hilltop (if increasing elevation) or a depression (if decreasing, often marked with hachures).
•  Evenly spaced contours indicate a uniform slope.
•  Water flows perpendicular to contour lines.
Slope is expressed as a percentage, ratio, or angle. For the LARE exam, percentage and ratio are most commonly used.
Example: If two contour lines are 4 feet apart in elevation over a horizontal distance of 80 feet: Slope = (4 / 80) x 100 = 5%
Slope Ratios: Expressed as horizontal:vertical (H:V). A 3:1 slope means 3 feet of horizontal distance for every 1 foot of vertical rise = 33.3%.

rows: Nearly flat; poor surface drainage; ponding risk; may require subsurface drainage
Ideal for most development; adequate drainage; ADA accessible routes (max 5% running slope)
Moderate slope; comfortable for walking paths; requires grading attention
Steep for development; limited building suitability; erosion concerns increase
Steep; significant grading/retaining walls needed; high erosion risk; limited recreation use
Very steep; maximum for mowable turf grass (3:1); development generally discouraged
Extremely steep; unsuitable for most development; preserve as open space/natural area

content.text: EXAM TIP: Key slope thresholds to memorize: 1-2% minimum for surface drainage; 5% max for ADA accessible routes; 8.33% (1:12) max for ADA ramps; 33% (3:1) max for mowable turf; 50% (2:1) max for stabilized slopes without structures.
Aspect is the compass direction that a slope faces. In the Northern Hemisphere:
•  South-facing slopes receive the most direct sunlight (warmest, driest, earliest snowmelt).
•  North-facing slopes receive the least direct sunlight (coolest, most moist, retain snow longest).
•  East-facing slopes receive morning sun (good for many plants; gentler light).
•  West-facing slopes receive afternoon sun (hottest, most intense; can stress plants).
Aspect affects plant selection, microclimate, building orientation, energy efficiency, and snow/ice management.
A watershed (drainage basin or catchment) is the area of land where all precipitation drains to a common outlet point. Understanding watershed boundaries and behavior is critical for site analysis.
Drainage Divide: The ridge or high point that separates adjacent watersheds. Water falling on either side flows to different outlets.

Time of Concentration (Tc): The time required for runoff to travel from the hydraulically most distant point in a watershed to the outlet. Longer Tc = lower peak flows; shorter Tc = higher peak flows.
Watershed Area: The total contributing drainage area, measured in acres or square miles. Directly affects runoff volume.
The Rational Method is the most commonly used formula for estimating peak stormwater runoff from small drainage areas (< 200 acres). It is essential LARE knowledge.

subsections.title: Q = C x i x A

content.text: Q: Peak runoff rate (cubic feet per second, cfs)
C: Runoff coefficient (dimensionless, 0 to 1). Represents the fraction of rainfall that becomes surface runoff. Higher C = more runoff.
i: Rainfall intensity (inches per hour). Based on the design storm frequency and the time of concentration.
A: Drainage area (acres)

EXAM TIP: Development increases the C coefficient by replacing pervious surfaces (forest, lawn) with impervious surfaces (roofs, pavement). This directly increases peak runoff Q, which is why stormwater management is required for new development.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) creates Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs) that delineate flood hazard areas. Understanding FIRM maps is critical for site analysis.

100-Year Floodplain (Zone A/AE): Area with a 1% annual chance of flooding. This does NOT mean it floods once every 100 years; it means there is a 1 in 100 chance of flooding in any given year. Construction in this zone is heavily regulated.
500-Year Floodplain (Zone X - Shaded): Area with a 0.2% annual chance of flooding. Moderate flood risk; fewer regulatory restrictions.
Zone X (Unshaded): Minimal flood risk. Areas outside the 500-year floodplain.
Floodway: The channel and adjacent land that must remain unobstructed to convey the base flood discharge. No development permitted in the floodway.
Base Flood Elevation (BFE): The elevation to which floodwater is expected to rise during the 100-year flood. Structures in Zone AE must have their lowest floor at or above the BFE.
EXAM TIP: The 100-year flood has a 1% annual chance of occurring, not a literal 100-year cycle. A property in the 100-year floodplain has a 26% chance of flooding during a 30-year mortgage.

Water Table: The upper surface of the zone of saturation in the ground. A high water table affects foundation design, basement feasibility, plant root development, and subsurface drainage requirements.
Perched Water Table: A localized zone of saturation above the regional water table, typically caused by an impermeable layer (such as clay or bedrock) that prevents downward water movement.
Aquifer: A geological formation that can store and transmit significant quantities of groundwater. Aquifer recharge areas should be protected from contamination.
Baseflow: Groundwater discharge into a stream. Maintains stream flow during dry periods.
Riparian Zone: The vegetated area along a stream, river, or water body. Riparian buffers filter pollutants, stabilize banks, reduce erosion, moderate water temperature, and provide wildlife habitat.
Vegetation patterns reveal underlying site conditions. Landscape architects must be able to read plant communities as indicators of soil moisture, drainage, disturbance, and ecological health.

rows: Wetland conditions / hydric soils / high water table
Disturbed sites, poor soils, early succession

content.text: Ecological succession is the predictable, sequential change in plant community composition over time.
Primary Succession: Occurs on newly formed or exposed surfaces with no prior soil (e.g., lava flows, retreating glaciers). Begins with pioneer species like lichens and mosses.
Secondary Succession: Occurs on sites where existing vegetation has been disturbed or removed, but soil remains (e.g., after fire, logging, or abandonment). Much faster than primary succession.
Climax Community: The stable, mature endpoint of succession that is in equilibrium with local conditions.
Typical Secondary Succession Sequence: Bare soil > Annual weeds/grasses > Perennial grasses/herbs > Shrubs/saplings > Shade-intolerant pioneer trees > Shade-tolerant climax forest
Habitat Corridor: A linear landscape feature (stream buffer, hedgerow, greenway) that connects fragmented habitat patches, allowing wildlife movement and gene flow between populations.
Edge Effect: The transition zone between two different habitats (e.g., forest and meadow). Edges support higher species diversity but can also allow invasive species to penetrate interior habitats.
Patch-Corridor-Matrix Model: A landscape ecology framework. Patches are distinct habitat areas; corridors connect them; the matrix is the dominant background land cover.
Endemic Species: Species native to and found only in a particular geographic area. Their habitats require special protection.
Invasive Species: Non-native species that spread aggressively, displacing native vegetation and disrupting ecosystems. Site inventory should document their presence and extent.
When inventorying trees on a project site, the following data should be collected for each significant tree:
•  Species (botanical and common name)
•  DBH (Diameter at Breast Height) measured at 4.5 feet above grade
•  Canopy spread (drip line diameter)
•  Condition (health, structural integrity, disease, pest damage)
•  Critical Root Zone (CRZ): The area around a tree where roots essential for stability and health are located. Typically extends 1 foot of radius per 1 inch of DBH, minimum.
Understanding sun angles and orientation is critical for site planning, plant selection, and energy-efficient design.
•  In the Northern Hemisphere, the sun is always in the southern sky.
•  Summer sun is high in the sky (high altitude angle) and rises/sets north of due east/west, resulting in long days.
•  Winter sun is low in the sky (low altitude angle) and rises/sets south of due east/west, resulting in short days.
•  South-facing building facades receive the most consistent year-round solar exposure.
•  Deciduous trees on the south and west sides of buildings provide summer shade while allowing winter solar gain.
Prevailing wind direction varies by region and season. In much of the continental US, prevailing winter winds come from the northwest, while summer breezes often come from the south or southwest.
•  Evergreen windbreaks should be placed on the windward side (typically northwest) to block winter winds.
•  Windbreaks are most effective at a height-to-distance ratio of about 1:10 (protection extends ~10x the height of the windbreak on the leeward side).
•  Buildings, walls, and dense vegetation can create wind tunnels that accelerate wind speed in narrow gaps.
Urban areas are significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas due to:
•  Large areas of dark-colored impervious surfaces (asphalt, rooftops) that absorb and re-radiate heat
•  Reduced vegetation and tree canopy that would otherwise provide cooling through evapotranspiration and shade
•  Waste heat from vehicles, HVAC systems, and industrial processes
•  Reduced wind flow due to building density
Mitigation strategies: Increase tree canopy, use high-albedo (reflective) paving and roofing materials, install green roofs, reduce impervious surface area, incorporate water features.

The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map divides North America into 13 zones based on average annual minimum winter temperature. Each zone spans a 10-degree F range, with 5-degree sub-zones (a and b). This is the standard reference for determining which plants can survive winter in a given location.

The frost line (frost depth) is the maximum depth to which soil freezes in winter. It varies by climate zone (from 0 inches in southern Florida to 72+ inches in northern Alaska). Footings, water lines, and other underground structures must be placed below the frost line to prevent frost heave damage.
During site inventory, the landscape architect must identify and document all existing utilities:
•  Water supply lines, sanitary sewer, storm sewer
•  Gas lines, electrical lines (overhead and underground), telecommunications
•  Easements and rights-of-way that restrict development
•  Utility setback requirements from structures and other improvements

811 "Call Before You Dig": Before any excavation, contractors are required to call 811 to have underground utilities marked. Landscape architects should reference utility plans and verify locations during site inventory.
EXAM TIP: Utility conflicts are a common source of project delays and change orders. Accurate utility location during inventory prevents costly surprises during construction.

s1_guide.title: Part 3: Inventory and Data Collection (21% of Exam)

content.text: This domain tests your knowledge of data sources, survey methods, mapping fundamentals, GIS, remote sensing, and legal documents used in site inventory.
Know which federal, state, and local agencies provide which types of data:

rows: Topographic maps (7.5-minute quadrangles), elevation data, geologic maps, water resource data, National Map
Soil surveys (Web Soil Survey), soil properties, hydrologic soil groups, hydric soils, land capability classes
Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs), floodplain boundaries, Base Flood Elevations, National Flood Hazard Layer
Population, demographics, housing, socioeconomic data, American Community Survey
Environmental regulations, Superfund sites, brownfield data, water quality standards
Wetlands inventory (National Wetlands Inventory), endangered species data, critical habitat designations
Climate data, precipitation records, weather patterns, coastal data
Historic resource inventories, National Register of Historic Places data, Section 106 coordination
Zoning maps, land use plans, setback requirements, overlay districts, development codes
Property records, plats, deeds, easements, rights-of-way

content.text: EXAM TIP: A common exam question format: 'Which agency/source would you consult to determine [specific data]?' Match the data type to the correct agency.
Base Map/Survey: A scaled drawing showing property boundaries, topography, existing structures, utilities, and other physical features. Prepared by a licensed surveyor.
Topographic Survey: A survey that maps the elevation and contours of a site, including spot elevations of key features.
Boundary Survey: A survey that establishes legal property lines and corners, referencing monuments and legal descriptions.
Field Reconnaissance: A firsthand site visit to observe and document conditions not shown on maps: vegetation, drainage patterns, views, microclimate, adjacent land uses, sensory qualities.
Photographic Documentation: Systematic photographs of site conditions keyed to a site plan. Provides a visual record for analysis and future reference.
Primary Data: Data collected firsthand through field surveys, observations, and measurements. More accurate but more expensive and time-consuming.
Secondary Data: Data from existing sources (maps, reports, databases). Efficient but may be outdated or at an inappropriate scale.
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are powerful tools for layering, analyzing, and visualizing spatial data. GIS is used extensively in site analysis, planning, and environmental assessment.

rows: Represents features as discrete points, lines, and polygons with precise coordinates. Best for features with defined boundaries (property lines, roads, buildings, utilities).
Represents data as a grid of cells (pixels), each with a value. Best for continuous data (elevation, temperature, land cover, satellite imagery).
Different datasets (topography, soils, vegetation, zoning) stored as separate layers that can be overlaid for analysis.
Operations like buffering, overlay, proximity analysis, and suitability modeling that combine layers to answer questions.
The mathematical method used to represent the 3D earth on a 2D map. Common projections include UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator) and State Plane.
Reference frameworks for locating features. Include geographic (latitude/longitude) and projected (UTM, State Plane) systems.
The process of aligning spatial data to a known coordinate system.

content.text: Ian McHarg's Overlay Method: Pioneered in 'Design with Nature' (1969), McHarg's suitability analysis involved overlaying transparent maps of different environmental factors (slope, soils, hydrology, vegetation) to identify areas suitable or unsuitable for development. GIS is the digital evolution of this method.

Aerial Photography: Photographs taken from aircraft or drones. Provides detailed, current imagery for vegetation mapping, land use analysis, and site documentation. Orthorectified photos are corrected for distortion and can be used at scale.
Satellite Imagery: Images captured by satellites (e.g., Landsat, Sentinel). Lower resolution than aerial photos but covers larger areas and includes multispectral bands.

NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index): A remote sensing metric that measures vegetation health and density using near-infrared and red light reflectance. Values range from -1 to +1; higher values indicate denser, healthier vegetation.

LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging): Uses laser pulses to create highly accurate 3D point clouds of terrain and vegetation. Produces precise Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and can penetrate tree canopy to map ground surface. Increasingly used for topographic surveys, floodplain mapping, and vegetation structure analysis.
Plat: A recorded legal map showing the subdivision of land into lots, blocks, streets, and easements.
Deed: A legal document that transfers property ownership. Contains legal descriptions of property boundaries.
Easement: A legal right to use another's land for a specific purpose (e.g., utility easement, access easement, conservation easement). Easements restrict what can be built within their boundaries.
Right-of-Way (ROW): A strip of land dedicated or granted for public use, typically for roads, sidewalks, and utilities.
Title Report: A document summarizing property ownership history, liens, encumbrances, and easements.
Covenant/Restriction: Private agreements that restrict land use (e.g., HOA covenants, deed restrictions). May limit building height, materials, land uses.
Zoning regulations govern how land can be used, what can be built, and where. Understanding zoning is essential for site analysis and project feasibility.

Zoning Categories: Common categories include Residential (R), Commercial (C), Industrial (I), Agricultural (A), and Mixed-Use (MU). Each category has specific permitted uses, conditional uses, and prohibited uses.
Setbacks: The minimum required distance between a structure and the property line (front, side, rear). Setbacks vary by zone.
FAR (Floor Area Ratio): The ratio of total building floor area to the total lot area. FAR = Total Floor Area / Lot Area. Higher FAR = more intense development.
Lot Coverage: The percentage of a lot that may be covered by buildings and/or impervious surfaces.
Overlay District: A special zoning district superimposed on base zoning to address specific concerns (historic preservation, floodplain, environmental protection, airport noise).
Variance: An exception to zoning requirements granted by a zoning board when strict compliance would cause undue hardship.
Conditional Use Permit (CUP): A permit that allows a use not normally permitted in a zone, subject to specific conditions and public review.
•  Requires federal agencies to assess the environmental impact of proposed actions before making decisions.

•  Three levels of review: Categorical Exclusion (CE) for minor actions; Environmental Assessment (EA) for uncertain impacts, leading to a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) or escalation; Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for major actions significantly affecting the environment.
•  Involves public comment periods and consideration of alternatives.
•  Regulates the discharge of dredged or fill material into "waters of the United States," including wetlands.
•  Permits issued by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE).
•  Requires avoidance and minimization of wetland impacts; unavoidable impacts must be mitigated (compensatory mitigation).
•  Requires federal agencies to consider the effects of their undertakings on historic properties (those listed on or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places).
•  Involves consultation with the State Historic Preservation Officer (SHPO) and the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP).
•  Applies when a project receives federal funding, licensing, or permits.
•  Protects threatened and endangered species and their critical habitats.
•  Administered by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) for terrestrial and freshwater species.
•  Section 7 consultation required for projects with a federal nexus; Section 10 permits for private projects.
•  Accessible routes: minimum 36 inches wide, maximum 5% running slope (1:20), maximum 2% cross slope.
•  Ramps: maximum 8.33% slope (1:12), maximum 30 inches of rise per run, handrails required on both sides for rises > 6 inches, level landings at top and bottom (60 inches minimum length).
•  Accessible parking: van-accessible spaces require 96-inch minimum width with 96-inch access aisle; standard accessible spaces require 60-inch access aisle.
•  Extends ADA principles to public sidewalks, crosswalks, curb ramps, and pedestrian signals.
•  Addresses conditions unique to public rights-of-way where terrain cannot be easily modified.
•  Requires detectable warning surfaces (truncated domes) at curb ramps.

subsections.title: 4.3.1 Kevin Lynch's Five Elements of Urban Form

content.text: From 'The Image of the City' (1960), Lynch identified five elements people use to construct their mental maps of cities:
Paths: Channels of movement (streets, walkways, transit lines, trails). The most dominant element in most people's mental maps.
Edges: Linear boundaries between areas (shorelines, railroad tracks, walls, changes in land use). Can be barriers or seams.
Districts: Medium-to-large areas with a common, identifiable character (Chinatown, a financial district, a residential neighborhood).
Nodes: Strategic focal points or junctions (major intersections, plazas, transit hubs, gathering places).
Landmarks: External reference points used for orientation (clock towers, monuments, distinctive buildings, prominent natural features). Usually visible from many angles.
Viewshed: The area visible from a specific vantage point. GIS-based viewshed analysis uses terrain data to map what can and cannot be seen from a point.
Visual Corridor: A linear view framed by landscape elements (tree-lined avenue, valley views, gaps between buildings).

Figure-Ground Analysis: A mapping technique showing the relationship between built form (figure, shown in black) and open space (ground, shown in white). Reveals urban fabric patterns, density, and spatial organization.
Level of Service (LOS): A qualitative measure of traffic flow, graded A (free flow) through F (forced flow/gridlock). Used in traffic impact studies.
Complete Streets: Streets designed to accommodate all users: pedestrians, cyclists, transit riders, and motorists of all ages and abilities.

Traffic Calming: Physical design measures to reduce vehicle speeds and volumes in residential and pedestrian areas. Includes speed tables, chicanes, curb extensions (bulb-outs), raised crosswalks, and lane narrowing.
Multimodal Transportation: Planning for multiple modes of travel (walking, cycling, transit, driving) within a coordinated network.
Site context analysis includes understanding the community served by a project:
•  Population density, age distribution, household size, income levels (U.S. Census / American Community Survey)

•  Environmental Justice: the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people regardless of race, income, or national origin in environmental decision-making. Projects should not disproportionately burden disadvantaged communities.
•  Cultural landscape considerations: understanding the cultural significance of places, traditions, and land use patterns.
The International Association for Public Participation (IAP2) developed the most widely recognized framework for understanding levels of public involvement in decision-making:

rows: Fact sheets, websites, open houses, presentations
Obtain public feedback on alternatives or decisions
We will listen and acknowledge your concerns
Surveys, public comment periods, focus groups, public meetings
Work directly with the public throughout the process
We will work with you to ensure your concerns are reflected
Partner with the public in each aspect of the decision
We will look to you for advice and incorporate it
Place final decision-making in the hands of the public
We will implement what you decide

content.text: The spectrum is not hierarchical; the appropriate level depends on the project goals, timeline, resources, and the community's stake in the outcome.
EXAM TIP: The exam may present scenarios and ask you to identify the most appropriate level of public participation. Consider the community's role in the decision and the project phase.
Public Meeting / Open House: Large-format meetings where information is presented and public comment is received. Can be one-way (presentation) or interactive (stations).
Design Charrette: An intensive, collaborative workshop where stakeholders work with designers to develop design concepts in a compressed timeframe.
Focus Group: A small, facilitated discussion with a targeted group of stakeholders to explore specific issues in depth.
Survey / Questionnaire: A structured set of questions distributed widely to collect quantitative and qualitative data from a broad audience.
Online Engagement: Web-based tools (interactive maps, online surveys, social media, virtual meetings) that expand participation beyond those who can attend in-person events.
Stakeholder Interviews: One-on-one or small-group conversations with key stakeholders to understand perspectives, concerns, and priorities.
Advisory Committee: A formally constituted group representing diverse stakeholder interests that meets regularly throughout the project.
Effective stakeholder engagement must be culturally responsive and remove barriers to participation:
•  Provide materials in multiple languages relevant to the community.
•  Hold meetings at times and locations accessible to working families.
•  Ensure ADA-accessible meeting venues and materials.
•  Provide childcare, food, and transportation assistance when possible.
•  Use culturally appropriate outreach methods to reach underrepresented communities.
•  Consider digital divides; supplement online engagement with in-person options.
All engagement activities must be thoroughly documented:
•  Meeting minutes capturing key decisions, action items, responsible parties, and deadlines.
•  Comment summaries and response matrices showing how public input was considered.
•  Attendance records and sign-in sheets.
•  Photographic and/or video documentation.
Although the lowest-weighted domain, Project Management questions are often straightforward and represent easy points to earn.
A typical landscape architecture project follows these phases:

rows: Define project goals, scope, budget, schedule; collect and analyze site data; develop program requirements; stakeholder engagement
Develop conceptual design alternatives; present concepts to client; select preferred direction; preliminary cost estimate (order-of-magnitude)
Refine selected design; select specific materials, furnishings, and systems; develop detailed design solutions; refined cost estimate
Prepare final drawings and specifications for bidding and construction; coordinate with consultants; detailed cost estimate
Distribute documents to contractors; answer bidder questions (addenda); evaluate bids; recommend award
Review submittals, respond to RFIs, conduct site observations, review payment applications, manage punch list, issue certificate of substantial completion

content.text: Scope of Work: A written description of the services to be provided, deliverables, and project boundaries. Scope creep (unauthorized expansion of scope) is a major project management challenge.
Work Breakdown Structure (WBS): A hierarchical decomposition of project work into manageable tasks and subtasks.
Gantt Chart: A bar chart showing project tasks plotted against a timeline, illustrating task duration, sequence, and overlap.

Critical Path Method (CPM): A scheduling technique that identifies the longest sequence of dependent tasks (the critical path). Tasks on the critical path have zero float; any delay in these tasks delays the entire project.
Float (Slack): The amount of time a non-critical task can be delayed without delaying the project completion. Critical path tasks have zero float.
Owner-Landscape Architect Agreement: Defines scope of services, compensation, schedule, responsibilities, and terms. Standard forms include ASLA and AIA documents.
Subconsultant Agreement: Agreement between the landscape architect and specialized consultants (civil engineer, structural engineer, lighting designer, etc.).
Fee Structures: Lump sum (stipulated sum), hourly with a cap, percentage of construction cost, or cost-plus-fixed-fee. The appropriate fee structure depends on the clarity of scope.

Standard of Care: The legal standard to which landscape architects are held: services performed with the same degree of skill and care that a reasonably competent professional would exercise in similar circumstances.
Landscape architects work within interdisciplinary teams. Key coordination roles include:

rows: Grading, drainage, stormwater management, utility design, roadway design
Retaining walls, bridges, foundations, structures exceeding landscape scope
Building-landscape interface, site access, building orientation, setbacks
Wetland delineation, habitat assessment, environmental permitting
Vehicular circulation, parking, pedestrian/bike facilities, traffic calming
Soil boring analysis, bearing capacity, slope stability, foundation design
Boundary surveys, topographic surveys, utility location, legal descriptions
Tree health assessment, preservation planning, root zone protection

s1_guide.title: Part 7: Key Formulas, Standards, and Quick Reference

content.text: Rational Method: Q = C x i x A (Q = peak runoff in cfs; C = runoff coefficient; i = rainfall intensity in/hr; A = area in acres)

subsections.title: Slope Ratio: Expressed as H:V (horizontal : vertical). 3:1 = 33.3%; 4:1 = 25%; 2:1 = 50%
FAR: Floor Area Ratio = Total Building Floor Area / Total Lot Area

rows: Requires environmental review of federal actions (CE, EA/FONSI, EIS)
Wetland fill permits issued by Army Corps of Engineers
Review effects on historic properties; consult SHPO
Protects listed species and critical habitats; USFWS consultation
Accessibility requirements for public accommodations and facilities
