s1_book.title: Preface: How to Use This Book

content.text: This study book is designed to give you everything you need to pass LARE Section 1: Inventory, Analysis, and Project Management. It is not a summary or an outline. It is a complete teaching resource that explains each topic from the ground up, as though you were learning it in a university classroom, and then connects that knowledge directly to what you will face on exam day.
The content is organized to mirror the five domains of the CLARB exam blueprint, weighted in order of importance. Each chapter contains:
•  Full explanatory text that teaches the concept, not just defines it
•  Real-world examples showing how concepts apply to professional practice
•  Memory aids and mnemonics to help you retain key information
•  Exam tips that flag exactly how topics are tested
•  Reference tables for quick lookup during study sessions
•  Chapter summaries listing everything you must know
•  Review questions with explained answers at the end of each chapter
The book is structured from the most heavily tested domain to the least:

Begin with the Physical Analysis chapters and spend the most time there. It is the single largest domain and the most technically demanding. Do not skip any domain, however. Even the 7% Project Management domain represents six questions that are often straightforward points to earn.

EXAM FORMAT:  Section 1 uses both standard multiple-choice questions and graphic Advanced Item Types (AITs). AITs present you with maps, diagrams, or images and ask you to interpret them. Practice reading topographic maps, soil surveys, FIRM maps, and aerial photographs before exam day. The free CLARB demo exam lets you practice the testing interface.

If there is one topic that defines LARE Section 1, it is soils. Soil conditions affect virtually every decision a landscape architect makes: where to place buildings and pavements, what plants will thrive, how water will move through a site, whether slopes will be stable, and whether stormwater can be managed on-site. The exam tests your ability to read soil data, understand what it means for design, and apply that understanding to site analysis problems.

This chapter teaches soil science from the ground up. By the end, you will be able to read an NRCS soil survey report, identify soil constraints and opportunities, and answer any soil-related question on the exam.
Soil is not simply dirt. It is a complex, living system made up of four components:

rows: Sand, silt, and clay derived from weathered rock. Determines texture, drainage, and structural properties.
Decomposed plant and animal material (humus). Improves water retention, nutrient supply, and soil structure.
Fills pore spaces between particles. Essential for plant growth and chemical processes. Amount varies with rainfall and drainage.
Fills pore spaces not occupied by water. Essential for root respiration and microbial activity.

content.text: The balance between water and air in the pore spaces is critical. In well-drained soils, water drains through and air fills the pores. In poorly drained soils, water fills the pores for extended periods, creating anaerobic (oxygen-deprived) conditions. This is the fundamental difference between upland soils and wetland (hydric) soils.

s1_book.title: 1.2 Soil Horizons: Reading the Soil Profile

content.text: If you were to dig a deep hole in undisturbed ground, you would see distinct horizontal layers called soil horizons. Together, these layers form the soil profile. Each horizon has different characteristics that affect how the soil performs.

O Horizon (Organic Layer): The thin surface layer of decomposing leaves, roots, and organic debris. Found primarily in forests and undisturbed grasslands. This layer is often absent in urban and agricultural sites where the surface has been disturbed.

A Horizon (Topsoil): The dark, mineral-rich layer where organic matter mixes with mineral particles. This is where most biological activity occurs — roots, earthworms, fungi, and bacteria are concentrated here. Topsoil is the most important layer for plant growth because it holds nutrients and moisture. It is typically 2 to 10 inches deep. In landscape construction, topsoil is often stripped, stockpiled, and replaced after grading to ensure the final surface can support planting.

B Horizon (Subsoil): The layer below topsoil where minerals leached from the A horizon accumulate — particularly clay, iron oxides, and calcium carbonate. The B horizon is often denser, more compact, and less fertile than topsoil. Its clay content can create a restrictive layer that impedes drainage. The B horizon's characteristics heavily influence a site's drainage performance and bearing capacity.

C Horizon (Parent Material): Partially weathered rock or sediment from which the soil above developed. It has little biological activity and retains many characteristics of the original geological material (glacial deposits, alluvium, bedrock fragments). Understanding the parent material helps explain why soils in a region behave the way they do.

R Horizon (Bedrock): Solid, unweathered rock. Shallow bedrock (close to the surface) is a major site constraint — it limits excavation, makes grading expensive, prevents deep root growth, and eliminates the possibility of subsurface stormwater infiltration. Depth to bedrock is a critical piece of site inventory data.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  During a site inventory for a new park, the landscape architect reviews soil borings and finds that bedrock is only 18 inches below grade across much of the site. This means the site cannot support deep-rooted trees without soil amendment, underground utilities will require rock excavation (expensive), and stormwater infiltration BMPs like rain gardens will not work without significant soil modification. The landscape architect would document this as a major site constraint and recommend surface-based stormwater strategies instead.

s1_book.title: 1.3 The Five Factors of Soil Formation

content.text: Why do soils vary so dramatically from place to place? Russian geologist Vasily Dokuchaev and later American scientist Hans Jenny identified five factors that control soil formation, remembered by the mnemonic CLORPT:

C — Climate: Temperature and precipitation are the dominant drivers. Warm, wet climates accelerate weathering and produce deep, highly developed soils. Cold or dry climates slow the process, producing thin, poorly developed soils. Climate also controls the rate of organic matter decomposition.

L — Living Organisms: Plants contribute organic matter through leaf litter and root decay. Burrowing animals (earthworms, gophers) mix soil layers. Microorganisms decompose organic matter and cycle nutrients. Human activity (agriculture, construction, urbanization) dramatically alters soil profiles.

O — Relief (Topography): Slope angle and aspect affect drainage, erosion, and microclimate. Hilltops and steep slopes tend to have thin soils because water runs off before it can infiltrate. Valley bottoms accumulate deep soils from eroded material above. South-facing slopes (in the Northern Hemisphere) are warmer and drier; north-facing slopes are cooler and moister.

R — Parent Material: The geological material from which soil develops. Soils derived from limestone tend to be alkaline (high pH). Soils from granite tend to be acidic. Glacial till produces mixed, often stony soils. Alluvial deposits (from rivers) tend to be deep, fertile, and well-sorted.

P/T — Time: Soil development takes hundreds to thousands of years. Young soils (recently deposited alluvium, volcanic ash) have poorly defined horizons. Old soils have deep, well-differentiated profiles. Urban soils are often "young" in the sense that grading has destroyed natural horizons.
MEMORY AID:  CLORPT: Climate, Living organisms, O (relief/topography), Rock (parent material), Time. Think "CLORox Plus Time" — these five factors bleach the rock into soil over time.

s1_book.title: 1.4 Soil Texture: Sand, Silt, and Clay

content.text: Soil texture refers to the relative proportions of the three mineral particle sizes: sand, silt, and clay. Texture is the single most important soil property because it controls drainage, water-holding capacity, nutrient retention, workability, and structural behavior. The USDA Soil Texture Triangle classifies soil into 12 texture classes based on the percentage of each particle size.

rows: Sticky when wet, hard when dry
Low — drains before plants can use it
Very high — but much is unavailable to plants
Low (particles too heavy to move easily)
Moderate when dry; low when aggregated

content.text: Loam is not a single particle size — it is a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay, typically around 40% sand, 40% silt, and 20% clay. Loam combines the advantages of all three particle sizes: the good drainage of sand, the moisture retention of silt, and the nutrient-holding capacity of clay. It is the ideal soil for most landscape planting and is often specified as the standard for topsoil in landscape construction.

Variations include sandy loam (drains faster, good for drought-tolerant plantings), silt loam (retains more moisture, good for gardens), and clay loam (holds nutrients well but may drain slowly). These texture classes are defined precisely on the USDA Soil Texture Triangle.

EXAM TIP:  When the exam describes soil behavior, you should be able to work backward to identify the probable texture. If a question says the soil drains rapidly and does not hold moisture, think sand. If it says the soil cracks when dry and is sticky when wet, think clay. If it says the soil feels smooth and erodes easily when wet, think silt.

The Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) classifies all mapped soils in the United States into four Hydrologic Soil Groups (A, B, C, and D) based on their infiltration rate when thoroughly wetted. These groups are essential for stormwater runoff calculations because they directly determine the runoff coefficient used in engineering formulas.

Group A — Low Runoff Potential: These soils have high infiltration rates even when thoroughly wetted. They are deep (more than 40 inches to any restrictive layer), well-drained to excessively drained, and have sandy or gravelly textures. Water moves through them rapidly. They produce the least surface runoff. Examples: deep sands, well-drained gravels. Group A soils are ideal for stormwater infiltration practices like rain gardens and infiltration basins.

Group B — Moderately Low Runoff Potential: These soils have moderate infiltration rates. They are moderately deep (20-40 inches to a restrictive layer), moderately well-drained, and have moderately fine to moderately coarse textures like silt loam and loam. Most agricultural soils fall into Group B. They can support many green infrastructure practices with proper design.

Group C — Moderately High Runoff Potential: These soils have slow infiltration rates due to a layer that impedes downward water movement — often a dense clay layer, a fragipan, or a shallow water table. Textures are typically sandy clay loam or clay loam. A significant portion of rainfall becomes surface runoff. Infiltration-based stormwater practices may require underdrains to function effectively.

Group D — High Runoff Potential: These soils have very slow infiltration rates. They are typically clay-heavy soils, soils with a permanently high water table, soils with a claypan or hardpan near the surface, or soils over shallow bedrock. Nearly all precipitation becomes surface runoff. Infiltration BMPs are generally not feasible without significant soil modification. Detention-based strategies (holding and slowly releasing water) are usually required instead.

MEMORY AID:  Think of the HSGs as a grading scale from best to worst infiltration: A is the best (like getting an A grade), D is the worst (failing at infiltration). A = Awesome drainage, D = Dreadful drainage.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A landscape architect is evaluating two potential sites for a community park that will use rain gardens for stormwater management. Site 1 has Group B soils (silt loam, moderate infiltration). Site 2 has Group D soils (heavy clay, very slow infiltration). The LA recommends Site 1 because the rain gardens will function effectively without underdrains, reducing construction cost and long-term maintenance. If the client must use Site 2, the LA explains that rain gardens will need underdrains connected to the storm sewer, significantly increasing cost, or the stormwater strategy should shift to detention basins.

The NRCS Web Soil Survey (websoilsurvey.nrcs.usda.gov) is the primary free tool for accessing detailed soil information for any location in the United States. Every landscape architect should be proficient with this tool, and the exam expects you to understand the types of data it provides.
When you enter a project location into the Web Soil Survey, you receive:
•  A soil map showing the geographic boundaries of distinct soil units (map units) across the site.

•  Soil properties for each map unit: texture, depth to bedrock, depth to water table, drainage class, permeability, available water capacity, pH, organic matter content, shrink-swell potential (linear extensibility).
•  Hydrologic Soil Group classification for runoff calculations.
•  Hydric soil ratings, which indicate potential wetland areas requiring regulatory review.
•  Suitability and limitation ratings for specific uses: building site development, septic systems, recreational development, roads, and more.
•  Erosion factors including the K-factor (inherent erodibility of the soil) and T-factor (tolerable soil loss rate).

EXAM TIP:  The exam may present soil survey data and ask you to interpret it. Practice using the Web Soil Survey before the exam. Navigate to a site, generate a soil report, and review the properties tables. Pay special attention to drainage class, HSG, depth to restrictive features, and hydric ratings.

Hydric soils are soils that formed under conditions of saturation, flooding, or ponding long enough during the growing season to develop anaerobic (oxygen-free) conditions in the upper part. The presence of hydric soils is one of three criteria used to delineate jurisdictional wetlands under the Clean Water Act:
•  Hydric soils (soils that formed under saturated conditions)
•  Hydrophytic vegetation (plants adapted to wet conditions — cattails, sedges, willows)
•  Wetland hydrology (evidence of prolonged saturation or inundation)

All three criteria must be present to delineate a jurisdictional wetland. However, the presence of any one indicator should alert the landscape architect to investigate further and potentially consult a wetland specialist.

Hydric soils often display distinctive visual indicators: a dark, mucky surface layer rich in organic matter; gray or bluish-gray colors (gleying) caused by the chemical reduction of iron under anaerobic conditions; and mottling (patches of rust-orange and gray) caused by fluctuating water levels.

EXAM TIP:  If the exam describes a soil as hydric, it is telling you the site may contain jurisdictional wetlands requiring Section 404 permits from the Army Corps of Engineers. Hydric soil = potential regulatory constraint. Always recommend further investigation.
Beyond agriculture and planting, soils have engineering properties that affect construction feasibility, structural design, and long-term performance of built features.

Bearing capacity is the ability of soil to support structural loads without excessive settlement or failure. Sandy and gravelly soils generally have high bearing capacity because their particles interlock and resist compression. Clay soils have variable bearing capacity — stiff, dry clay can support heavy loads, but the same clay when wet may lose strength dramatically. Organic soils (peat, muck) have very low bearing capacity and are generally unsuitable for structural support without extensive remediation.

Certain clay minerals, particularly montmorillonite (smectite), absorb water and expand significantly, then shrink and crack when they dry out. This volumetric change creates enormous forces that can crack foundations, heave sidewalks, break utility lines, and tilt retaining walls. Shrink-swell potential is measured by the COLE (Coefficient of Linear Extensibility) value in the soil survey.

High shrink-swell soils require: deeper footings, flexible pavement joints, moisture barriers around foundations, avoidance of large trees near structures (tree roots extract moisture and cause differential settlement), and careful irrigation management.

When water in the soil freezes, it expands and pushes the ground surface upward (frost heave). Frost heave damages foundations, sidewalks, retaining walls, and fence posts that are not placed below the frost line (the maximum depth of soil freezing). Silty soils are the most susceptible to frost heave because their pore sizes are just right for drawing water upward through capillary action, feeding the formation of ice lenses.

Frost line depths vary by region: From 0 inches in southern Florida to 72+ inches in northern Minnesota and Alaska. The local building code specifies the required depth for footings and frost-protected structures. All footings for walls, deck posts, and freestanding structures must extend below the frost line.

A soil's vulnerability to erosion by water is quantified by the K-factor in the Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE). Silty soils have the highest K-factors (most erodible) because silt particles are light enough to be transported by water but lack the cohesion of clay that would hold them together. Sandy soils resist erosion because particles are too heavy to move easily. Well-aggregated clay soils also resist erosion, but dispersed clays on steep slopes can erode rapidly.

The T-factor represents the maximum rate of soil loss that can be sustained without degrading long-term productivity — typically 3 to 5 tons per acre per year. Erosion and sediment control plans must keep soil loss below this threshold.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Soil is composed of mineral particles, organic matter, water, and air in roughly 45/5/25/25 proportions. ✔  Soil horizons (O-A-B-C-R) form a vertical profile; the A horizon (topsoil) is most important for plant growth. ✔  CLORPT: Climate, Living organisms, Relief, Parent material, Time control soil formation. ✔  Sand drains fast but holds few nutrients; clay drains slowly but holds nutrients and has shrink-swell risk; silt is most erodible; loam is the balanced ideal. ✔  Hydrologic Soil Groups range from A (best infiltration, least runoff) to D (worst infiltration, most runoff). ✔  The NRCS Web Soil Survey provides texture, drainage, HSG, hydric status, and engineering properties for any US site. ✔  Hydric soils indicate potential wetlands requiring regulatory review (Section 404 CWA). ✔  Key engineering properties: bearing capacity, shrink-swell (COLE), frost susceptibility (silts worst), erosion (K-factor, silts worst).
1. A soil survey report classifies a site's soils as Hydrologic Soil Group D. What does this mean for site development?
A)  The site has excellent conditions for stormwater infiltration
B)  The soils have high runoff potential and very slow infiltration rates
C)  The soils are well-drained and suitable for rain gardens without modification
D)  The soils have high bearing capacity for structural foundations
Answer: B. Group D soils have very slow infiltration and high runoff potential. Infiltration-based stormwater BMPs will likely need underdrains or alternative detention strategies.

subsections.title: 2. Which soil particle size is MOST susceptible to erosion by water?

content.text: A)  Sand
B)  Gravel
C)  Silt
D)  Clay
Answer: C. Silt particles are light enough to be transported by water but lack the cohesion of clay, making them the most erodible. Silt soils have the highest K-factors.
3. During a site inventory, the landscape architect reviews the NRCS Web Soil Survey and finds that several soil map units are classified as hydric. This finding is significant because:
A)  Hydric soils indicate excellent bearing capacity for building foundations
B)  Hydric soils indicate potential wetland areas that may require regulatory permits
C)  Hydric soils indicate the site has no flooding risk
D)  Hydric soils indicate the site is ideal for septic systems
Answer: B. Hydric soils are one of three indicators of jurisdictional wetlands (along with hydrophytic vegetation and wetland hydrology) that trigger Section 404 Clean Water Act permitting.

subsections.title: 4. A soil described as having high montmorillonite clay content poses the greatest risk of:

content.text: A)  Rapid percolation and groundwater contamination
B)  Shrink-swell damage to foundations and pavements
C)  Excessive drainage causing plant stress
D)  Low nutrient availability for plantings
Answer: B. Montmorillonite clay has high shrink-swell potential. It expands when wet and contracts when dry, creating forces that crack foundations, heave pavements, and damage utilities.

subsections.title: 5. Which soil horizon is MOST important for supporting plant growth in a landscape?

content.text: A)  A horizon (topsoil)
B)  B horizon (subsoil)
C)  C horizon (parent material)
D)  R horizon (bedrock)
Answer: A. The A horizon (topsoil) is where organic matter mixes with minerals, creating the nutrient-rich, biologically active layer essential for plant root growth.

Topography — the shape of the land surface — is the framework upon which all site design decisions are built. The lay of the land determines where water flows, which areas receive sunlight, where views open up, where erosion threatens, and which areas can economically support development. On the LARE exam, you will be asked to read topographic maps, calculate slopes, identify drainage patterns, evaluate slope suitability for various uses, and understand how landform affects microclimate.
This chapter teaches you to read terrain as fluently as you read text.

s1_book.title: 2.1 Contour Lines: The Language of Terrain

content.text: Contour lines are the fundamental tool for representing three-dimensional terrain on a two-dimensional map. Each contour line connects all points at the same elevation above a reference datum (typically mean sea level). The contour interval is the vertical distance between consecutive contour lines — commonly 1, 2, 5, or 10 feet depending on the map scale and terrain variability.
Mastering contour interpretation requires understanding these principles:

1. Contour lines never cross. Each line represents a single elevation. Two different elevations cannot exist at the same point (the rare exception is an overhanging cliff, which you will not encounter on the exam).

2. Close spacing = steep slope; wide spacing = gentle slope. This is the most fundamental principle. Imagine walking across a site: if you cross ten contour lines in a short horizontal distance, the ground is rising (or falling) steeply. If you cross the same ten lines over a much longer horizontal distance, the slope is gentle. On a topographic map, closely spaced contour lines indicate steep terrain, and widely spaced lines indicate gentle terrain.

3. V-shapes pointing uphill indicate valleys; V-shapes pointing downhill indicate ridges. When contour lines bend into a V shape with the point aiming toward higher elevation, they are following the bottom of a valley or drainage swale where water collects and flows. When the V points downhill (toward lower elevation), the contour is wrapping around a ridge or spur — a high point that sheds water to both sides. This is one of the most commonly tested contour principles.

4. Concentric closed contours indicate a hill or depression. If the elevations increase toward the center, it is a hilltop. If the elevations decrease toward the center (often marked with hachure lines — small tick marks pointing inward), it is a depression or closed basin.

5. Water flows perpendicular to contour lines. Water always takes the steepest path downhill, which means it crosses contour lines at right angles. This principle is essential for understanding drainage patterns and designing grading plans.

6. Evenly spaced contours indicate a uniform slope. If the spacing between contour lines changes, the slope is changing. Lines that start wide and get progressively closer together indicate a concave slope (getting steeper). Lines that start close and get wider indicate a convex slope (getting gentler).

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  You are reviewing a topographic map for a proposed trail alignment. In one area, the contour lines are so close together they nearly merge. You know this represents a cliff or very steep embankment. Your trail cannot cross here without switchbacks, stairs, or a significant reroute. In another area, the contour lines are widely and evenly spaced. This is gentle, uniform terrain ideal for an accessible trail meeting ADA slope requirements.
Slope is the ratio of vertical change (rise) to horizontal distance (run). It can be expressed three ways:
Percentage: Slope (%) = (Rise ÷ Run) × 100. This is the most common format in landscape architecture. A 5% slope rises 5 feet for every 100 feet of horizontal distance.
Ratio: Written as horizontal:vertical (H:V). A 3:1 slope has 3 feet of horizontal distance for every 1 foot of vertical rise. To convert to percentage: (1 ÷ 3) × 100 = 33.3%.

Degrees: The angle of the slope measured from horizontal. Used less frequently in landscape architecture but occasionally appears. A 45-degree slope equals 100% (1:1). A 100% slope does NOT mean vertical — it means the rise equals the run.
Two contour lines are labeled 250 and 254 (a 4-foot elevation difference). They are 200 feet apart (measured horizontally on the map, using the map scale).
This 2% slope is gentle, suitable for accessible routes (max 5%), lawn areas, and most development.
Two points are separated by 12 feet of elevation over 40 feet of horizontal distance.
This is a very steep slope, approaching the limit for mowable turf (3:1 = 33%). It would require retaining walls for usable development and would have high erosion risk without stabilization.
Different land uses require different slope ranges. Knowing these thresholds is essential for both professional practice and the exam.

rows: Nearly flat. Risk of ponding and poor surface drainage. May need subsurface drainage. Suitable for sports fields with tile drainage.
Minimum slope for adequate surface drainage of paved areas and lawns. Ideal for parking lots (1-2% min) and building pads.
Comfortable for walking, lawn recreation, and accessible routes. Maximum running slope for ADA accessible routes is 5% (1:20). Ideal for most site development.
Moderate slope. Comfortable for walking paths but not ADA accessible routes. Portions of ramps may be up to 8.33% (1:12) with handrails and landings.
Steep. Difficult for pedestrians. Development requires significant grading, retaining walls, or stepped designs. Erosion risk is substantial.
Very steep. Limit for most constructed slopes with erosion control. Buildings possible but expensive. Not suitable for recreation.
Approaching the limit for mowable turf (3:1). Maintenance equipment cannot safely operate. Vegetated with groundcover or stabilized with geotextile.
Maximum for stabilized earth slopes without structural retaining. Requires erosion mat, hydroseeding, or bioengineering techniques.
Extreme. Retaining structures or natural rock slopes only. Preserve as natural area or open space.

content.text: MEMORY AID:  Key slope thresholds: 1-2% = minimum drainage; 5% = max ADA accessible route; 8.33% (1:12) = max ADA ramp; 25% = max practical constructed slope; 33% (3:1) = max mowable turf. Write these five numbers on your scratch paper when the exam begins.

s1_book.title: 2.4 Aspect: The Direction a Slope Faces

content.text: Aspect is the compass direction that a slope faces, and it dramatically affects microclimate, plant selection, snow behavior, and energy use. In the Northern Hemisphere:

South-facing slopes receive the most direct sunlight year-round. They are warmer, drier, and experience earlier snowmelt. Plants on south-facing slopes are exposed to more heat stress and drought. These slopes are ideal for solar-oriented buildings but may require drought-tolerant plantings.

North-facing slopes receive the least direct sunlight. They are cooler, more moist, and retain snow and ice longest. Vegetation tends to be denser and more shade-tolerant. These slopes may experience persistent ice in winter and are generally less suitable for solar energy or warm-season outdoor spaces.

East-facing slopes receive gentle morning sun. This is favorable for many plants because the gradual warming reduces thermal shock. East-facing slopes tend to be moderately warm without the intense heat of afternoon exposure.

West-facing slopes receive intense afternoon sun. This is the hottest exposure, which can cause heat stress in plants and overheating of outdoor spaces. West-facing building facades have the highest cooling loads in summer. West-facing slopes also receive the full force of afternoon thunderstorms in many regions.

EXAM TIP:  If a question asks which slope orientation is warmest and driest, the answer is south-facing. If it asks which is coolest and most moist, the answer is north-facing. If it asks which receives the most intense heat, the answer is west-facing (afternoon sun).
Interpolation is the process of estimating the elevation of a point that falls between two known contour lines. This is a fundamental skill for grading design and is commonly tested on the exam.

Method: If a point is located 60% of the distance from the 100-foot contour to the 105-foot contour, its estimated elevation is 100 + (0.60 × 5) = 103 feet. This assumes a uniform slope between the two contour lines, which is a standard assumption in practice.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Contour lines connect points of equal elevation. Close spacing = steep; wide spacing = gentle. ✔  V-shapes pointing uphill = valley/swale; V-shapes pointing downhill = ridge. ✔  Water flows perpendicular to contour lines, always taking the steepest path downhill. ✔  Slope (%) = (Rise / Run) x 100. Slope ratio is expressed as H:V. ✔  Key thresholds: 1-2% min drainage; 5% max ADA route; 8.33% max ADA ramp; 33% (3:1) max mowable turf. ✔  Aspect affects microclimate: south-facing = warmest/driest; north-facing = coolest/moistest in Northern Hemisphere. ✔  Interpolation estimates elevation between known contour lines assuming uniform slope.
1. On a topographic map, contour lines are very closely spaced on the west side of a hill and widely spaced on the east side. This indicates:
A)  The west side is gently sloped and the east side is steep
B)  The west side is steep and the east side is gently sloped
C)  Both sides have the same slope
D)  The east side has higher elevation
Answer: B. Close contour spacing indicates steep terrain. The west side with closely spaced contours is steep; the east side with widely spaced contours is gentle.
2. A landscape architect needs to design an ADA-accessible pedestrian route. What is the maximum allowable running slope?
Answer: B. ADA accessible routes have a maximum running slope of 5% (1:20). Slopes steeper than 5% must be designed as ramps (max 8.33% or 1:12) with handrails and landings.
3. The elevation at Point A is 116 feet and the elevation at Point B is 108 feet. The horizontal distance between them is 200 feet. What is the slope?

subsections.title: 4. In the Northern Hemisphere, which slope aspect receives the LEAST direct sunlight?

content.text: A)  South-facing
B)  West-facing
C)  East-facing
D)  North-facing
Answer: D. North-facing slopes face away from the sun in the Northern Hemisphere, receiving the least direct sunlight. They are cooler and moister.

subsections.title: 5. What is the maximum slope for mowable turf grass?

content.text: Answer: D. Slopes steeper than 3:1 (33%) are too steep for safe mowing equipment operation. Steeper slopes should use groundcover or stabilization instead of mowed turf.

Water is the most powerful force shaping landscapes, and understanding how water moves across and through a site is fundamental to landscape architecture. Hydrology — the study of water movement — connects directly to grading, drainage design, stormwater management, plant selection, erosion control, and regulatory compliance. This chapter covers watersheds, runoff calculations, floodplains, groundwater, and the relationship between development and water.

A watershed (also called a drainage basin or catchment) is the area of land from which all precipitation drains to a single outlet point — a stream confluence, a lake, or an outfall pipe. Every point on the landscape falls within a watershed. The boundary between adjacent watersheds is called the drainage divide, which follows ridgelines and high points.

Understanding watershed boundaries matters because what happens upstream affects everything downstream. If a development upstream increases runoff, downstream properties may flood. If pollutants enter a stream upstream, they affect all downstream users. Landscape architects must think in terms of whole watersheds, not just individual sites.

To delineate a watershed on a topographic map, start at the outlet point (the lowest point where water leaves the area of interest) and trace uphill along ridgelines in both directions, following the highest points that separate water flowing toward your outlet from water flowing elsewhere. The watershed boundary always crosses contour lines at right angles, following the line of highest elevation. This is a common AIT (graphic) question type on the exam.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A proposed park site drains to a small stream that feeds a community lake used for recreation. The landscape architect delineates the stream's watershed on a topographic map and discovers that a large commercial development is planned upstream. The LA recommends coordinating with the upstream developer to ensure their stormwater management plan will not degrade water quality in the lake. This is watershed-scale thinking.

The Rational Method is the most widely used formula for estimating peak stormwater runoff from small drainage areas (generally under 200 acres). It is one of the most important formulas for the LARE exam.
Q = Peak runoff rate in cubic feet per second (cfs). This is the maximum flow rate you need to design for.

C = Runoff coefficient. A dimensionless number between 0 and 1 that represents the fraction of rainfall that becomes surface runoff. A C of 0.95 means 95% of rainfall runs off (nearly impervious surface like a rooftop). A C of 0.10 means only 10% runs off (well-drained lawn). When a drainage area has multiple surface types, you calculate a weighted average C.

i = Rainfall intensity in inches per hour. Determined from local rainfall data (IDF curves — Intensity-Duration-Frequency curves) based on the design storm frequency (e.g., 10-year, 25-year, 100-year storm) and the time of concentration.

rows: About half to two-thirds becomes runoff
Most rain infiltrates but clay reduces absorption
Steep slope + clay = significantly more runoff
Leaf litter and root systems absorb most rainfall
Mix of roofs, driveways, and lawns

content.text: A 5-acre site is being developed. Currently, the site is forest (C = 0.15). After development, it will be 40% buildings and pavement (C = 0.90) and 60% lawn on clay soil (C = 0.15). The design storm intensity is 4 inches per hour.

Development tripled the peak runoff from 3.0 to 9.0 cfs. This is why stormwater management regulations require developers to control post-development runoff so it does not exceed pre-development rates. The difference (6.0 cfs) must be managed through detention, retention, or infiltration.

EXAM TIP:  The exam loves to test the concept that development increases runoff. The key mechanism is simple: replacing pervious surfaces (forest, meadow) with impervious surfaces (roofs, pavement) increases the runoff coefficient C, which directly increases Q. This is the fundamental justification for stormwater management requirements.

The time of concentration (Tc) is the time required for runoff to travel from the hydraulically most distant point in a watershed to the outlet. It matters because it determines how intense the design rainfall should be: shorter Tc means you must design for higher-intensity, shorter-duration storms, which produce higher peak flows.
Factors that affect Tc:
•  Watershed size: Larger watersheds have longer flow paths, so longer Tc.
•  Slope: Steeper slopes move water faster, reducing Tc.
•  Surface roughness: Rough surfaces (forest floor, dense grass) slow water, increasing Tc. Smooth surfaces (pavement, pipes) speed water, decreasing Tc.
•  Channel characteristics: Paved channels and pipes convey water faster than natural streams with vegetation.

Development typically decreases Tc because it replaces rough, pervious surfaces with smooth, impervious ones and replaces natural channels with efficient storm sewers. This shorter Tc means higher design rainfall intensities and higher peak flows — another reason development increases flooding risk.

The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), administered by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), maps flood hazard areas across the United States using Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs). These maps are essential site analysis tools and understanding them is required for the exam.

rows: Flood insurance required for federally backed mortgages. Structures must be elevated to or above the Base Flood Elevation (BFE). Substantial fill and development restrictions.
The active flow channel within Zone A/AE
NO development permitted. This area must remain unobstructed to convey the base flood discharge. Even minor encroachment is prohibited.
Moderate risk. Fewer restrictions but flood insurance recommended. Important for critical facilities (hospitals, schools).
Lowest risk. No flood insurance requirement. Standard development practices apply.

content.text: Base Flood Elevation (BFE): The computed elevation to which floodwater is anticipated to rise during the 100-year (1% annual chance) flood. In Zone AE, the BFE is shown on the FIRM map. Structures in Zone AE must have their lowest habitable floor at or above the BFE. Many local codes require 1-2 feet of additional elevation above the BFE for safety (called freeboard).

MEMORY AID:  The "100-year flood" has a 1% chance of occurring in any given year. It does NOT mean it floods once every 100 years. Over a 30-year mortgage, a property in the 100-year floodplain has approximately a 26% chance of experiencing at least one flood — a much higher risk than most people realize. This is a commonly tested misconception.

While surface hydrology deals with water moving across the land surface, groundwater hydrology deals with water moving through the subsurface. The water table is the upper surface of the zone where all pore spaces in the soil and rock are fully saturated.

High water table: When the water table is close to the surface (within a few feet), it creates significant design constraints: basements are not feasible, deep foundations require dewatering during construction, plants must tolerate saturated root zones, subsurface utilities may require special waterproofing, and stormwater infiltration is limited because water has nowhere to go.

Perched water table: Sometimes water accumulates above the regional water table because an impermeable layer (hardpan, clay lens, or bedrock) blocks downward movement. This creates a localized saturated zone that can surprise construction crews and affect foundation design.

Aquifer recharge: Areas where precipitation infiltrates to replenish aquifers are called recharge zones. These areas are often protected from impervious development and contamination risk because they supply drinking water to communities.

Riparian buffers: Vegetated strips along streams and rivers serve multiple functions: they filter sediment and pollutants from surface runoff before it reaches waterways, stabilize stream banks through root systems, shade the water to moderate temperature (critical for aquatic habitat), provide wildlife corridors, and reduce flood damage by absorbing and slowing floodwater. Most jurisdictions require minimum riparian buffer widths (commonly 25-100 feet) based on stream classification.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  A watershed is the area draining to a common outlet, bounded by drainage divides along ridgelines. ✔  Q = CiA: the Rational Method calculates peak runoff from drainage area, rainfall intensity, and runoff coefficient. ✔  Development increases runoff by increasing impervious surfaces (higher C) and decreasing time of concentration. ✔  FEMA FIRM maps show flood zones: Zone A/AE (1% annual chance, regulated), Floodway (no development), Zone X (lower risk). ✔  BFE is the elevation floodwater reaches during the 100-year flood; structures must be built at or above it. ✔  The 100-year flood has a 1% annual probability, NOT a 100-year return interval. ✔  High water table limits basements, infiltration BMPs, and deep foundations. ✔  Riparian buffers filter pollutants, stabilize banks, moderate temperature, and provide wildlife corridors.

1. A 10-acre site currently has a weighted runoff coefficient (C) of 0.20. After development, the weighted C will be 0.60. If the design rainfall intensity is 3 in/hr, what is the increase in peak runoff?
A)  6 cfs
B)  12 cfs
C)  18 cfs
D)  24 cfs
Answer: B. Pre-development Q = 0.20 x 3 x 10 = 6 cfs. Post-development Q = 0.60 x 3 x 10 = 18 cfs. Increase = 18 - 6 = 12 cfs.
2. A property is located in FEMA Zone AE with a Base Flood Elevation of 42.0 feet. What is the minimum elevation for the lowest habitable floor?
A)  40.0 feet
B)  42.0 feet or higher per local code
C)  44.0 feet exactly
D)  There is no minimum
Answer: B. In Zone AE, structures must have their lowest floor at or above the BFE. Many local codes add 1-2 feet of freeboard above the BFE.

subsections.title: 3. The Regulatory Floodway on a FEMA FIRM map is significant because:

content.text: A)  It is an area of minimal flood risk
B)  Development is permitted with a variance
C)  No development or encroachment is permitted to ensure flood conveyance
D)  Flood insurance is optional
Answer: C. The Regulatory Floodway must remain unobstructed to convey the base flood discharge. No development is permitted.

subsections.title: 4. Development typically decreases the time of concentration (Tc) of a watershed because:

content.text: A)  Impervious surfaces and storm sewers move water faster than natural surfaces
B)  Development adds more vegetation
C)  Development flattens all slopes
D)  Buildings block wind and slow water
Answer: A. Smooth impervious surfaces and piped storm systems convey water much faster than natural ground cover and channels, reducing Tc.

Vegetation is both a resource and an indicator. Existing plant communities tell the landscape architect about soil moisture, drainage, disturbance history, and ecological health without digging a single hole. The exam tests your ability to read vegetation patterns, understand ecological processes, and recognize the landscape-scale systems that connect habitats.
Experienced landscape architects learn to read vegetation the way a physician reads symptoms. Different plant species and communities indicate specific environmental conditions:

rows: Wetland / hydric soil / high water table
Likely jurisdictional wetland. Regulatory review required. Limit disturbance. Section 404 permit may be needed.
Former farmland, cleared land, or abandoned site. Soils may be compacted. Opportunity for restoration.
High ecological value. Strong candidate for preservation. Deep, fertile soils.
Unique ecosystem. Highly sensitive to disturbance. Likely jurisdictional.
Cool microclimate. Limited sun exposure. Consider shade-tolerant plants.
Tidally influenced. Critical habitat. Coastal regulations apply.
Opportunity for restoration but significant removal effort needed.

content.text: EXAM TIP:  The exam may describe vegetation and ask you to infer site conditions. If a question mentions cattails and sedges, the answer almost certainly involves wetlands, hydric soils, or regulatory constraints. If it mentions oaks and hickories, think well-drained upland.

Succession is the predictable process by which plant communities change over time, from simple pioneer communities to complex mature ecosystems. Understanding succession helps landscape architects predict how disturbed sites will recover and how to manage vegetation over time.

Primary succession occurs on entirely new surfaces where no soil exists: cooled lava flows, retreating glaciers, newly exposed rock. Pioneer organisms like lichens and mosses colonize first, slowly breaking down rock and building soil. Over centuries, grasses, shrubs, and eventually trees establish. Primary succession is rarely relevant to typical landscape architecture projects.

Secondary succession occurs on sites where vegetation has been removed but soil remains: abandoned farmland, fire-cleared forest, graded construction sites, cleared lots. Secondary succession proceeds much faster because soil is already present. The typical sequence in temperate regions is:

Bare soil → Annual weeds and grasses (Year 1-2) → Perennial grasses and wildflowers (Years 2-5) → Shrubs and tree seedlings (Years 5-15) → Pioneer trees like birch, poplar, pine (Years 15-50) → Shade-tolerant hardwoods like oak, maple, beech (Years 50-200+)

Climax community: The stable, self-perpetuating plant community that represents the endpoint of succession for a given climate and soil. In the eastern United States, the climax community is typically deciduous forest (beech-maple or oak-hickory, depending on region). In the Pacific Northwest, it is coniferous forest. Climax communities persist unless disturbed by fire, logging, development, or climate change.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A landscape architect is designing a 50-acre conservation park on a former farm abandoned 10 years ago. The site is currently dominated by goldenrod, young red cedars, and patches of blackberry. Recognizing this as early secondary succession, the LA designs a management plan that accelerates succession in some areas (planting native hardwood trees) while maintaining meadow habitat in others (mowing annually to prevent tree colonization) to create ecological diversity.
Landscape ecology studies spatial patterns at the landscape scale — how patches of habitat, corridors connecting them, and the surrounding matrix interact to support biodiversity.

Patches: Distinct areas of habitat (a forest, a wetland, a prairie remnant). Larger patches support more species and more stable populations than small patches. The relationship between patch area and species diversity is described by the species-area relationship: larger areas support exponentially more species.

Corridors: Linear landscape features that connect patches, allowing wildlife to move between them. Stream buffers, hedgerows, greenways, and highway wildlife crossings function as corridors. Corridors are critical for maintaining genetic diversity and allowing species to respond to habitat loss, seasonal resource changes, and climate shifts. Corridors should be as wide and continuous as possible.

Matrix: The dominant background land use surrounding patches and corridors (agricultural land, suburban development, highway networks). A hostile matrix (dense urban development) makes corridors more important because wildlife cannot safely cross open areas.

Edge effect: The boundary zone between two habitat types (e.g., forest edge meeting a meadow). Edges support high species diversity because species from both habitats coexist. However, edges also expose interior-dwelling species to predators, invasive species, and altered microclimates (more wind, light, and temperature fluctuation). In conservation design, minimizing the ratio of edge to interior area preserves sensitive interior habitats.
Trees are often the most valuable biological and aesthetic assets on a project site. A thorough tree inventory documents each significant tree and provides the data needed for preservation decisions.

DBH (Diameter at Breast Height): The trunk diameter measured at 4.5 feet above grade on the uphill side. DBH is the standard measure of tree size in the United States. A tree with a 24-inch DBH is a significant specimen in most species.

Critical Root Zone (CRZ): The area around a tree essential for structural support and health. As a general rule, the CRZ extends 1 foot of radius for each 1 inch of DBH. A 24-inch DBH tree has a CRZ with a 24-foot radius. No grading, trenching, paving, or soil compaction should occur within the CRZ if the tree is to be preserved.

Condition assessment: Each tree should be rated for health (crown density, leaf color, dieback percentage), structural integrity (trunk wounds, decay, lean, root damage), and risk (likelihood of failure and consequences of failure based on targets below). An arborist may be needed for detailed assessments.

Tree protection during construction: Preservation-worthy trees must be protected with tree protection fencing installed at the drip line or CRZ boundary before any construction activity begins. No equipment, materials, or soil may be stored within the fenced area. Grade changes, trenching, and root cutting within the CRZ can kill a tree within 3-7 years.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Vegetation patterns indicate underlying site conditions: cattails = wetland; oaks/hickories = well-drained upland; red cedar/goldenrod = disturbed early succession. ✔  Succession follows a predictable sequence: bare soil > weeds > grasses > shrubs > pioneer trees > climax forest. ✔  Landscape ecology uses the patch-corridor-matrix model to understand habitat connectivity. ✔  Corridors (stream buffers, greenways) connect habitat patches and are critical for wildlife movement and genetic diversity. ✔  Edge effects increase diversity at boundaries but can harm interior-specialist species. ✔  Tree inventory records: species, DBH (at 4.5 ft), canopy spread, condition, CRZ (1 ft radius per 1 inch DBH). ✔  Tree protection fencing at the CRZ/drip line must be installed before any construction begins.

Climate shapes every aspect of landscape design: what plants survive, how people use outdoor spaces, how much irrigation is needed, where snow accumulates, and how buildings should be oriented. Microclimate — the localized climate variations within a site — is even more directly relevant to design decisions. A south-facing courtyard sheltered from wind can be comfortable in spring while an exposed north-facing slope nearby remains frozen.
The sun's position changes daily and seasonally, and understanding these patterns is essential for site planning, building orientation, and planting design.

Altitude angle: The sun's height above the horizon. In the Northern Hemisphere, the sun reaches its highest altitude angle at the summer solstice (June 20-21) and its lowest at the winter solstice (December 21-22). At 40°N latitude, the noon sun altitude is approximately 73.5° at summer solstice and 26.5° at winter solstice.

Azimuth angle: The sun's compass bearing. At the equinoxes (March 20-21, September 22-23), the sun rises due east and sets due west. In summer, it rises north of east and sets north of west, creating long days. In winter, it rises south of east and sets south of west, creating short days.
Design implications:
•  Place outdoor gathering spaces where they receive winter sun (south-facing, protected from north winds) for year-round comfort.
•  Use deciduous trees on south and west sides of buildings: they provide summer shade (reducing cooling costs) while allowing winter sun through bare branches (reducing heating costs).
•  Avoid placing shade-intolerant plants on the north side of buildings or walls where they will receive little direct sunlight.
•  Design canopy openings and building gaps to allow winter sun to penetrate streets and plazas at low angles.
Wind patterns affect thermal comfort, plant health, snow drifting, erosion, and the structural design of exposed elements.

Prevailing winds: In much of the continental United States, prevailing winter winds blow from the northwest, bringing cold air. Summer breezes often come from the south or southwest. Local topography, water bodies, and urban form can significantly modify regional wind patterns.

Windbreaks: Rows of trees or structures placed perpendicular to prevailing winds. Evergreen windbreaks are most effective for year-round protection. An effective windbreak reduces wind speed on the leeward side for a distance of approximately 10 times its height. A 30-foot-tall windbreak provides meaningful wind reduction for about 300 feet downwind.
Wind tunnels: When wind is forced through a narrow gap between buildings or walls, it accelerates (the Venturi effect). Site plans should avoid creating narrow passages aligned with prevailing winds.
Urban areas are typically 2-10°F warmer than surrounding rural areas, a phenomenon called the urban heat island (UHI) effect. This temperature difference is caused by:
•  Large areas of dark-colored impervious surfaces (asphalt, rooftops) that absorb solar radiation during the day and re-radiate it as heat at night.
•  Reduced vegetation and tree canopy that would otherwise cool the air through evapotranspiration (plants release water vapor, which absorbs heat as it evaporates) and shade.
•  Waste heat generated by vehicles, air conditioning systems, and industrial processes.
•  Reduced wind flow due to buildings that trap heat in urban canyons.
•  Canyon geometry of tall buildings that absorb and reflect heat between surfaces.
Landscape architecture plays a central role in UHI mitigation:
•  Increase tree canopy cover (a single large tree can transpire 100+ gallons of water per day, providing significant cooling).
•  Use high-albedo (light-colored, reflective) paving and roofing materials that reflect solar radiation instead of absorbing it.
•  Install green roofs that insulate buildings and cool through evapotranspiration.
•  Reduce impervious surface area through compact development and pervious paving.
•  Incorporate water features that provide evaporative cooling.

EXAM TIP:  If a question asks about reducing urban temperatures or mitigating the heat island effect, look for answers involving trees, vegetation, high-albedo materials, green roofs, or reduced impervious surfaces. Answers involving more pavement, removing trees, or dark materials are always wrong.

The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map divides North America into 13 zones (1a through 13b) based on average annual extreme minimum winter temperature. Each zone represents a 10°F range, and each sub-zone (a and b) a 5°F range. This is the single most important reference for determining whether a plant species can survive winter at a given location.

Frost line (frost depth): The maximum depth to which soil freezes in winter. Ranges from 0 inches in the southernmost US to 72+ inches in northern Alaska. All footings for walls, decks, fence posts, and other structures must extend below the local frost line to prevent frost heave damage. The local building code specifies the required depth.

Growing season: The number of frost-free days per year, bounded by the last spring frost and first fall frost dates. Longer growing seasons allow more plant diversity and longer periods of outdoor use.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  South-facing slopes and walls receive the most sun; north-facing receive the least (Northern Hemisphere). ✔  Deciduous trees on south/west building faces provide summer shade and winter solar access. ✔  Evergreen windbreaks on the northwest side protect against prevailing winter winds for ~10x their height downwind. ✔  Urban heat island: cities are 2-10°F warmer due to impervious surfaces, reduced vegetation, and waste heat. ✔  UHI mitigation: tree canopy, high-albedo materials, green roofs, reduced impervious area, water features. ✔  USDA Hardiness Zones indicate minimum winter temperature survivability for plants. ✔  Frost line depth determines minimum footing depth; silty soils are most susceptible to frost heave.

s1_book.title: Chapter 6: Data Sources and Site Inventory

content.text: Effective site analysis depends on knowing where to find the right data. The exam frequently presents scenarios asking which agency or tool provides specific information. This chapter is your definitive reference.

rows: Topographic maps (7.5-minute quadrangles), Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), geologic maps, water resource data, National Map viewer
Need elevation data, terrain analysis, geologic hazards, or a base topographic map for a site
Web Soil Survey, soil properties (texture, drainage class, HSG, hydric rating), land capability classes, erosion factors
Need soil data for grading, planting, stormwater infiltration, or septic feasibility
Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs), floodplain boundaries, Base Flood Elevations, National Flood Hazard Layer
Need to determine flood risk, regulatory constraints, or required building elevations
National Wetlands Inventory (NWI), endangered species data, critical habitat designations
Need to identify wetlands or threatened/endangered species on or near the site
Superfund site locations, brownfield data, water quality standards, environmental regulations
Need to assess contamination risk or understand environmental regulatory requirements
Climate data, precipitation records, IDF curves, coastal data, sea level rise projections
Need rainfall data for stormwater design or climate data for planting decisions
Population, demographics, housing, income, American Community Survey
Need demographic data for programming, environmental justice analysis, or community profiles
Historic resource inventories, National Register listings, Section 106 consultation
Site may contain or be near historic resources; project has federal funding or permits
Zoning maps, land use plans, setbacks, FAR, overlay districts, subdivision regulations
Need to understand what can be built on the site and development requirements
Property records, plats, deeds, easements, rights-of-way, title history
Need to verify property boundaries, find easements, or understand legal constraints
Aerial imagery, LiDAR data, parcel data, environmental layers
Need high-resolution spatial data for GIS analysis or detailed site mapping
State wetland regulations, water quality permits, stormwater regulations
State regulations may exceed federal requirements; need state-level permits

content.text: MEMORY AID:  Match the data to the source: Topo = USGS. Soils = NRCS. Floods = FEMA. Wetlands = USFWS. Demographics = Census. Climate = NOAA. Contamination = EPA. History = SHPO. Zoning = Local Planning. Property = County Recorder.

Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are the primary technology for spatial data analysis in landscape architecture. GIS allows you to layer, query, and analyze multiple datasets simultaneously — the digital evolution of Ian McHarg's overlay method from Design with Nature (1969).

Vector data represents features as discrete geometric objects: points (wells, trees, survey monuments), lines (roads, streams, utilities), and polygons (property boundaries, soil units, land use zones). Vector data has precise coordinates and clean boundaries. Use vector data for features with well-defined locations.

Raster data represents information as a continuous grid of cells (pixels), each assigned a value. Raster is ideal for continuous phenomena: elevation (Digital Elevation Models), temperature, rainfall, land cover, satellite imagery. Each cell might represent one square meter or one square kilometer, depending on resolution.

Key GIS operations: Buffer analysis (creating zones around features — e.g., 100-foot buffer around a stream), overlay analysis (combining layers to find intersections — e.g., where steep slopes AND hydric soils overlap), suitability analysis (scoring areas based on multiple criteria to identify best sites for a given use), and viewshed analysis (determining visible areas from a given point based on terrain).

Remote sensing tools: LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) uses laser pulses from aircraft to create precise 3D point clouds of terrain and vegetation. It can penetrate tree canopy to map the ground surface beneath. NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) uses satellite multispectral imagery to measure vegetation health and density, with values ranging from -1 to +1 (higher = denser, healthier vegetation).

Boundary survey: Establishes legal property lines and corners, referencing survey monuments and legal descriptions. Prepared by a licensed surveyor. Required before any design work to define the project's legal extent.
Topographic survey: Maps elevation changes using contour lines and spot elevations. Shows existing structures, trees, utilities, and physical features. The foundation for grading design.

ALTA/NSPS survey: A comprehensive survey combining boundary and topographic information with easements, encroachments, zoning setbacks, and flood zone designations. Often required for commercial real estate transactions.

Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (ESA): Identifies potential environmental contamination through records review, site reconnaissance, and interviews — without intrusive testing (no soil borings or groundwater sampling). If potential contamination is found, a Phase II ESA involves actual sampling and laboratory analysis.

Legal documents: Plats (recorded subdivision maps), deeds (transfer property ownership), easements (grant specific use rights to others), rights-of-way (dedicated strips for public use), and covenants/restrictions (private agreements limiting land use).

Landscape architects must navigate a complex web of federal, state, and local regulations. The exam tests your knowledge of the major environmental laws, accessibility standards, and regulatory processes that affect site analysis and project management.

Enacted in 1970, NEPA requires all federal agencies to evaluate the environmental effects of their proposed actions before making decisions. Any project that receives federal funding, requires a federal permit, or occurs on federal land triggers NEPA review.
NEPA establishes three levels of review, depending on the expected environmental impact:

Categorical Exclusion (CE): For routine actions that individually and cumulatively have no significant environmental impact. Examples: minor maintenance, small-scale construction, and administrative actions. No detailed analysis required.

Environmental Assessment (EA): For actions where environmental significance is uncertain. The EA is a concise document analyzing the proposed action, alternatives, and environmental effects. If the EA finds no significant impact, the agency issues a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) and proceeds. If significant impacts are identified, a full EIS is required.

Environmental Impact Statement (EIS): For major federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment. An EIS is a comprehensive document analyzing the purpose and need, the proposed action, a range of reasonable alternatives (including a No Action alternative), the affected environment, and the environmental consequences of each alternative. EIS preparation involves extensive public comment periods and can take 1-3+ years.
Section 404 of the Clean Water Act regulates the discharge of dredged or fill material into "waters of the United States," which includes wetlands, streams, rivers, lakes, and their tributaries.
Who issues permits: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) administers the Section 404 permit program. The EPA has veto authority over USACE decisions (Section 404(c)).

Permit process follows a sequence: (1) Avoid wetland impacts if possible, (2) Minimize unavoidable impacts, (3) Mitigate remaining impacts through compensatory mitigation (creating, restoring, or preserving wetlands elsewhere to offset losses). This avoid-minimize-mitigate sequence is fundamental to Section 404 compliance.

Wetland delineation: The boundaries of jurisdictional wetlands are established through a formal delineation process that documents three criteria: hydric soils, hydrophytic vegetation, and wetland hydrology. All three must be present.

Section 106 of the NHPA requires federal agencies to consider the effects of their actions on historic properties — properties listed on or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places. The process involves:
•  Identifying the undertaking and its Area of Potential Effect (APE)
•  Identifying historic properties within the APE through survey and consultation
•  Assessing effects (No Historic Properties Affected, No Adverse Effect, or Adverse Effect)
•  Resolving adverse effects through consultation with the State Historic Preservation Officer (SHPO) and affected parties

Section 106 applies when a project has a federal nexus: federal funding, federal permits, or federal land. Cultural landscapes (designed landscapes, vernacular landscapes, and historic sites) fall within Section 106's scope.

The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires that public accommodations, commercial facilities, and state/local government facilities be accessible to people with disabilities. The Public Rights-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines (PROWAG) extend these requirements to sidewalks, crosswalks, curb ramps, and pedestrian signals.

rows: Required on both sides when rise exceeds 6 inches
60 inches minimum length, width of ramp
60 inches wide at intervals of 200 feet max
Truncated domes required, 24 inches deep minimum

content.text: Endangered Species Act (ESA): Protects federally listed threatened and endangered species and their critical habitats. USFWS administers for terrestrial/freshwater species. Section 7 consultation required for projects with federal nexus. Section 10 Habitat Conservation Plans for private projects.

Coastal Zone Management Act (CZMA): Requires federal actions in coastal zones to be consistent with state coastal management programs. Addresses erosion, storm surge, sea level rise, and coastal habitat protection.

Phase I Environmental Site Assessment: Follows ASTM E1527 standards to identify Recognized Environmental Conditions (RECs) through records review, site reconnaissance, and interviews. Does not involve sampling. Required for most commercial real estate transactions to establish liability protection.

Landscape architecture is fundamentally a public-serving profession, and the ability to engage stakeholders meaningfully is both a professional obligation and a tested competency. This chapter covers the frameworks, methods, and principles of effective public participation.

s1_book.title: 8.1 The IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation

content.text: The International Association for Public Participation (IAP2) developed the most widely adopted framework for understanding levels of community involvement. The spectrum ranges from least to most public influence:

Level 1 — INFORM: One-way communication. The goal is to provide balanced, objective information so the public understands the project. The promise: "We will keep you informed." Methods: fact sheets, websites, newsletters, open houses with display boards, presentations. Use when the decision is already made or the public's role is limited to being aware.

Level 2 — CONSULT: Two-way communication seeking feedback. The goal is to obtain public feedback on analysis, alternatives, or decisions. The promise: "We will listen to and acknowledge your concerns and aspirations." Methods: public comment periods, surveys, focus groups, public meetings with Q&A. Use during alternatives analysis when you want input but decision-making remains with the project team.

Level 3 — INVOLVE: Active participation throughout the process. The goal is to work directly with the public to ensure their concerns are consistently understood and considered. The promise: "We will work with you to ensure your concerns and aspirations are directly reflected in alternatives and decisions." Methods: workshops, design charrettes, deliberative polling, community advisory groups. Use when public values should shape alternatives.

Level 4 — COLLABORATE: Partnership in decision-making. The goal is to partner with the public in each aspect of the decision, including developing alternatives and identifying the preferred solution. The promise: "We will look to you for advice and innovation and incorporate your advice into decisions to the maximum extent possible." Methods: consensus-building committees, joint design teams, participatory budgeting.

Level 5 — EMPOWER: The public makes the final decision. The promise: "We will implement what you decide." Methods: citizen juries, delegated decisions, referendums. Rarely used in landscape architecture but important to understand the full spectrum.

EXAM TIP:  The exam may present a project scenario and ask which level of participation is most appropriate. Match the level to the public's role: if the decision is made and you are sharing information, that is Inform. If you are seeking feedback, that is Consult. If stakeholders are co-designing, that is Collaborate. A design charrette = Involve or Collaborate level.
Effective engagement must reach all segments of the community, especially historically underrepresented populations. Barriers to participation include:
•  Language barriers — provide translated materials and interpreters
•  Meeting times that conflict with work schedules — offer evening and weekend options
•  Inaccessible venues — ensure ADA compliance, provide childcare and food
•  Digital divides — supplement online tools with in-person alternatives
•  Distrust of institutions — partner with trusted community organizations
•  Environmental justice considerations — ensure projects do not disproportionately burden low-income communities or communities of color

Project management is the lowest-weighted domain (7%, approximately 6 questions) but represents reliable points because the concepts are straightforward and drawn from standard professional practice. Do not skip this material.
A landscape architecture project typically follows six phases, each building on the deliverables of the previous one:

1. Pre-Design / Programming: Define project goals, scope, budget, and schedule. Conduct site inventory and analysis. Develop the program (a list of desired uses, spaces, and requirements). Engage stakeholders to understand needs and priorities. This is the phase most directly tested in Section 1.

2. Schematic Design (SD): Translate the program into conceptual design alternatives showing spatial organization, circulation, and major features. Present concepts to the client for feedback and selection. Prepare an order-of-magnitude cost estimate.

3. Design Development (DD): Refine the selected concept. Choose specific materials, furnishings, and planting. Develop detailed design solutions. Coordinate with consultants (civil, structural, electrical). Prepare a more detailed cost estimate.

4. Construction Documents (CD): Prepare the final drawings and written specifications that contractors will use to bid and build the project. Coordinate all consultant documents for consistency. Prepare a detailed cost estimate.
5. Bidding and Negotiation: Distribute CDs to contractors. Answer questions through addenda. Evaluate bids. Recommend contract award.

6. Construction Administration (CA): Observe construction for conformance with design intent. Review submittals and shop drawings. Respond to RFIs. Review payment applications. Conduct punch list and issue certificate of substantial completion.

Critical Path Method (CPM): A network-based scheduling technique that identifies the longest sequence of dependent tasks from project start to finish. This longest sequence is the critical path. Tasks on the critical path have zero float (slack) — any delay in a critical path task directly delays the entire project. Non-critical tasks have float, meaning they can be delayed by the float amount without affecting the project end date.
Gantt Chart: A horizontal bar chart plotting tasks against time. Shows duration, sequence, overlap, and milestones. The most common visual scheduling tool in professional practice.

Work Breakdown Structure (WBS): A hierarchical decomposition of all project work into smaller, manageable tasks and subtasks. The WBS is the foundation for building the schedule and tracking progress.

Standard of care: The legal standard for landscape architects: services performed with the same degree of skill and care that a reasonably competent professional would exercise under similar circumstances. This is not a guarantee of perfection — it is a duty of competence.

Scope creep: The unauthorized, incremental expansion of project scope beyond the original agreement. Scope creep is the most common cause of fee overruns and client disputes. The solution: document scope clearly in the contract, recognize scope changes promptly, and negotiate amendments before performing additional work.

Fee structures: Lump sum (fixed price for defined scope — best when scope is clear); hourly with a not-to-exceed cap (best when scope is uncertain); percentage of construction cost (best for larger projects where scope will evolve); cost-plus-fixed-fee (actual costs plus a guaranteed fee — best for complex or uncertain projects).
Landscape architects coordinate with numerous disciplines. Know who is responsible for what:

rows: Grading, drainage, stormwater infrastructure, utility layout, roadway geometry
Retaining walls over 4-6 feet, bridges, large pergolas, foundations for heavy structures
Building design, building-site interface, interior spaces adjacent to landscape
Soil borings, bearing capacity analysis, slope stability, foundation recommendations
Wetland delineation, habitat surveys, environmental permitting (NEPA, Section 404)
Vehicular circulation, intersection design, parking requirements, traffic calming
Boundary surveys, topographic surveys, utility location, construction staking
Detailed tree health and risk assessment, root zone protection, pruning specifications

content.text: CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Six project phases: Pre-Design, SD, DD, CD, Bidding, CA. Section 1 primarily tests pre-design knowledge. ✔  CPM identifies the critical path (longest task sequence). Critical tasks have zero float; delays cascade. ✔  Standard of care = reasonable competence, not perfection. ✔  Scope creep is prevented by clear contracts and documented change management. ✔  Fee structures: lump sum (clear scope), hourly/cap (uncertain scope), percentage (evolving scope). ✔  Landscape architects coordinate with civil, structural, geotech, environmental, traffic engineers, architects, surveyors, and arborists.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect enters into a contract with a client using AIA or ASLA standard form agreements. Which of the following is the landscape architect's PRIMARY obligation under such agreements?

choices.text: Provide professional services with reasonable skill and care
Guarantee the project will be completed on time and within budget
Assume liability for the contractor's means and methods of construction
Ensure the contractor's work is free from all defects

s1_exam.explanation: Landscape architects are held to a standard of reasonable skill and care, not perfection or guarantees.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect is negotiating fees for a public park project. Which fee structure would BEST protect the landscape architect when the scope of work is not clearly defined?

choices.text: Lump sum (stipulated sum)
Percentage of construction cost
Hourly with a not-to-exceed cap
Cost plus a fixed fee

s1_exam.explanation: Hourly with a not-to-exceed cap protects the LA when scope is undefined, limiting client exposure while compensating for actual time spent.

s1_exam.question: In a standard owner-landscape architect agreement, "Additional Services" typically includes which of the following?

choices.text: Preparation of construction documents
Expert witness testimony
Schematic design presentations to the client
Construction administration site visits

s1_exam.explanation: Expert witness testimony is typically an additional service; schematic design, CD preparation, and CA are basic services.

s1_exam.question: Which contract delivery method gives the owner a single point of responsibility for both design and construction?

choices.text: Design-Bid-Build
Construction Manager at Risk
Multiple Prime Contracts
Design-Build

s1_exam.explanation: Design-Build provides a single entity responsible for both design and construction.

s1_exam.question: Under a stipulated sum (lump sum) contract, who bears the greatest financial risk if unforeseen conditions arise?

choices.text: The contractor
The owner
The landscape architect
The surety company

s1_exam.explanation: Under a lump sum contract, the contractor assumes the risk of unforeseen conditions since the price is fixed.

s1_exam.question: During construction administration, a landscape architect observes that the contractor is installing a retaining wall foundation at a depth shallower than shown on the construction documents. The landscape architect should FIRST:

choices.text: Issue a stop-work order immediately
Contact the structural engineer for a revised design
Inform the owner that the contractor is in default
Notify the contractor of the discrepancy and document the observation

s1_exam.explanation: The LA should first notify the contractor of the observed discrepancy and document it. The LA typically does not have stop-work authority.

s1_exam.question: A contractor submits a Request for Information (RFI) asking for clarification on a grading detail. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Respond verbally on the next site visit to save time
Provide a written response within a reasonable time as defined in the contract
Direct the contractor to interpret the drawings as they see fit
Issue a change order to address the RFI

s1_exam.explanation: RFIs should be responded to in writing within the timeframe established in the contract to maintain a proper project record.

s1_exam.question: Which of the following is the PRIMARY purpose of a submittal review during construction?

choices.text: To verify the contractor's compliance with means and methods
To guarantee the quality of all materials being installed
To transfer liability for product selection to the contractor
To confirm that materials and products are consistent with the design intent

s1_exam.explanation: Submittal review confirms materials are consistent with design intent, not a guarantee of quality or review of means and methods.

s1_exam.question: A contractor requests a substitution for a specified tree species, claiming the specified species is unavailable. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Evaluate the proposed substitution for design intent, quality, and suitability before responding
Approve the substitution immediately to avoid project delays
Reject the substitution outright since it was not specified
Require the contractor to find the originally specified species regardless of availability

s1_exam.explanation: The LA should evaluate the substitution against design intent, quality, and suitability before making a decision.
