s1_exam.question: During a punch list walkthrough, the landscape architect identifies several items of incomplete work. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Recommend the owner withhold the entire remaining payment until all items are complete
Accept the work as substantially complete and release all remaining payment
Direct the contractor on how to complete each item
Document the incomplete items and establish a timeline for completion before final payment

s1_exam.explanation: Document incomplete items and establish a timeline for completion; retainage is typically held to cover punch list work.

s1_exam.question: A critical path method (CPM) schedule shows that landscape installation has zero float. This means:

choices.text: The landscape installation can be delayed without affecting the project completion date
Any delay in landscape installation will delay the overall project completion
The landscape installation is not important to the project
The landscape architect should request more time for this activity

s1_exam.explanation: Zero float on a CPM schedule means the activity is on the critical path; any delay will delay the project.

s1_exam.question: Which of the following is the BEST method for tracking project budget during the design phase?

choices.text: Comparing invoices to the original fee proposal at project completion
Waiting until the end of each phase to review costs
Relying on the client to track the budget
Monitoring hours and expenses against budget at regular intervals

s1_exam.explanation: Regular monitoring of hours and expenses against budget allows for timely adjustments.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect discovers that the scope of a project has significantly expanded beyond the original agreement. The MOST appropriate action is to:

choices.text: Absorb the additional work to maintain a good client relationship
Notify the client, document the scope change, and negotiate an amendment to the contract
Complete the additional work and bill at a higher hourly rate
Reduce the quality of other deliverables to compensate for the extra work

s1_exam.explanation: Scope changes should be documented and the contract amended through proper negotiation.

s1_exam.question: Which of the following is a PRIMARY benefit of phasing a large construction project?

choices.text: It eliminates the need for a construction manager
It allows portions of the project to be used while other portions are still under construction
It guarantees lower overall construction costs
It reduces the landscape architect's liability exposure

s1_exam.explanation: Phasing allows partial occupancy or use while other portions are still under construction.

s1_exam.question: A project has a fast-track schedule. Which of the following is a characteristic of fast-tracking?

choices.text: Design and construction phases overlap, with construction beginning before design is fully complete
All construction documents are completed before bidding begins
The project is guaranteed to cost less than a traditional delivery
The landscape architect has reduced responsibility during construction

s1_exam.explanation: Fast-tracking overlaps design and construction phases, beginning construction before design is fully complete.

s1_exam.question: Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), which of the following is the MAXIMUM allowable running slope for an accessible route?
s1_exam.explanation: ADA requires a maximum running slope of 1:20 (5%) for accessible routes. Ramps (which are steeper portions) may be up to 1:12.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect seals and signs a set of construction documents. By doing so, the landscape architect is:

choices.text: Certifying that the documents were prepared under their responsible charge
Guaranteeing the project will be built exactly as drawn
Assuming liability for the contractor's construction methods
Warranting that no changes will be needed during construction

s1_exam.explanation: Sealing documents certifies they were prepared under the LA's responsible charge; it does not guarantee outcomes.

s1_exam.question: Which of the following activities would MOST LIKELY require the landscape architect to coordinate with a local zoning authority?

choices.text: Selecting plant species for a residential garden
Designing a parking lot layout that must meet minimum landscaping requirements
Choosing furniture for an outdoor dining area
Specifying an irrigation controller brand

s1_exam.explanation: Parking lot landscaping requirements are typically regulated through local zoning ordinances.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect learns that a proposed project may impact wetlands regulated under the Clean Water Act. The MOST appropriate action is to:

choices.text: Proceed with the design and address wetland issues during construction
Redesign the project to avoid all natural areas
Advise the client of the regulatory requirements and coordinate with appropriate agencies early in the process
Recommend the client hire a lawyer before any design work begins

s1_exam.explanation: Early coordination with regulatory agencies regarding wetland impacts is essential and a professional responsibility.

s1_exam.question: In most jurisdictions, a landscape architect's license can be revoked or suspended for which of the following?

choices.text: Losing a project to a competitor
Designing a project that exceeds the client's budget
Practicing outside the scope of licensure or professional misconduct
Refusing to take on a project outside their area of expertise

s1_exam.explanation: Practicing outside the scope of licensure or professional misconduct are grounds for license revocation or suspension.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect is asked by a developer to certify that a project meets local tree preservation ordinance requirements. Upon review, the landscape architect determines the project does NOT fully comply. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Refuse to certify and inform the client of the specific areas of non-compliance
Certify the project to maintain the client relationship
Recommend the client find another landscape architect to certify the project
Certify the project with a disclaimer noting the areas of concern

s1_exam.explanation: The LA has an ethical and legal obligation to refuse to certify non-compliant work and inform the client of deficiencies.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect discovers a potential conflict of interest because they own stock in a company that manufactures a product they intend to specify. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Specify the product without disclosing the financial interest
Avoid specifying the product entirely, even if it is the best option
Disclose the conflict of interest to the client and allow the client to decide how to proceed
Sell the stock before specifying the product

s1_exam.explanation: Conflicts of interest must be disclosed to the client, who can then make an informed decision.

s1_exam.question: A former client asks a landscape architect for copies of construction documents from a completed project to give to a new designer. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Refuse to provide any documents
Provide the documents, as they always belong to the client
Charge triple the original fee for the documents
Provide the documents in accordance with the terms of the original contract regarding document ownership

s1_exam.explanation: Document ownership and distribution rights are governed by the original contract terms.

s1_exam.question: During a public bidding process, a landscape architect receives a question from one bidder requesting clarification on the specifications. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Issue an addendum with the clarification to all bidders
Answer the question privately to that bidder only
Ignore the question since the documents should speak for themselves
Recommend the bidder include an allowance for the unclear item

s1_exam.explanation: In public bidding, all clarifications must be issued as addenda to all bidders to ensure fairness.

s1_exam.question: Which of the following bond types protects the owner in the event the contractor fails to complete the project?

choices.text: Bid bond
Payment bond
Performance bond
Maintenance bond

s1_exam.explanation: A performance bond guarantees the contractor will complete the work per the contract.

s1_exam.question: An owner on a private project wants to negotiate directly with a single contractor rather than competitively bid the project. This approach is known as:

choices.text: Design-Build
Invitation to bid
Negotiated contract
Competitive sealed proposal

s1_exam.explanation: Directly negotiating with a single contractor is a negotiated contract approach.

s1_exam.question: "Substantial completion" in a construction project is BEST defined as:

choices.text: The point at which 100% of the work is finished with no remaining punch list items
The stage at which the work is sufficiently complete that the owner can occupy or use the project for its intended purpose
The date on which the contractor submits the final payment application
The point at which the landscape architect completes the final site inspection

s1_exam.explanation: Substantial completion is when the work is sufficiently complete for the owner to use it for its intended purpose.

s1_exam.question: A change order is typically used to:

choices.text: Correct errors in the contractor's bid
Replace the original contract between owner and contractor
Transfer design responsibility from the landscape architect to the contractor
Document agreed-upon changes to the contract sum, contract time, or scope of work

s1_exam.explanation: Change orders document agreed-upon changes to contract sum, time, or scope.

s1_exam.question: Which of the following types of specifications gives the contractor the MOST flexibility in selecting products?

choices.text: Proprietary (closed) specification
Prescriptive specification
Reference standard specification
Performance specification

s1_exam.explanation: Performance specifications define required outcomes, giving the contractor maximum flexibility in product selection.

s1_exam.question: Retainage in a construction contract refers to:

choices.text: The contractor's profit margin on the project
The amount the landscape architect retains for construction administration services
A percentage of each progress payment withheld by the owner until project completion
Funds set aside for warranty repairs after project completion

s1_exam.explanation: Retainage is a percentage of each payment withheld until project completion to ensure the contractor completes all work.

s1_exam.question: Professional liability insurance (errors and omissions insurance) for a landscape architect covers:

choices.text: Injuries to workers on the construction site
Damage to the contractor's equipment
Claims arising from negligent professional services
Environmental contamination caused by construction activities

s1_exam.explanation: Professional liability (E&O) insurance covers claims arising from negligent professional services.

s1_exam.question: Which of the following is the MOST effective way for a landscape architect to manage risk on a project?

choices.text: Avoid putting anything in writing
Accept all client requests without question
Delegate all decisions to the contractor
Maintain thorough documentation throughout all project phases

s1_exam.explanation: Thorough documentation is the most effective risk management strategy for design professionals.

s1_exam.question: During the schematic design phase, which type of cost estimate is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Detailed quantity takeoff
Order-of-magnitude estimate
Contractor's bid
Parametric or unit-cost estimate

s1_exam.explanation: Order-of-magnitude estimates are appropriate for schematic design when limited detail is available.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect's construction cost estimate exceeds the client's budget. The MOST appropriate course of action is to:

choices.text: Proceed with construction documents and hope bids come in lower
Reduce the landscape architect's fee to offset the cost overrun
Discuss value engineering options with the client to reduce costs while maintaining design intent
Recommend the client increase the budget without exploring alternatives

s1_exam.explanation: Value engineering explores cost reductions while maintaining design intent, which is the appropriate professional response.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a project seeking LEED certification. Which of the following site-related credits would the landscape architect MOST likely be responsible for?

choices.text: Reducing light pollution through exterior lighting design
Energy-efficient HVAC systems
Indoor air quality management
Building envelope insulation

s1_exam.explanation: Exterior lighting design to reduce light pollution (Sustainable Sites credit) falls within the LA's scope of work.

s1_exam.question: When designing a public playground, which of the following standards should the landscape architect reference for safety compliance?

choices.text: ASTM and CPSC playground safety guidelines
OSHA construction standards
MUTCD traffic control standards
ANSI elevator safety codes

s1_exam.explanation: ASTM F1487 and CPSC Publication 325 are the primary playground safety standards.

s1_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a stormwater management facility for a public park. The PRIMARY consideration for public safety is:

choices.text: Maximizing the water storage capacity
Designing the facility to prevent public access at all times
Balancing stormwater function with safe public access, including appropriate grading, signage, and barriers where needed
Using the least expensive construction materials

s1_exam.explanation: Stormwater facilities in public spaces must balance function with safe public access through appropriate design measures.

s1_exam.question: During a multi-disciplinary project, the landscape architect discovers a conflict between the civil engineer's grading plan and the landscape planting plan. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Modify the civil engineer's grading plan without consulting them
Coordinate with the civil engineer to resolve the conflict before issuing construction documents
Ignore the conflict and let the contractor resolve it in the field
Issue both plans and include a note that the contractor should follow whichever plan they prefer

s1_exam.explanation: Conflicts between disciplines should be resolved through coordination before issuing documents.

s1_exam.question: Meeting minutes from a client meeting should include which of the following?

choices.text: Only the landscape architect's design recommendations
A verbatim transcript of everything discussed
Only items that the landscape architect considers important
Key decisions, action items, responsible parties, and deadlines

s1_exam.explanation: Effective meeting minutes capture key decisions, action items, responsible parties, and deadlines.

s1_exam.question: A contractor claims additional compensation for work they say was not included in the original contract documents. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Review the original contract documents to determine if the work was included and respond accordingly
Approve the claim immediately to maintain good relations
Deny the claim without review
Tell the contractor to take the issue up with the owner directly

s1_exam.explanation: The LA should review the original documents to determine if the claimed extra work was already included before responding.

content.text: Aligned to the CLARB Exam Blueprint (Effective December 2023)
85 Scored Items  |  Computer-Based  |  Multiple Choice + Multiple Response  |  3 Hours

LARE Section 2 tests your ability to plan and design landscape architectural projects. It covers the full design process from stewardship principles through master planning, schematic design, and design development.

The exam includes both multiple-choice and multiple-response questions. Multiple-response questions require you to select all correct answers from a list. You must select every correct option and no incorrect options to receive credit.
This domain tests your understanding of the ethical, environmental, and cultural responsibilities of the landscape architect during the planning and design process.
•  SITES (Sustainable SITES Initiative) — rating system for landscape sustainability
–  Developed by ASLA, Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center, and U.S. Botanic Garden
–  8 credit categories: Site Context, Pre-Design Assessment + Planning, Water, Soil + Vegetation, Materials Selection, Human Health + Well-Being, Construction, Operations + Maintenance
–  4 certification levels: Certified, Silver, Gold, Platinum
–  Applies to landscapes with or without buildings
•  LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) — building-focused but includes Sustainable Sites credits
–  SS credits address: site selection, development density, brownfield redevelopment, stormwater, heat island effect, light pollution
•  Living Building Challenge — regenerative design framework; Net Positive approach
•  Triple Bottom Line — evaluating projects across people, planet, profit
•  Ecosystem services — benefits nature provides: provisioning, regulating, supporting, cultural
•  Resilience — capacity of a system to absorb disturbance and reorganize while retaining function
•  Regenerative design — goes beyond sustainability; aims to restore and improve ecological function
•  Low Impact Development (LID) — managing stormwater at the source through small-scale BMPs
•  Native plant communities — using regionally appropriate species to support local ecosystems
•  Habitat connectivity — linking habitat patches through corridors and greenways
•  Adaptive management — iterative approach: design → monitor → evaluate → adjust
•  Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties
–  Four treatment approaches: Preservation, Rehabilitation, Restoration, Reconstruction
•  Cultural Landscape Reports (CLR) — documents used to guide treatment of historic landscapes
•  National Register of Historic Places — listing criteria and implications for design
•  Section 106 of NHPA — requires federal agencies to consider effects on historic properties
•  Cultural landscape types: historic designed, historic vernacular, ethnographic, archaeological
•  Elements of design: line, form, color, texture, scale
•  Principles of design: unity, balance, proportion, rhythm, emphasis, sequence
•  Spatial organization: axis, symmetry, hierarchy, datum, transformation
•  Kevin Lynch's five elements: paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks
•  Pattern Language (Christopher Alexander) — timeless spatial patterns
•  Genius loci — spirit of place; designing in response to a site's unique character
•  Universal design — creating spaces usable by all people to the greatest extent possible
•  Biophilic design — incorporating nature and natural patterns into the built environment

The largest domain on the exam. Master planning encompasses programming, site analysis, land use planning, and plan preparation. You must understand the entire process from identifying client goals through developing a master plan.
•  Defining project goals, objectives, and priorities with stakeholders
•  Needs assessment — identifying user groups, activities, and spatial requirements
•  Program development — quantifying spaces, areas, and functional relationships
•  Space standards — dimensions for parking, athletic fields, playgrounds, plazas, paths
–  Parking: standard stall 9'×18', ADA accessible stall 8'×18' + 5' access aisle (van: 8' aisle)
–  Two-way drive aisle: 24', one-way: 12–14'
–  ADA parking ratio: 1 per 25 total (1-25 spaces), 2 per 50 (26-50), etc.
–  Playground safety zones: 6' minimum use zone around equipment
•  Precedent studies — analyzing comparable projects for lessons learned
•  Budget parameters — understanding how design scope relates to available funding
•  Opportunities and constraints mapping — synthesizing site inventory into design implications
•  Suitability analysis (Ian McHarg overlay method) — layering factors to find best-fit areas
–  McHarg's Design with Nature (1969) — foundational text for ecological planning
–  Layer maps of slope, soils, hydrology, vegetation, viewsheds, cultural resources
–  Identify zones of highest and lowest development suitability
•  Carrying capacity — maximum use a site can sustain without degradation
•  Visual analysis — viewshed mapping, visual absorption capacity, scenic quality assessment
•  Circulation analysis — pedestrian, vehicular, bicycle, and service access patterns
•  Solar analysis — sun angles, shadow patterns, building orientation for passive solar
•  Wind analysis — prevailing winds, wind channeling, windbreaks, ventilation corridors
•  Comprehensive plans — long-range community planning documents
•  Zoning — land use districts, setbacks, FAR, lot coverage, height limits, density
–  Euclidean zoning — traditional use-based districts
–  Form-based codes — regulate building form rather than use
–  Planned Unit Development (PUD) — flexible zoning for mixed-use projects
–  Overlay districts — additional regulations for special areas (historic, environmental, etc.)
•  Smart Growth principles — mixed use, compact, walkable, transit-oriented development
•  New Urbanism — traditional neighborhood design, interconnected streets, town centers
•  Transect-based planning — T1 Natural through T6 Urban Core
•  Green infrastructure planning — regional networks of parks, trails, stream corridors, urban forests
•  Greenway and trail planning — connecting communities through multi-use corridors
•  Site organization — arranging program elements based on functional relationships
•  Bubble diagrams — schematic layouts showing spatial relationships and adjacencies
•  Functional diagrams — refining relationships, circulation, and spatial hierarchy
•  Land use compatibility — separating conflicting uses, buffering incompatible adjacencies
•  Density and intensity calculations — dwelling units per acre, floor area ratio (FAR)
•  Open space requirements — percentage, distribution, types (active, passive, conservation)
•  Phasing plans — sequencing development to manage growth and funding
•  Concept plans — illustrating design intent through diagrams and sketches
•  Alternative analysis — developing and evaluating multiple design options
•  Master plan components: site plan, circulation plan, planting concept, grading concept, utilities, phasing
•  Presentation techniques — graphic standards, rendering, 3D visualization, digital tools
•  Written narratives — design rationale and project descriptions
•  Community presentations — communicating design to public audiences
•  Design review processes — board presentations, agency review, entitlement applications

Schematic design translates the master plan concept into a more detailed design that establishes spatial organization, form, character, and functional relationships. This domain tests your ability to evaluate and refine design proposals.
•  Translating program requirements into three-dimensional spatial concepts
•  Establishing design vocabulary — materials palette, forms, spatial character
•  Scale and proportion — human scale, building scale, landscape scale
•  Spatial definition — using plantings, walls, grade changes, and structures to define space
•  Enclosure ratios — D/H ratio (distance-to-height) and its effect on spatial quality
–  1:1 (D/H = 1) — intimate, enclosed space
–  2:1 — comfortable, balanced space
–  3:1 — open, expansive feeling
–  4:1+ — spaciousness, loss of spatial definition
•  Focal points — creating visual hierarchy through emphasis elements
•  Hierarchy of movement — primary, secondary, and tertiary paths
•  Pedestrian circulation — walkways, promenades, trails, sidewalks
–  Minimum accessible path width: 5' (36" minimum clear, but 5' required for two-way passing)
–  ADA maximum running slope: 5% (1:20) for accessible routes, cross slope: 2% maximum
–  Ramps: 8.33% maximum (1:12), 30' maximum run between landings, 5'×5' landing minimum
•  Vehicular circulation — access points, internal roads, fire lanes, service access
–  Fire lane: typically 20' minimum width, 13'6" vertical clearance
–  Sight distance triangles at intersections — maintain clear vision area
•  Bicycle facilities — bike lanes, cycle tracks, shared-use paths, bike parking
•  Complete Streets — designing roads that serve all users: pedestrians, cyclists, transit, vehicles
•  Traffic calming — speed tables, chicanes, narrowing, roundabouts, textured paving
•  Slope categories and typical uses:
–  0-2%: athletic fields, plazas, ponding risk if not properly drained
–  2-5%: ideal for most development (buildings, parking, lawns)
–  5-10%: suitable for informal recreation, requires erosion consideration
–  10-25%: limited development, significant grading required, high erosion risk
–  25%+: conservation, potential slope stability issues, avoid development
•  Spot elevations — establishing key grades at buildings, corners, intersections, drain inlets
•  Drainage patterns — sheet flow, concentrated flow, swales, area drains, catch basins
•  Positive drainage — grading to direct water away from structures (minimum 2% within 10')
•  ADA-compliant grading — balancing accessibility requirements with drainage needs
•  Plant selection criteria: climate zone, soil conditions, water requirements, mature size, maintenance
•  Planting design principles: layering, massing, repetition, rhythm, seasonal interest
•  Functional planting: screening, windbreaks, shade, erosion control, habitat creation
•  Native vs. adapted species — ecological benefits vs. expanded palette
•  Xeriscape principles — water-efficient landscape design (7 principles)
–  Planning/design, soil improvement, practical turf areas, appropriate plants, efficient irrigation, mulch, maintenance
•  Urban forestry — tree canopy goals, species diversity, structural soil, suspended pavement
•  Green infrastructure strategies: rain gardens, bioswales, permeable paving, green roofs, cisterns
•  Stormwater quantity — managing peak flow and total volume
•  Stormwater quality — first flush treatment, pollutant removal, TSS reduction
•  BMP selection criteria — soil type, space, depth to groundwater, maintenance capacity
•  LID principles — minimize impervious area, disconnect impervious surfaces, maximize infiltration
•  Rain garden sizing — typically 5-10% of contributing impervious area
•  Bioretention components — ponding area, mulch layer, engineered soil media, underdrain (if needed)

Design development refines the schematic design into a detailed, buildable project. This domain tests your understanding of materials, cost implications, maintenance, sustainability, and legal considerations.
•  Hardscape materials: concrete, unit pavers, natural stone, asphalt, decomposed granite, permeable options
–  Concrete: versatile, durable, many finishes; control joints at 10-12' max spacing
–  Unit pavers: flexible, replaceable, good for freeze-thaw areas; require edge restraints
–  Natural stone: high-quality, durable; cost varies greatly by type and source
–  Permeable paving: reduces runoff; requires clean aggregate base and maintenance
•  Site furnishings: benches, trash receptacles, bollards, bike racks, signage
–  ADA requirements: clear floor space at benches, accessible routes to all amenities
•  Fencing and walls: materials, heights, sight lines, security, screening
•  Lighting: types (ambient, task, accent, security), photometrics, dark sky compliance
–  IDA Dark Sky: full cutoff fixtures, minimize light trespass, reduce sky glow
•  Sustainable materials: recycled content, regional sourcing, FSC-certified wood, life cycle assessment
•  Order-of-magnitude estimates — early project phase, ±30-50% accuracy
•  Schematic design estimates — based on unit costs and quantities, ±15-25% accuracy
•  Design development estimates — more refined quantities, ±10-15% accuracy
•  Construction cost components: site preparation, grading, paving, planting, irrigation, structures, site furnishings, utilities
•  Soft costs: design fees, permits, testing, surveys, contingencies
•  Value engineering — reducing costs while maintaining design intent and function
•  Life cycle cost analysis — comparing initial cost vs. maintenance and replacement costs over project life
•  Design for maintainability — specifying materials and systems that reduce long-term maintenance
•  Maintenance intensity levels: high (annual beds, turf), medium (shrubs, mulched areas), low (native plantings, meadows)
•  Irrigation system types: drip, spray, rotor, smart controllers, rain sensors
•  Maintenance access — ensuring equipment can reach all areas (mower widths, vehicle access)
•  Plant establishment period — typically 1-3 years for trees and shrubs; irrigation essential during establishment
•  Maintenance plans and budgets — projecting long-term costs for client decision-making
•  ADA and PROWAG — accessible routes, slopes, surfaces, detectable warnings, signage
–  PROWAG: Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines — curb ramps, crosswalks, pedestrian signals
•  Building codes — setbacks, fire access, occupancy, height limits
•  Zoning compliance — permitted uses, density, lot coverage, open space, parking requirements
•  Environmental regulations — wetland buffers, floodplain restrictions, tree preservation ordinances
•  Stormwater regulations — MS4 permits, post-construction requirements, water quality standards
•  Professional liability — standard of care, errors and omissions, duty to warn
•  Easements and rights-of-way — utility easements, access easements, conservation easements
•  Energy conservation — building orientation, shading, wind protection, microclimate design
•  Water conservation — rainwater harvesting, graywater reuse, drought-tolerant planting, efficient irrigation
•  Heat island mitigation — high-albedo surfaces, shade trees, green roofs, open grid paving
•  Carbon sequestration — tree planting, soil building, preserving existing vegetation
•  Waste reduction — recycling construction waste, specifying recycled materials, composting
•  Post-occupancy evaluation — assessing whether design goals are met after construction

rows: 8' wide + 5' access aisle (8' aisle for van)
Required at curb ramps and transit platforms

s2_guide.title: Typical Slope Ranges for Site Uses

content.text: •  Focus the most time on Master Planning (33%) — it is the single largest domain and covers the broadest range of topics.
•  Practice reading site plans, bubble diagrams, and concept plans. Section 2 often tests your ability to interpret graphic information.
•  Memorize ADA dimensional standards. These appear frequently and the answers are precise numbers.
•  Understand sustainability rating systems (especially SITES) at a conceptual level — know what each system emphasizes.
•  Know your slope ranges — which slopes are appropriate for which uses.
•  Study stormwater BMP selection — know which practices work on which soil types and site conditions.
•  Review cost estimating phases and accuracy ranges — these are commonly tested.
•  Practice the free CLARB demo exam to familiarize yourself with the testing interface and question formats.
•  Review the Secretary of the Interior's Standards — know the four treatment types.
•  Understand design theory vocabulary — D/H ratios, spatial enclosure, Lynch's elements, genius loci.
Aligned to the CLARB Exam Blueprint (Effective December 2023)
85 Scored Items  |  Computer-Based  |  Multiple Choice + Multiple Response  |  3 Hours

s2_book.title: Preface: How to Use This Book

content.text: This study book is designed to give you everything you need to pass LARE Section 2: Planning and Design. It is a complete teaching resource that explains each topic from the ground up, as though you were learning it in a university studio, and then connects that knowledge directly to what you will face on exam day.

Section 2 tests your ability to apply planning and design knowledge across the full arc of a project — from stewardship principles that guide ethical practice, through master planning that organizes land use and program, through schematic design that gives form to spatial ideas, to design development that refines those ideas into buildable, maintainable, and legally compliant projects.
The content is organized to mirror the four domains of the CLARB exam blueprint, weighted in order of importance. Each chapter contains:
•  Full explanatory text that teaches the concept, not just defines it
•  Real-world examples showing how concepts apply to professional practice
•  Memory aids and mnemonics to help you retain key information
•  Exam tips that flag exactly how topics are tested
•  Reference tables for quick lookup during study sessions
•  Chapter summaries listing everything you must know
•  Review questions with explained answers at the end of each chapter

Begin with the Master Planning chapters and spend the most time there — it is the single largest domain at 33%. But do not neglect Stewardship, which establishes the ethical and theoretical foundation that informs every design decision. The Schematic Design and Design Development domains are where your practical design judgment will be tested most directly.

EXAM FORMAT:  Section 2 uses both standard multiple-choice questions and multiple-response questions. Multiple-response questions ask you to select ALL correct answers from a list. You must select every correct option and no incorrect options to receive full credit. Read each question carefully to determine if it asks for the single best answer or all that apply.

The practice of landscape architecture is fundamentally an act of stewardship. Every design decision you make — where to place a building, what materials to specify, how to manage stormwater, which trees to preserve — has consequences for the health of ecosystems, the well-being of communities, and the resilience of landscapes over time. The LARE exam tests whether you understand these responsibilities and can apply sustainability principles to real design problems.
This chapter teaches the frameworks, rating systems, and ecological concepts that define sustainable landscape practice.

s2_book.title: 1.1 What Sustainability Means in Landscape Architecture

content.text: Sustainability in landscape architecture goes beyond simply being "green." It means designing landscapes that meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — the definition established by the Brundtland Commission in 1987. In practice, this requires balancing three interconnected dimensions, often called the Triple Bottom Line:

Environmental: Protecting and restoring ecosystems, conserving natural resources, reducing pollution, managing stormwater naturally, preserving biodiversity, and minimizing the carbon footprint of construction and maintenance.

Social: Creating equitable, accessible, healthy, and culturally meaningful spaces that serve diverse communities. This includes environmental justice — ensuring that the burdens and benefits of development are distributed fairly across all populations.

Economic: Designing projects that are financially viable over their full life cycle, including initial construction costs, ongoing maintenance, and eventual replacement. A beautiful design that the client cannot afford to maintain is not sustainable.
MEMORY AID:  Triple Bottom Line = People, Planet, Profit. A truly sustainable project scores well on all three. If any leg of the stool is missing, the project will eventually fail.

Ecosystem services are the benefits that natural systems provide to humans. Understanding these services is essential because sustainable design aims to protect and enhance them. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) organized ecosystem services into four categories:

rows: Food production (community gardens, urban agriculture), timber, clean water, medicinal plants
Benefits from ecosystem regulation of natural processes
Stormwater management by wetlands, air quality improvement by urban forests, climate regulation by tree canopy, pollination by native insects
Services necessary for production of all other services
Soil formation, nutrient cycling, photosynthesis, water cycling, habitat provision
Recreation, aesthetic enjoyment, spiritual value, sense of place, educational opportunities, tourism

content.text: When a landscape architect proposes preserving a wetland on a development site, they are protecting regulating services (flood attenuation, water quality treatment), supporting services (habitat for wildlife), and cultural services (nature viewing, education). Quantifying these services helps justify preservation decisions to clients and regulatory agencies.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A developer proposes filling a 2-acre wetland to create additional parking. The landscape architect calculates that the wetland provides approximately $50,000 per year in stormwater management services (by attenuating peak flows and filtering pollutants), plus habitat for migratory birds that attracts visitors. The cost of replacing these services with engineered infrastructure would exceed $800,000. This ecosystem services analysis helps the client see the wetland as an asset rather than a liability.

The Sustainable SITES Initiative (SITES) is the most important sustainability rating system for landscape architects to understand for the exam. While LEED focuses on buildings, SITES focuses specifically on landscapes and outdoor spaces — with or without buildings. It was developed by the American Society of Landscape Architects (ASLA), the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center, and the United States Botanic Garden.
SITES v2 is organized into ten sections, eight of which contain credits that earn points toward certification:

rows: Understanding the site's ecological and community context before design begins
Baseline conditions, stakeholder engagement, sustainability goals
Reducing water use, managing stormwater, protecting water resources
Protecting and restoring soils, using appropriate vegetation, managing invasives
Sustainable sourcing, recycled content, regional materials, life cycle assessment
Promoting physical activity, mental health, social interaction, cultural connections
Minimizing construction impacts, protecting existing features, reducing waste
Sustainable maintenance practices, monitoring, adaptive management
Mandatory requirements that all projects must meet before earning credits

content.text: Certification levels are based on total points earned: Certified (70 points), Silver (85 points), Gold (100 points), and Platinum (135 points) out of a possible 200 points. All projects must meet mandatory prerequisites before earning any credits.

EXAM TIP:  Know the difference between SITES and LEED. SITES is landscape-focused and can certify projects without buildings. LEED is building-focused but includes site-related credits. On the exam, if a question asks about certifying a park, plaza, or streetscape, SITES is the correct framework — not LEED.

Regenerative design goes beyond sustainability. While sustainability aims to do no harm — maintaining the status quo — regenerative design aims to actively improve ecological and social systems. A regenerative project leaves the site and community in better condition than it found them.
Key regenerative strategies in landscape architecture include:
•  Restoring degraded ecosystems to healthy, self-sustaining conditions (e.g., converting a parking lot to a functioning wetland)
•  Building soil health through composting, biochar, and mycorrhizal inoculation rather than relying on synthetic fertilizers
•  Creating habitat that supports biodiversity beyond what existed on the pre-development site
•  Designing stormwater systems that recharge groundwater, improving the hydrologic cycle
•  Producing more energy, water, or food than the site consumes (net-positive design)

The Living Building Challenge embodies regenerative principles. It requires projects to achieve net-positive performance in seven "Petals": Place, Water, Energy, Health + Happiness, Materials, Equity, and Beauty. Unlike LEED, which awards points on a scale, the Living Building Challenge requires actual measured performance over a 12-month operating period.

Low Impact Development is a stormwater management philosophy that manages rainfall at the source using decentralized, small-scale practices that mimic natural hydrology. Rather than collecting all runoff in pipes and sending it off-site, LID distributes stormwater management across the landscape.
The core principles of LID are:
•  Preserve existing natural features — wetlands, forests, drainage patterns, permeable soils
•  Minimize impervious surfaces — reduce parking, use narrower streets, cluster development
•  Disconnect impervious surfaces — direct roof and pavement runoff to pervious areas, not pipes
•  Manage stormwater at the source — treat and infiltrate runoff where it falls using bioretention, permeable paving, and other distributed practices
•  Extend time of concentration — slow runoff down to reduce peak discharge rates
MEMORY AID:  LID = Little Individual Devices everywhere, instead of one Big Pipe to somewhere else. Distribute, don't concentrate.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Sustainability encompasses environmental, social, and economic dimensions (Triple Bottom Line: People, Planet, Profit). ✔  Ecosystem services fall into four categories: provisioning, regulating, supporting, and cultural. ✔  SITES is the primary sustainability rating system for landscapes; LEED is primarily for buildings. ✔  SITES has 8 credit categories, 4 certification levels, and applies to landscapes with or without buildings. ✔  Regenerative design goes beyond sustainability to actively improve ecological and social systems. ✔  The Living Building Challenge requires net-positive performance measured over 12 months of actual operation. ✔  LID manages stormwater at the source using distributed, small-scale practices that mimic natural hydrology.
1. A landscape architect is designing a public park on a former industrial site. Which sustainability rating system is MOST appropriate for certifying the overall landscape?
A)  LEED
B)  SITES
C)  WELL
D)  Energy Star

Answer: B. SITES is specifically designed for landscapes and outdoor spaces, with or without buildings. LEED focuses on buildings, WELL focuses on indoor health, and Energy Star focuses on energy efficiency.
2. A wetland on a development site provides flood attenuation, water quality treatment, and wildlife habitat. These benefits are examples of:
A)  Carrying capacity
B)  Ecosystem services
C)  Design development deliverables
D)  Environmental impact mitigation
Answer: B. Ecosystem services are the benefits that natural systems provide. Flood attenuation and water quality treatment are regulating services; habitat is a supporting service.

subsections.title: 3. Which design philosophy aims to leave a site in BETTER ecological condition than it was found?

content.text: A)  Sustainable design
B)  Low Impact Development
C)  Regenerative design
D)  Adaptive management
Answer: C. Regenerative design goes beyond sustainability (which maintains the status quo) to actively improve ecological systems. It aims for net-positive outcomes.

subsections.title: 4. The core principle of Low Impact Development (LID) is to:

content.text: A)  Collect all stormwater in underground detention systems
B)  Manage rainfall at the source using distributed, small-scale practices
C)  Maximize impervious surface to prevent soil erosion
D)  Direct all runoff to regional stormwater treatment facilities
Answer: B. LID manages stormwater at the source using decentralized practices that mimic natural hydrology, rather than concentrating runoff in conventional pipe systems.

subsections.title: 5. What distinguishes the Living Building Challenge from LEED certification?

content.text: A)  It only applies to commercial buildings
B)  It requires actual measured net-positive performance over 12 months
C)  It focuses exclusively on energy efficiency
D)  It does not address water management

Answer: B. The Living Building Challenge requires projects to demonstrate net-positive performance in seven Petals through 12 months of actual measured operation, unlike LEED which awards points based on design intent.

s2_book.title: Chapter 2: Design Theory and Cultural Landscapes

content.text: Design theory provides the vocabulary and conceptual framework that landscape architects use to create meaningful, beautiful, and functional spaces. The LARE exam does not test whether you can produce beautiful designs — it tests whether you understand the principles, vocabulary, and theories that inform design decisions, and whether you can apply them to evaluate and communicate about design proposals.
The elements of design are the basic visual building blocks that every composition uses. Think of them as the alphabet of design — individual components that combine to create meaning.

Line: The most fundamental element. Lines define edges, create movement, establish direction, and divide space. In landscape architecture, lines appear as paths, walls, hedgerows, edges of water bodies, and grade changes. Straight lines convey formality and order. Curved lines suggest naturalism and movement. Diagonal lines create tension and dynamism.

Form: The three-dimensional shape of objects and spaces. Forms can be geometric (cubes, spheres, cones) or organic (free-flowing, irregular). A clipped boxwood hedge is a geometric form; a naturalistic meadow planting is an organic form. The form of spaces — concave (bowl-shaped, enclosing) versus convex (mound-shaped, exposing) — profoundly affects how people experience them.

Color: Used in planting, materials, and lighting. Color has three properties: hue (the color itself — red, blue, green), value (lightness or darkness), and chroma (intensity or saturation). Warm colors (reds, oranges, yellows) advance visually and feel energetic. Cool colors (blues, greens, purples) recede and feel calming. Color theory helps designers create harmonious palettes and draw attention to focal points.

Texture: The surface quality of materials and plants, ranging from fine to coarse. Fine textures (ornamental grasses, smooth concrete) make spaces feel larger and more refined. Coarse textures (large-leaved plants, rough stone) make spaces feel smaller and more intimate. Texture contrast creates visual interest — a smooth water feature against a rough stone wall, for example.

Scale: The size of objects and spaces relative to each other and to the human body. Human scale means spaces and elements feel comfortable and proportionate to people. Monumental scale intentionally exceeds human proportions to create awe (civic plazas, memorials). Intimate scale creates small, sheltered spaces that feel personal.
The principles of design are the rules for combining elements into effective compositions. They are the grammar that gives meaning to the alphabet of elements.

Unity: The sense that all parts of a design belong together. Unity is achieved through consistency of materials, repetition of forms, and a coherent design vocabulary. A project that uses twelve different paving materials and five different bench styles lacks unity. Dominance of one material or form family with selective contrast creates a unified composition.

Balance: The visual equilibrium of a composition. Symmetrical balance (bilateral symmetry) places equal visual weight on either side of an axis — it conveys formality, order, and permanence (the National Mall, Versailles). Asymmetrical balance uses unequal elements that achieve visual equilibrium through contrast — a large tree balanced by a cluster of smaller shrubs. Asymmetrical balance feels more dynamic and natural.

Proportion: The size relationship between parts. The Golden Ratio (approximately 1:1.618) appears throughout nature and has been used in design for millennia. More practically, proportion in landscape architecture means ensuring that the size of a plaza relates to the height of its enclosing walls, that a bench relates to the path it serves, and that a tree canopy relates to the space beneath it.

Rhythm: Repetition and pattern that create movement and continuity. A row of evenly spaced street trees creates simple rhythm. Alternating large and small trees creates complex rhythm. Rhythm pulls the eye and the body through space — it is the design principle that makes paths feel like journeys with beginning, middle, and end.

Emphasis: Creating a focal point — an element that draws attention because it contrasts with its surroundings. A sculpture in a garden, a specimen tree at the end of a vista, or a water feature at a plaza's center all create emphasis. Without emphasis, a composition feels monotonous. With too many focal points, a composition feels chaotic.

Sequence: The experience of moving through a series of spaces over time. Sequence is uniquely important in landscape architecture because landscapes are experienced dynamically — people walk, drive, and cycle through them. A successful sequence creates anticipation, surprise, and resolution. Frederick Law Olmsted was a master of sequence, designing park drives that alternated between enclosed and open views.
Beyond elements and principles, designers use specific spatial strategies to organize compositions:

Axis: An imaginary line that establishes direction and organizes elements along its length. Axes create visual and physical connections between features. A tree-lined allée is a landscape axis. Axes can be formal (straight, symmetrical) or implied (a view corridor toward a distant mountain).

Hierarchy: Establishing relative importance among spaces and elements. A campus design might have a primary quad (most important, largest), secondary courtyards (medium importance), and tertiary pocket gardens (smallest, most intimate). Hierarchy helps users navigate and understand a place intuitively.

Datum: A line, plane, or volume that runs through a composition and to which other elements relate. A long wall, a continuous tree canopy, or a consistent ground plane can serve as a datum — the unifying thread that ties diverse elements together.

Enclosure (D/H Ratio): The relationship between the distance across a space (D) and the height of its enclosing elements (H) profoundly affects how people experience it. This is one of the most exam-tested design concepts.

rows: Narrow European street, Japanese garden path
Open field, large parking lot without trees

content.text: MEMORY AID:  D/H ratio: think of it as the room you are standing in. A 1:1 ratio feels like a narrow hallway — the walls are as tall as the room is wide. A 4:1 ratio feels like standing in a field — the edges are too far away to define the space.

Kevin Lynch's The Image of the City (1960) introduced the concept of urban legibility — how easily people can understand and navigate the built environment. Lynch identified five elements that people use to form mental maps of places:

Paths: The channels along which people move — streets, walkways, trails, transit lines. Paths are the most important element because most people experience cities by moving through them. Clear, well-connected paths make a place legible. Dead-ends, confusing intersections, and discontinuous routes destroy legibility.

Edges: Linear boundaries between two areas — shorelines, railroad tracks, highway walls, edges of parks. Edges can be barriers (a highway that divides neighborhoods) or seams (a waterfront promenade that connects a city to its river).

Districts: Medium-to-large areas with a recognizable, consistent character — Chinatown, the warehouse district, a university campus. People mentally "enter" districts and know they are in a distinct place because of consistent architecture, signage, paving, or vegetation.

Nodes: Strategic points people enter and navigate from — major intersections, transit hubs, town squares, plazas. Nodes are decision points and gathering places. A well-designed node is both a destination and an orientation point.

Landmarks: Distinctive physical objects used for orientation — a clock tower, a large sculpture, a prominent building, a specimen tree. Unlike nodes, landmarks are typically viewed from a distance and serve as external reference points. They help people know where they are and which direction they are facing.
MEMORY AID:  Lynch's 5 elements: PEDAL — Paths, Edges, Districts, nodes (And), Landmarks. Or think PEDNL: People Enter Districts Near Landmarks.

EXAM TIP:  The exam frequently tests Lynch's elements. If a question describes a major intersection where several paths converge, the answer is NODE. If it describes a distinctive tower visible from across a park, the answer is LANDMARK. If it describes a linear boundary between two neighborhoods, the answer is EDGE.
A cultural landscape is a geographic area that has been shaped by the interaction between human activity and natural processes. The National Park Service recognizes four types of cultural landscapes:

Historic Designed Landscape: A landscape intentionally designed by a landscape architect, gardener, or horticulturist according to design principles and aesthetic values. Examples: Central Park, the gardens at Dumbarton Oaks, Monticello's landscape.

Historic Vernacular Landscape: A landscape that evolved through use by the people whose activities shaped it. It reflects the cultural values, traditions, and everyday activities of a community. Examples: agricultural landscapes, rural villages, fishing communities, mining towns.

Ethnographic Landscape: A landscape containing natural and cultural resources that a traditionally associated group defines as heritage resources. These landscapes often hold spiritual or sacred significance. Examples: Native American sacred sites, traditional gathering areas.

Archaeological Landscape: A landscape where the evidence of past human activity is primarily below ground. The cultural significance is in what lies beneath the surface rather than what is visible. Examples: buried village sites, ancient agricultural terraces.

When working with historic or cultural landscapes, the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties provide four treatment approaches. Choosing the right treatment depends on the significance of the landscape, its physical condition, and the proposed use:

rows: Maintain the existing form, features, and materials through stabilization, protection, and repair. No new additions.
When the landscape retains high integrity and significance. The goal is to keep it as it is.
Preserve significant features while allowing compatible alterations and additions for contemporary use.
When the landscape needs to accommodate new functions while retaining its historic character. The most flexible and common treatment.
Remove features from other periods and reconstruct missing features from the period of significance.
When the specific period of significance is well-documented and the goal is to return to that specific historic appearance.
Recreate a vanished landscape based on documentary and physical evidence.
When the original landscape no longer exists but documentation is sufficient to recreate it accurately.

content.text: MEMORY AID:  Secretary's Standards: P-R-R-R. Preservation (keep it), Rehabilitation (adapt it), Restoration (return it to a specific period), Reconstruction (rebuild what's gone). Rehabilitation is the most commonly used because it allows new uses while respecting historic character.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Elements of design (line, form, color, texture, scale) are the basic visual building blocks. ✔  Principles of design (unity, balance, proportion, rhythm, emphasis, sequence) govern how elements are combined. ✔  D/H ratio: 1:1 = intimate/enclosed, 2:1 = comfortable, 3:1 = open, 4:1+ = undefined space. ✔  Kevin Lynch's 5 elements (Paths, Edges, Districts, Nodes, Landmarks) describe how people read and navigate places. ✔  Four types of cultural landscapes: historic designed, historic vernacular, ethnographic, archaeological. ✔  Secretary of the Interior's four treatments: Preservation, Rehabilitation, Restoration, Reconstruction. ✔  Rehabilitation is the most flexible and commonly used treatment for historic landscapes.

subsections.title: 1. A plaza surrounded by buildings with a D/H ratio of approximately 2:1 would feel:

content.text: A)  Claustrophobic and confining
B)  Comfortable, well-proportioned, and human-scaled
C)  Vast and lacking spatial definition
D)  Threatening and exposed
Answer: B. A D/H ratio of 2:1 creates a comfortable, well-proportioned sense of enclosure — the space is twice as wide as the enclosing elements are tall.
2. A landscape architect is redesigning a historic town square to accommodate a new farmers market while preserving the square's Civil War-era character. Which treatment approach is MOST appropriate?
A)  Preservation
B)  Rehabilitation
C)  Restoration
D)  Reconstruction
Answer: B. Rehabilitation allows compatible new uses (farmers market) while preserving the historic character. It is the most flexible of the four treatments.
3. In Kevin Lynch's framework, a major transit hub where several bus routes converge would be classified as a:
A)  Path
B)  Edge
C)  District
D)  Node
Answer: D. Nodes are strategic decision points that people enter and navigate from — major intersections, transit hubs, and gathering places.
4. A rural farming community where the arrangement of fields, barns, and roads reflects generations of agricultural practice is an example of a:
A)  Historic designed landscape
B)  Historic vernacular landscape
C)  Ethnographic landscape
D)  Archaeological landscape
Answer: B. Historic vernacular landscapes evolved through everyday use by the people whose activities shaped them, reflecting cultural traditions and practices.

subsections.title: 5. Which design principle creates visual movement and continuity through repetition and pattern?

content.text: A)  Unity
B)  Balance
C)  Rhythm
D)  Emphasis
Answer: C. Rhythm uses repetition and pattern (e.g., evenly spaced trees along a path) to create visual movement and pull the eye through space.

Programming is the systematic process of identifying the requirements that a design must satisfy. It is the bridge between a client's goals and the designer's response. Without thorough programming, even a brilliantly designed landscape can fail because it does not meet the actual needs of its users. On the LARE exam, you must understand how to develop a program, what it contains, and how it guides design decisions.

Programming happens before design begins. The landscape architect gathers, analyzes, and organizes information from multiple sources to create a document that defines what the project must accomplish. The process typically follows these steps:

1. Identify stakeholders: Who will use, maintain, fund, and be affected by the project? Stakeholders include the client (owner/developer), end users (residents, visitors, employees), maintenance staff, regulatory agencies, neighboring property owners, and the broader community.

2. Define goals and objectives: Goals are broad aspirations ("create a vibrant community gathering space"). Objectives are specific, measurable outcomes that support goals ("provide seating for 200 people" or "reduce stormwater runoff by 30%"). Good objectives are SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

3. Conduct a needs assessment: Determine what activities will occur, who will participate, and what spatial and functional requirements each activity demands. Methods include surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation studies, and demographic analysis.

4. Establish space requirements: Quantify the area needed for each program element — playgrounds, athletic fields, parking, trails, plazas, gardens, buildings, maintenance facilities, stormwater management.

5. Determine functional relationships: Which program elements need to be adjacent? Which need separation? A playground should be visible from seating areas (adjacency). A service yard should be screened from public view (separation). A dog park should be buffered from a children's play area.

6. Set priorities and constraints: Budget, schedule, regulatory requirements, site limitations, and phasing needs all constrain the program. The landscape architect helps the client understand trade-offs when the program exceeds available resources.

The exam tests your knowledge of common dimensional standards for landscape elements. These are not arbitrary — they come from building codes, ADA requirements, sport governing bodies, and established practice.

rows: 8' wide + 5' access aisle; van accessible = 8' wide + 8' access aisle
5' minimum (4' absolute minimum with passing spaces)
6' minimum from equipment in all directions
Required under and around equipment to ASTM/CPSC standards

content.text: EXAM TIP:  Memorize ADA parking requirements. They appear frequently. Know: 1 accessible space per 25 total, van-accessible spaces need 8' access aisles, and all accessible spaces must be on the shortest accessible route to the building entrance.

Precedent studies involve analyzing completed projects that are comparable to the one being designed. They help the design team learn from successes and failures, identify best practices, and inspire creative solutions. A good precedent study examines:
•  Site conditions and context — how similar are they to the current project?
•  Program elements — what activities and spaces does the precedent include?
•  Design strategies — what spatial organization, materials, and planting approaches were used?
•  Performance outcomes — does the project function well? Are users satisfied?
•  Maintenance and durability — how has the project held up over time?
•  Budget and construction — was it built within budget? What value engineering was done?

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A landscape architect designing a new riverfront park in a midsize city conducts precedent studies of Louisville's Waterfront Park, the San Antonio River Walk, and Pittsburgh's Three Rivers Heritage Trail. Each precedent offers different lessons: Louisville shows how to use flood-resilient design in a floodplain; San Antonio shows how to integrate commerce and recreation along a waterway; Pittsburgh shows how to convert rail corridors into multi-use trails. The precedent analysis informs programming decisions and helps the client visualize possibilities.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Programming defines project requirements before design begins — it answers 'what' before 'how.' ✔  Good objectives are SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. ✔  Space standards come from codes, ADA, and governing bodies — memorize key dimensions. ✔  ADA parking: 1 accessible space per 25 total, van spaces need 8' access aisles. ✔  Functional relationships define which spaces need adjacency and which need separation. ✔  Precedent studies analyze comparable completed projects for lessons and best practices.

subsections.title: 1. A parking lot has 80 total spaces. What is the MINIMUM number of ADA-accessible spaces required?

content.text: Answer: C. Per ADA: 1-25 spaces = 1 accessible, 26-50 = 2, 51-75 = 3, 76-100 = 4. An 80-space lot requires 4 accessible spaces.

2. During programming, the landscape architect determines that the dog park should be separated from the children's playground but both should be visible from the central pavilion. This is an example of establishing:
A)  Space standards
B)  Functional relationships
C)  Precedent analysis
D)  Cost estimates
Answer: B. Functional relationships define which program elements need adjacency (visibility from pavilion) and which need separation (dog park from playground).

subsections.title: 3. The MINIMUM width of a two-way vehicular drive aisle in a parking lot is:

content.text: A)  12 feet
B)  18 feet
C)  24 feet
D)  30 feet
Answer: C. Two-way drive aisles require a minimum of 24 feet to allow vehicles to pass each other safely.

Site analysis transforms raw inventory data into design implications. While site inventory asks "what is here?," site analysis asks "what does it mean for the project?" This is the analytical core of master planning and one of the most heavily tested areas on the exam.
Every site feature is either an opportunity (an asset the design can leverage) or a constraint (a limitation the design must accommodate). Many features are both, depending on the project goals.

rows: Shade, habitat, aesthetic value, preservation as amenity
Limits building footprint, root zone protection required, maintenance cost
Erosion risk, limits access, expensive to grade, slope instability
Amenity, habitat, stormwater conveyance, trail alignment
Floodplain/buffer restrictions, regulatory permits, erosion setbacks
Potential for rain gardens, wetland creation
Limits foundations, basements, underground utilities, infiltration
Pedestrian access, reduced parking demand, connectivity
Noise, visual clutter, security concerns at off-peak hours
Connections to utilities, reduce new construction
Easements restrict building, capacity limitations, relocation costs

content.text: Ian McHarg, in his seminal book Design with Nature (1969), pioneered the overlay method of suitability analysis. The approach is straightforward in concept but powerful in practice:
Step 1: Identify all site factors relevant to the proposed land use (slope, soils, hydrology, vegetation, wildlife, views, cultural resources, access, utilities).
Step 2: Map each factor on a separate transparent overlay, classifying each area as high, moderate, or low suitability for the proposed use.

Step 3: Stack the overlays. Areas where multiple factors align as "high suitability" are the best candidates for development. Areas where multiple factors align as "low suitability" should be conserved.

McHarg's method was revolutionary because it grounded land use decisions in ecological data rather than purely economic considerations. Today, this overlay analysis is performed digitally using Geographic Information Systems (GIS), but the logic is identical to McHarg's original hand-drawn overlays.

EXAM TIP:  If the exam describes a process of layering multiple site factors (slope, soil, hydrology, etc.) on transparent maps to determine where development is most appropriate, the answer is McHarg's suitability analysis or overlay method.
Visual analysis evaluates what people see from and toward a site. It is critical for projects where views, scenic quality, and visual impact are design considerations.

Viewshed analysis: Mapping all areas visible from a specific point. A viewshed from a proposed overlook determines what visitors will see and what the design should emphasize or screen. GIS tools and LiDAR data can generate precise viewshed maps.

Visual absorption capacity (VAC): The ability of a landscape to absorb visual change without significant loss of scenic quality. Forested slopes have high VAC — a new structure is easily hidden. Open meadows and ridgelines have low VAC — any change is highly visible.

Scenic quality assessment: Evaluating the visual quality of a landscape based on factors like variety, vividness, intactness, and unity. Federal land management agencies (USFS, BLM) use formal visual resource management systems to classify scenic quality and set management objectives.
Carrying capacity is the maximum amount of use a site can sustain without unacceptable degradation of the resource or the user experience. It applies to both ecological and social dimensions:

Ecological carrying capacity: How much use can the natural system absorb? A meadow trail can handle a certain number of hikers before soil compaction, vegetation trampling, and erosion become unacceptable. A lake can absorb a limited amount of recreational boating before water quality, wildlife habitat, and shoreline stability are compromised.

Social carrying capacity: How crowded can a space become before users feel the experience is diminished? A wilderness trail has low social carrying capacity — users expect solitude. A boardwalk at a beach resort has high social carrying capacity — users expect crowds.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A national park trail shows signs of exceeding its carrying capacity: widening from 4 feet to 12 feet as hikers avoid muddy sections, vegetation die-back 10 feet on either side, root exposure, and social trails cutting switchbacks. The landscape architect recommends hardening the trail surface, installing boardwalks over wet areas, defining clear edges, and implementing a permit system to limit daily use.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Every site feature is either an opportunity, a constraint, or both — depending on project goals. ✔  McHarg's overlay method (Design with Nature, 1969) layers site factors to find areas of highest development suitability. ✔  Modern suitability analysis uses GIS to digitally perform what McHarg did with hand-drawn overlays. ✔  Viewshed analysis maps all visible areas from a given point; VAC measures ability to absorb visual change. ✔  Carrying capacity has both ecological (resource degradation) and social (user experience) dimensions.
1. Ian McHarg's method of layering transparent maps of slope, soils, hydrology, and other factors to determine the best areas for development is called:
A)  Carrying capacity analysis
B)  Overlay suitability analysis
C)  Visual resource management
D)  Life cycle assessment
Answer: B. McHarg pioneered the overlay suitability analysis in Design with Nature (1969), layering multiple factors to identify areas of highest and lowest development suitability.
2. A forested hillside can absorb the visual impact of a new structure more easily than a bare ridgeline. This quality is described as:
A)  Viewshed
B)  Scenic quality
C)  Visual absorption capacity
D)  Carrying capacity
Answer: C. Visual absorption capacity (VAC) measures a landscape's ability to absorb visual change. Forested areas have high VAC; bare ridgelines have low VAC.
3. A wilderness trail is experiencing widening, root exposure, and social trails cutting switchbacks. These are signs that the trail has exceeded its:
A)  Design development scope
B)  Visual absorption capacity
C)  Ecological carrying capacity
D)  Functional relationship threshold
Answer: C. Trail widening, vegetation damage, root exposure, and social trail formation are classic signs of exceeding ecological carrying capacity.

s2_book.title: Chapter 5: Land Use and Community Planning

content.text: Landscape architects work at every scale — from a residential garden to a regional park system. At the community and regional scale, understanding zoning, comprehensive planning, and contemporary planning movements is essential. The exam tests your ability to apply these frameworks to real planning scenarios.

Zoning is the primary regulatory tool that communities use to control land use. A zoning ordinance divides a municipality into districts and specifies what uses are permitted, conditionally permitted, or prohibited in each district. Zoning also regulates dimensional standards:

rows: Minimum distance from property lines to structures
Maximum percentage of lot covered by impervious surface or structures
Ratio of building floor area to lot area
FAR 2.0 = 20,000 SF building on 10,000 SF lot
35 feet or 3 stories, whichever is less
Number of dwelling units per acre
1 space per 300 SF commercial; 2 per dwelling unit
Minimum landscape or open space percentage
20% of lot must be landscaped open space

content.text: Euclidean Zoning: The traditional, most common form. Named after Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. (1926), the Supreme Court case that upheld zoning's constitutionality. Separates land uses into distinct districts (residential, commercial, industrial). Criticized for encouraging sprawl and automobile dependence by segregating uses.

Form-Based Codes: A newer approach that regulates building form (height, setback, facade articulation, street relationship) rather than use. Form-based codes allow mixed uses and focus on creating predictable physical character. They are associated with New Urbanism and walkable mixed-use neighborhoods.

Planned Unit Development (PUD): A flexible zoning tool that allows a developer to propose a custom set of standards for a specific site, typically in exchange for providing community benefits like open space, affordable housing, or infrastructure improvements. PUDs allow mixing uses and varying densities within a single development.

Overlay Districts: Additional regulations layered on top of base zoning for areas with special characteristics — historic districts, floodplain overlay, environmental protection overlay, transit-oriented development overlay. Overlay regulations supplement (and may supersede) the underlying base zoning.
Smart Growth is a set of planning principles that counter suburban sprawl by promoting compact, walkable, mixed-use development. The ten Smart Growth principles are:
•  Mix land uses
•  Take advantage of compact building design
•  Create a range of housing opportunities and choices
•  Create walkable neighborhoods
•  Foster distinctive, attractive communities with a strong sense of place
•  Preserve open space, farmland, natural beauty, and critical environmental areas
•  Strengthen and direct development towards existing communities
•  Provide a variety of transportation choices
•  Make development decisions predictable, fair, and cost-effective
•  Encourage community and stakeholder collaboration in development decisions
New Urbanism promotes walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods with a clear center (town square, main street), well-defined edges, and a network of interconnected streets. Key principles include:
•  Interconnected street network (grid or modified grid) — discourages culs-de-sac
•  Narrow streets with street trees, on-street parking, and traffic calming
•  Buildings oriented to the street with shallow setbacks and active ground-floor uses
•  A mix of housing types (single-family, townhomes, apartments) within walking distance of shops and services
•  Public spaces (parks, plazas, greens) within a 5-minute walk (approximately 1/4 mile) of every residence
The rural-to-urban transect organizes the built environment into six zones, from most natural to most urban. It is the organizing framework for many form-based codes:

rows: Undeveloped land in its natural state
Farms, scattered buildings, country roads, hedgerows
Single-family homes, lawns, curving streets, some mixed use
Townhomes, apartments, shops, street trees, sidewalks
Mid-rise buildings, plazas, wide sidewalks, transit
High-rises, civic buildings, squares, major transit hubs

content.text: MEMORY AID:  The transect goes from trees to towers: T1 (Nature) → T2 (Rural) → T3 (Suburban) → T4 (Urban) → T5 (Center) → T6 (Core). Each zone gets progressively denser and more urban.

Green infrastructure is a strategically planned and managed network of natural and semi-natural areas that deliver ecosystem services. At the regional scale, green infrastructure connects parks, stream corridors, wetlands, forests, and farmland into a continuous network that supports biodiversity, manages stormwater, provides recreation, and improves quality of life.
Key components of a green infrastructure network:
•  Hubs — large anchor areas that provide habitat and serve as origins and destinations (large parks, nature preserves, forests)
•  Links — linear connections between hubs (stream corridors, greenways, trail corridors, hedgerows)
•  Sites — smaller individual areas that provide localized benefits (pocket parks, rain gardens, green roofs, street trees)

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A city's green infrastructure plan identifies three large regional parks as hubs, connects them through a stream corridor greenway system (links), and fills in the gaps with neighborhood pocket parks and bioswales along major streets (sites). The plan ensures that every resident lives within a 10-minute walk of green space and that stormwater is managed through the connected green network rather than solely through pipes.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Zoning controls land use through districts, setbacks, FAR, lot coverage, height limits, density, and parking requirements. ✔  Euclidean zoning separates uses; form-based codes regulate building form; PUDs offer custom flexibility; overlays add extra regulations. ✔  Smart Growth promotes compact, walkable, mixed-use development as an alternative to sprawl. ✔  New Urbanism emphasizes interconnected streets, mixed housing, shallow setbacks, and walkable neighborhoods. ✔  The Transect (T1-T6) organizes environments from natural to urban core. ✔  Green infrastructure connects hubs, links, and sites into a network that provides ecosystem services at the regional scale.
1. A developer proposes a mixed-use project that does not conform to the existing single-use residential zoning. Which zoning tool would MOST likely allow this project to proceed?
A)  Euclidean zoning variance
B)  Planned Unit Development (PUD)
C)  Overlay district
D)  Setback reduction
Answer: B. PUDs allow developers to propose custom standards for a specific site, including mixing uses and varying densities, typically in exchange for community benefits.

subsections.title: 2. The Transect zone T4 (General Urban) is characterized by:

content.text: A)  Undeveloped natural land
B)  Low-density single-family homes with large lots
C)  Mixed-use, moderate density with townhomes, shops, and street trees
D)  High-rise buildings and major transit hubs
Answer: C. T4 (General Urban) is a mixed-use zone with moderate density — townhomes, small apartments, neighborhood shops, street trees, and sidewalks.
3. A zoning ordinance specifies a Floor Area Ratio (FAR) of 1.5 on a 20,000 SF lot. What is the maximum total building floor area?
Answer: C. FAR = building floor area ÷ lot area. So maximum floor area = FAR × lot area = 1.5 × 20,000 = 30,000 SF.

s2_book.title: Chapter 6: Master Plan Preparation and Communication

content.text: A master plan synthesizes all of the programming, site analysis, and planning work into a comprehensive design document that guides the future development of a site. Creating and communicating a master plan requires both design skill and professional judgment. The exam tests whether you understand the process of developing, evaluating, and presenting a master plan.

The transition from analysis to design begins with concept development. A design concept is the central organizing idea that drives all spatial decisions. It answers the question: "What is the big idea?"

Bubble diagrams: The first step in translating program requirements into spatial organization. Each program element is represented as a "bubble" showing its relative size and position. Lines between bubbles indicate desired adjacencies. The bubble diagram is intentionally abstract — it shows relationships, not design.

Concept diagrams: Refine bubble diagrams by introducing site-specific geometry — axes, circulation routes, spatial edges, entry points, and key view corridors. The concept diagram begins to show how the program fits the actual site.

Schematic alternatives: Multiple design options developed from the concept diagrams.
