Typically two to three alternatives are developed to explore different spatial organizations, circulation strategies, and character approaches. Presenting alternatives gives the client meaningful choice and demonstrates that the designer has explored the problem thoroughly.

EXAM TIP:  If the exam asks what tool shows spatial relationships and adjacencies between program elements at the earliest design stage, the answer is bubble diagram. If it asks what comes next, the answer is concept diagram or functional diagram.
Evaluating alternatives requires systematic comparison against program requirements, site constraints, and project goals. Common evaluation methods include:
•  Matrix scoring — rating each alternative against weighted criteria (cost, accessibility, environmental impact, aesthetic quality, maintenance, phasing)
•  SWOT analysis — Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats for each option
•  Cost comparison — order-of-magnitude cost estimates for each alternative
•  Stakeholder preference — input from user groups, community members, and the client
The preferred alternative is typically a hybrid that combines the best elements of multiple options rather than adopting any single alternative wholesale.
A complete master plan package typically includes:
•  Site plan — the primary drawing showing the layout of all proposed elements
•  Circulation plan — vehicular, pedestrian, bicycle, service, and emergency access
•  Grading concept — overall drainage strategy and major grade changes
•  Planting concept — canopy plan, planting character areas, preservation zones
•  Utility plan — water, sewer, storm, electric, gas, and telecommunications
•  Phasing plan — sequencing development into manageable, fundable stages
•  Written narrative — design rationale, project description, goals and objectives
•  Cost estimate — order-of-magnitude budget for the overall plan and each phase
•  Illustrative renderings — perspective views, sections, and 3D visualizations
A master plan must communicate effectively to diverse audiences — elected officials, community members, funding agencies, and technical reviewers. Key communication strategies include:
•  Graphic standards — consistent line weights, colors, legends, north arrows, and scales across all drawings
•  Layered information — presenting complex plans in digestible layers rather than one overwhelming drawing
•  Before/after visualizations — showing the transformation from existing to proposed conditions
•  Sections and elevations — revealing three-dimensional relationships that plan views cannot show
•  Process documentation — showing the steps that led to the plan, building credibility and trust

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Design concepts evolve from bubble diagrams (relationships) → concept diagrams (site-specific geometry) → schematic alternatives. ✔  Two or three alternatives are typically developed to give the client meaningful choice. ✔  Alternative evaluation uses matrix scoring, SWOT analysis, cost comparison, and stakeholder input. ✔  A master plan includes site plan, circulation, grading, planting, utilities, phasing, narrative, cost estimate, and renderings. ✔  Effective communication uses graphic standards, layered information, before/after views, and process documentation.
1. At the earliest stage of design, the landscape architect creates a diagram showing relative sizes of program elements and their desired adjacencies. This diagram is called a:
A)  Site plan
B)  Bubble diagram
C)  Construction document
D)  Grading plan
Answer: B. Bubble diagrams show spatial relationships and adjacencies between program elements in abstract form — they are the first step in translating program into spatial organization.
2. When evaluating design alternatives, a landscape architect rates each option against weighted criteria such as cost, accessibility, and environmental impact. This method is called:
A)  SWOT analysis
B)  Precedent study
C)  Matrix scoring
D)  Value engineering
Answer: C. Matrix scoring rates each alternative against weighted criteria, producing a systematic comparison that supports objective decision-making.

Circulation — how people, vehicles, and services move through a site — is one of the most critical design decisions a landscape architect makes. A well-designed circulation system is safe, efficient, intuitive, and accessible to all users. A poorly designed one creates confusion, conflict between users, and barriers for people with disabilities. The exam tests your knowledge of circulation design standards, ADA requirements, and Complete Streets principles.

The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires that all public facilities and places of public accommodation be accessible to people with disabilities. The ADA Standards for Accessible Design establish minimum requirements that landscape architects must incorporate into every project.

rows: Both sides of ramps with rise > 6"
Truncated domes at curb ramps and transit platforms
Clear floor space at accessible elements
Shortest accessible route to building entrance

content.text: PROWAG (Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines) extends ADA requirements to the public right-of-way — sidewalks, crosswalks, curb ramps, pedestrian signals, and street furnishings. While PROWAG was proposed as guidelines, many jurisdictions have adopted them as enforceable standards.
MEMORY AID:  ADA slopes: 5-2-8. Maximum running slope = 5%. Maximum cross slope = 2%. Maximum ramp slope = 8.33% (1:12). These three numbers answer most ADA slope questions on the exam.

EXAM TIP:  When the exam mentions a walking surface that exceeds 5% running slope, it is no longer an accessible route — it becomes a ramp. Ramps require handrails, landings, and edge protection. If a surface exceeds 8.33%, it does not comply with ADA at all.
Designing walkways requires balancing width, slope, surface material, and connectivity to create a system that is safe, comfortable, and accessible.

rows: Higher pedestrian volumes require wider paths
AASHTO standard; separate modes when possible
Natural surface; may not meet full ADA

content.text: Vehicular circulation design must balance access, safety, and pedestrian priority. Key standards:

Sight distance triangles: At every intersection, a clear area must be maintained where drivers can see approaching vehicles and pedestrians. Nothing taller than 30 inches (shrubs, walls, signs) should be placed within the sight triangle. The triangle dimensions depend on the design speed of the road.

Traffic calming: Physical design measures that reduce vehicle speeds and volumes in pedestrian areas. Speed tables (flat-topped speed bumps) slow traffic at crosswalks. Chicanes (alternating curb extensions) force vehicles to follow a winding path. Neck-downs (curb extensions at intersections) shorten pedestrian crossing distances. Roundabouts slow vehicles while maintaining traffic flow. Textured paving signals a change in environment.

Fire access: Fire lanes must be a minimum of 20 feet wide with 13 feet 6 inches of vertical clearance. All buildings must be accessible by fire apparatus. Dead-end fire lanes over 150 feet require a turnaround (hammerhead or cul-de-sac).

Complete Streets is a transportation policy and design approach that requires streets to be designed for all users — not just automobiles. A complete street accommodates pedestrians, cyclists, transit riders, motorists, freight, and people of all ages and abilities. Typical elements include:
•  Wide sidewalks with street trees and a buffer zone between pedestrians and traffic
•  Protected bike lanes (cycle tracks) separated from motor vehicle traffic
•  Transit stops with shelters, benches, and accessible boarding platforms
•  On-street parking providing a buffer between travel lanes and bike lanes
•  Curb extensions (bulb-outs) at crosswalks to shorten pedestrian crossing distance
•  Median refuges allowing pedestrians to cross wide streets in two stages
•  Street trees providing shade, reducing heat island effect, and calming traffic

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  ADA slopes: 5% max running slope (accessible route), 2% max cross slope, 8.33% max ramp slope (1:12). ✔  Ramps: max 30' run between landings, 5' × 5' minimum landings, handrails both sides. ✔  PROWAG extends ADA requirements to the public right-of-way (sidewalks, crosswalks, curb ramps). ✔  Shared-use paths: 10' minimum (12' preferred); residential sidewalks: 5' preferred. ✔  Sight distance triangles must be clear of objects over 30" at all intersections. ✔  Fire lanes: 20' wide minimum, 13'6" clearance, turnaround required for dead-ends > 150'. ✔  Complete Streets design accommodates all users: pedestrians, cyclists, transit, and vehicles.

subsections.title: 1. A walkway has a running slope of 6.5%. Under ADA, this surface is classified as a:

content.text: A)  Accessible route
B)  Ramp
C)  Non-compliant surface
D)  Cross slope
Answer: B. Any walking surface exceeding 5% running slope is classified as a ramp under ADA. Ramps require handrails, landings, and edge protection, and cannot exceed 8.33%.

subsections.title: 2. The maximum cross slope allowed on an accessible route under ADA is:

content.text: Answer: B. ADA limits cross slope to 2% (1:50) on accessible routes to prevent wheelchair drift.
3. At an intersection, the landscape architect ensures no plantings over 30 inches tall are placed within the sight triangle. The purpose is to:
A)  Reduce maintenance costs
B)  Maintain clear sight lines for drivers and pedestrians
C)  Comply with irrigation setback requirements
D)  Reduce wind tunnel effects
Answer: B. Sight distance triangles must be clear of visual obstructions above 30" to allow drivers and pedestrians to see each other at intersections.

subsections.title: 4. A shared-use path serving both pedestrians and bicyclists should have a minimum width of:

content.text: A)  5 feet
B)  8 feet
C)  10 feet
D)  14 feet
Answer: C. AASHTO standards require a minimum 10-foot width for shared-use paths, with 12-14 feet preferred in high-use areas.

s2_book.title: Chapter 8: Grading, Drainage, and Stormwater Design

content.text: Grading shapes the land to serve design intent — directing water, creating accessible routes, defining spaces, and building landforms. Stormwater management determines how rainfall is captured, treated, and conveyed. Together, grading and stormwater design transform a site from a natural landscape into a functioning built environment. These topics span both the Schematic Design and Design Development domains on the exam.
Every land use has an acceptable slope range. Designing outside these ranges creates functional problems — ponding on flat surfaces, erosion on steep ones, and accessibility barriers everywhere.

rows: Must be consistent for fair play; crown or slope one direction
Steeper causes discomfort; flatter causes ponding
ADA accessible route across lot ≤ 2% cross slope
Steeper than 3:1 is unsafe for riding mowers
50% is practical limit for most ground covers
Slopes steeper than 2:1 typically need structural support
Minimum 2% slope away from buildings for 10 feet

content.text: MEMORY AID:  Slope limits to memorize: Athletic fields = 1-2%. Parking = 1-5%. Accessible route = max 5%. Ramps = max 8.33%. Mowed turf = max 25% (3:1). Unmowed = max 50% (2:1). Building perimeter = min 2% away for 10 feet.
Good grading follows several fundamental principles that apply to every project:

Positive drainage: All surfaces must slope to direct water away from buildings, toward collection points (swales, drains, BMPs). Water should never pond against a structure. Minimum 2% slope away from building foundations for at least 10 feet.

Balance earthwork: The ideal grading plan moves earth from cut areas to fill areas within the site, minimizing the need to import or export soil. Importing fill is expensive. Exporting excess cut generates hauling costs and disposal fees. A balanced cut/fill plan reduces both cost and truck traffic.

Preserve existing features: Minimize disturbance to existing trees (protect root zones — drip line or larger), wetlands, stream buffers, and rock outcrops. Every preserved feature reduces restoration cost and protects ecological function.

Match existing grades at property lines: Grading cannot alter drainage patterns onto adjacent properties. The proposed grade must match the existing grade at all property boundaries to avoid liability for flooding or erosion damage to neighbors.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A landscape architect is grading a new school campus. The existing site slopes 8% from northeast to southwest. The design places the building pad at the uphill end of the site (less cut required), the parking lot on a 3% slope in the middle, and the athletic fields on a 1.5% slope at the low end (where fill from the building pad cut can be deposited). A bioswale along the southern property line collects site runoff. The grading plan is balanced — no import or export needed.

Green infrastructure uses natural processes — infiltration, evapotranspiration, and biological treatment — to manage stormwater. These systems mimic natural hydrology and provide multiple benefits beyond stormwater management: habitat, aesthetics, heat island reduction, and air quality improvement.

rows: Collects and infiltrates runoff through engineered soil media
Allows rain to pass through surface into aggregate base
Vegetated channel that conveys and filters runoff
Vegetation layer absorbs and evapotranspires rainfall
Captures and stores roof runoff for reuse
Shallow, vegetated basin with permanent pool
Gravel-filled trench allows runoff to soak into ground
Size for infiltration rate × storm volume

content.text: EXAM TIP:  When an exam question asks which BMP is appropriate for a clay soil (HSG D) site, eliminate infiltration-based practices (rain garden without underdrain, infiltration trench, permeable pavement without underdrain). Choose detention-based or evapotranspiration-based practices (constructed wetland, green roof, cistern, or bioretention with underdrain).

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Every land use has a minimum and maximum slope range — memorize the key values. ✔  Positive drainage: minimum 2% slope away from buildings for at least 10 feet. ✔  Balance cut and fill on-site to minimize import/export costs. ✔  Match existing grades at property lines to avoid altering drainage to neighbors. ✔  Green infrastructure uses infiltration, evapotranspiration, and biological treatment to manage stormwater. ✔  On clay (HSG D) soils, use detention-based or underdrained practices — not infiltration-only BMPs. ✔  Rain garden sizing: typically 5-10% of the contributing impervious area.

subsections.title: 1. The minimum slope required away from building foundations is:

content.text: A)  0.5% for 5 feet
B)  1% for 8 feet
C)  2% for 10 feet
D)  5% for 20 feet
Answer: C. Grading standards require a minimum 2% slope away from buildings for at least 10 feet to ensure positive drainage and prevent water intrusion.

subsections.title: 2. A site has Hydrologic Soil Group D (heavy clay). Which stormwater BMP is MOST appropriate?

content.text: A)  Infiltration trench
B)  Permeable pavement without underdrain
C)  Bioretention with underdrain
D)  Dry well
Answer: C. HSG D soils have very slow infiltration, making infiltration-only practices infeasible. Bioretention with an underdrain provides treatment while draining through the pipe system.

subsections.title: 3. The maximum slope for a mowed turf area is approximately:

content.text: Answer: C. Mowed turf areas should not exceed 25% (3:1 slope) — steeper slopes are unsafe for riding mowers and prone to scalping.

Planting design is where landscape architecture most clearly distinguishes itself from architecture and civil engineering. Plants are living, growing, changing materials that define space, control climate, manage water, support wildlife, and create beauty. The exam tests whether you understand how to select, arrange, and specify plants to achieve functional and aesthetic goals.
Selecting the right plant for the right place requires matching plant characteristics to site conditions and design intent. The factors a landscape architect must consider include:

Hardiness zone: The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map divides North America into 13 zones based on average annual minimum winter temperature. Each zone represents a 10°F range. Plants must be hardy to the project's zone or they will not survive winter.

Heat tolerance: The American Horticultural Society Heat Zone Map rates plants for heat tolerance, measured by the average number of days per year above 86°F. In southern regions, heat tolerance may be more limiting than cold hardiness.

Soil requirements: pH preferences (acid-loving plants like azaleas vs. alkaline-tolerant plants like hackberry), drainage tolerance (wet-tolerant vs. drought-tolerant), and salt tolerance (critical for coastal and roadside plantings).

Light requirements: Full sun (6+ hours direct sunlight), partial shade (3-6 hours), full shade (less than 3 hours). The building shadow study and site orientation determine light availability across the site.

Mature size: Trees and shrubs must be specified based on their mature dimensions — height, canopy spread, root zone extent. A common design error is spacing plants based on their nursery size rather than their mature size, leading to overcrowding, maintenance problems, and conflicts with utilities and structures.

Maintenance requirements: High-maintenance plants (formal hedges, annual beds, hybrid turf) require regular irrigation, fertilization, pruning, and pest management. Low-maintenance plants (native species, adapted groundcovers, naturalistic meadows) require minimal inputs once established. The maintenance budget and staffing capacity must match the planting design.

Xeriscape (from the Greek xeros, meaning dry) is a water-efficient approach to landscape design. Developed in Denver during the 1981 drought, it has become a standard practice in arid and semi-arid regions and increasingly in all climate zones as water conservation becomes a universal priority.
The seven principles of xeriscape are:
1. Planning and design: Group plants by water needs (hydrozoning). Place high-water-use plants in visible, high-use areas. Use low-water plants in large background areas.
2. Soil improvement: Amend soil with compost to improve water-holding capacity in sandy soils and drainage in clay soils.
3. Practical turf areas: Limit turf to functional areas (play, recreation, gathering) and use groundcovers or native grasses elsewhere.
4. Appropriate plant selection: Choose species adapted to the local climate that can survive on natural rainfall once established.
5. Efficient irrigation: Use drip irrigation for planting beds, matched-precipitation-rate heads for turf, and smart controllers with rain sensors.
6. Mulching: Apply 3-4 inches of organic mulch to reduce evaporation, moderate soil temperature, and suppress weeds.
7. Appropriate maintenance: Mow at proper heights, avoid over-fertilization, and adjust irrigation seasonally.

MEMORY AID:  Xeriscape 7 principles: P-S-T-P-I-M-M. Planning, Soil improvement, Turf limits, Plant selection, Irrigation efficiency, Mulch, Maintenance. Think: "Pretty Smart To Plant In Mulched Meadows."
Plants serve many functions beyond aesthetics. The exam often tests whether you can identify which planting strategy solves a specific functional problem:

rows: Windbreak — 3-5 rows of staggered evergreen trees and shrubs
Dense, year-round foliage; tolerant of wind exposure; varied heights
Deciduous canopy trees on south and west sides of buildings
Broad canopy; high branching for clearance; fast to moderate growth
Dense evergreen hedges or mass plantings
Year-round foliage; dense branching; appropriate mature height
Ground covers, deep-rooted grasses, bioengineering (live stakes, fascines)
Fibrous root systems; rapid establishment; tolerance of poor soils
Tolerant of alternating wet/dry; deep roots to maintain infiltration
Dense plantings of evergreen trees and shrubs, 50-100' deep
Dense foliage mass; limited noise reduction (3-5 dB per 100' of dense planting)
Native plant communities with structural diversity (canopy, understory, groundcover, snags)
Native species; fruit/seed/nectar production; nesting/cover structure

content.text: EXAM TIP:  If the exam asks how to reduce energy costs for a building in a cold climate, the answer involves deciduous shade trees on the south and west (summer cooling) plus an evergreen windbreak on the north and northwest (winter wind protection). Deciduous trees allow solar gain in winter when their leaves drop.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Plant selection considers hardiness zone, heat tolerance, soil, light, mature size, and maintenance requirements. ✔  Xeriscape has 7 principles: planning, soil, turf limits, plants, irrigation, mulch, maintenance. ✔  Hydrozoning groups plants by water needs to optimize irrigation efficiency. ✔  Functional planting serves wind protection, shade, screening, erosion control, stormwater, noise reduction, and habitat. ✔  Deciduous shade trees on south/west + evergreen windbreak on north/northwest = energy-efficient building design. ✔  Native plant communities support biodiversity and typically require less maintenance once established.

subsections.title: 1. Grouping plants by water needs so that irrigation can be applied efficiently is called:

content.text: A)  Xeriscaping
B)  Hydrozoning
C)  Companion planting
D)  Monoculture
Answer: B. Hydrozoning groups plants with similar water requirements together so irrigation can be matched to need, avoiding overwatering low-need plants or underwatering high-need ones.

subsections.title: 2. To reduce summer cooling costs for a building, the landscape architect should plant:

content.text: A)  Evergreen trees on the south and west sides
B)  Deciduous trees on the south and west sides
C)  Deciduous trees on the north side
D)  Evergreen trees on all sides
Answer: B. Deciduous trees on south and west sides provide shade in summer (reducing cooling costs) and allow solar gain in winter when leaves drop.

subsections.title: 3. The primary purpose of a windbreak planting is to:

content.text: A)  Create visual screening from neighbors
B)  Reduce wind speed and protect buildings and outdoor spaces
C)  Provide wildlife habitat corridors
D)  Absorb stormwater runoff
Answer: B. Windbreaks are designed to reduce wind speed, protecting buildings from heat loss, outdoor spaces from discomfort, and crops/plants from desiccation.

Design development refines schematic design by specifying actual materials, detailing systems, and coordinating with engineering disciplines. At this stage, the design moves from what it looks like to how it is built. The exam tests your understanding of material properties, selection criteria, and the construction implications of design decisions.

Concrete: The most versatile hardscape material. It can be cast in any shape, colored, stamped, sandblasted, exposed aggregate, or polished. Concrete requires control joints to manage cracking — spaced at intervals of 2-3 times the slab thickness in feet (a 4-inch slab needs joints every 8-12 feet, typically 10-foot maximum). Expansion joints separate concrete from fixed structures (buildings, walls). Concrete performs poorly in freeze-thaw cycles without air-entrainment (microscopic air bubbles that accommodate ice expansion).

Unit pavers: Interlocking concrete pavers or clay brick set on a compacted aggregate base with sand-set joints. Advantages: flexible (accommodates minor settlement without cracking), individual units are replaceable, available in many colors and patterns, excellent for pedestrian areas. Require edge restraints to prevent spreading. Permeable interlocking concrete pavers (PICP) have wider joints filled with aggregate that allow water to infiltrate.

Natural stone: Granite (hardest, most durable, expensive), bluestone (moderate hardness, excellent for walkways and patios), limestone (softer, can etch in acid rain), sandstone (variable hardness, warm colors), slate (splits into thin sheets, good for paving but can be slippery). Natural stone adds a sense of permanence and quality but costs significantly more than concrete or pavers.

Asphalt: Lower cost than concrete, flexible (tolerates minor settlement), quiet, dark color absorbs heat (heat island concern). Requires periodic sealcoating and crack repair. Porous asphalt allows stormwater infiltration through an open-graded mix placed over a stone reservoir base.

Permeable paving systems: Include permeable interlocking pavers, porous concrete, porous asphalt, and open grid systems (grass or gravel in plastic or concrete grids). All require a clean aggregate base for water storage and must be protected from fine sediment that clogs the pore structure. Not appropriate for high-traffic roads but excellent for parking lots, plazas, driveways, and low-speed streets.
Site lighting serves four purposes: safety, security, wayfinding, and aesthetics. The landscape architect specifies fixture types, mounting heights, light levels, and distribution patterns.

rows: General illumination of paths, parking, plazas
Illuminate walkways, create sense of comfort
High output, uniform coverage, no shadows
Low-level path marking, not primary illumination

content.text: Dark sky compliance (International Dark-Sky Association standards) requires full cutoff fixtures that direct all light downward, eliminating uplight that contributes to sky glow. Landscape architects should specify dark-sky-compliant fixtures for all exterior lighting to minimize light pollution, reduce energy waste, and protect nocturnal wildlife.
Cost estimates become more accurate as design progresses and more information is available:

rows: Comparable project costs, cost per acre, cost per SF
Unit costs × approximate quantities (SF of paving, LF of wall, etc.)
Refined quantities, specific material selections, subcontractor input
Final quantities, current material prices, contractor market conditions

content.text: Value engineering: The systematic review of a design to reduce costs while maintaining function and quality. Value engineering is NOT simply cutting scope — it is finding alternative materials, methods, or configurations that achieve the same performance at lower cost. Examples: substituting concrete pavers for natural stone (same durability, lower cost), reducing irrigated turf in favor of native plantings (lower installation and maintenance cost), or simplifying custom-designed site furnishings into standard catalog items.

Life cycle cost analysis: Comparing the total cost of ownership — initial construction plus maintenance, repair, and replacement over the project's lifespan. A material with higher initial cost may have a lower life cycle cost if it requires less maintenance and lasts longer. Stainless steel bollards cost more than painted steel but never need repainting. Permeable pavers cost more than asphalt but reduce stormwater infrastructure costs.
EXAM TIP:  Know the accuracy ranges for each design phase. If the exam asks about the accuracy of a schematic-level cost estimate, the answer is ±15-25%. These ranges are commonly tested.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Concrete control joints: every 10-12' max (2-3× slab thickness in feet). ✔  Unit pavers need edge restraints; permeable pavers (PICP) have aggregate-filled joints for infiltration. ✔  Dark sky compliance requires full cutoff fixtures that direct all light downward. ✔  Cost estimate accuracy improves as design progresses: ±50% (concept) → ±25% (SD) → ±15% (DD) → ±10% (CD). ✔  Value engineering reduces cost while maintaining function — it is not simply cutting scope. ✔  Life cycle cost analysis compares total cost of ownership including maintenance, repair, and replacement.
1. A landscape architect's schematic design cost estimate should have an accuracy range of approximately:
Answer: C. Schematic design estimates are based on unit costs and approximate quantities, yielding ±15-25% accuracy.

subsections.title: 2. Concrete control joints should be spaced at a maximum of:

content.text: A)  4-6 feet
B)  10-12 feet
C)  20-25 feet
D)  30 feet
Answer: B. Control joints in concrete should be spaced at 10-12 feet maximum (2-3 times slab thickness in feet for a typical 4" slab).

subsections.title: 3. Value engineering is BEST described as:

content.text: A)  Eliminating program elements to reduce cost
B)  Finding alternative materials and methods that achieve the same performance at lower cost
C)  Reducing construction quality to meet budget
D)  Delaying construction to a future phase
Answer: B. Value engineering systematically identifies alternatives that reduce cost while maintaining function and quality — it is not simply cutting scope or quality.

Landscape architects work within a dense web of regulations, codes, and legal requirements. The exam tests whether you understand the major regulatory frameworks that affect site design and can identify when a design decision triggers a regulatory requirement.

The Americans with Disabilities Act (1990, updated 2010) is the foundational accessibility law. The ADA Standards for Accessible Design establish minimum requirements for accessible routes, ramps, parking, seating, and signage. PROWAG (Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines) extends these requirements to sidewalks, crosswalks, curb ramps, and pedestrian signals in the public right-of-way.

Key ADA requirements covered throughout this book include accessible route dimensions, maximum slopes, ramp requirements, parking standards, and clear floor space at accessible elements. The landscape architect is responsible for ensuring that every public outdoor space meets these standards.

Clean Water Act (CWA) Section 404: Requires a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for any discharge of dredged or fill material into waters of the United States, including wetlands. If a project involves filling, grading, or disturbing a jurisdictional wetland or stream, a Section 404 permit is required. Wetland mitigation (creating or restoring wetlands to compensate for losses) is typically a condition of the permit.

National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA): Requires federal agencies to assess the environmental impact of proposed actions through Environmental Assessments (EA) or Environmental Impact Statements (EIS). Projects with federal funding, on federal land, or requiring federal permits may trigger NEPA review. NEPA does not apply to purely private or state/local projects without a federal nexus.

Endangered Species Act (ESA): Prohibits actions that would harm threatened or endangered species or destroy their critical habitat. If a site survey reveals protected species, the project may need to modify its design to avoid, minimize, or mitigate impacts.

National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) Section 106: Requires federal agencies to consider the effects of their actions on properties listed in or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places. Section 106 review involves identifying historic properties, assessing potential effects, and consulting with stakeholders to resolve adverse effects.

Stormwater regulations (MS4 permits): The Clean Water Act requires municipalities with Municipal Separate Storm Sewer Systems (MS4s) to obtain NPDES permits that include post-construction stormwater management requirements. Most local jurisdictions now require development projects to manage stormwater quality and quantity on-site through BMPs.

Standard of care: Landscape architects are held to the standard of care — the level of skill and competence that a reasonably competent professional in the same field would exercise under similar circumstances. This is not perfection — it is reasonable competence. Errors and omissions liability arises when a professional's performance falls below this standard and causes harm.

Duty to warn: A landscape architect who discovers a hazardous condition during site analysis (contaminated soil, unstable slopes, unsafe structures) has a duty to warn the client, even if the condition is outside the scope of the current engagement. Failing to warn of a known hazard creates liability.

Easements: An easement grants a party the right to use another's property for a specific purpose. Utility easements allow utility companies to access, maintain, and repair their infrastructure. Conservation easements restrict development to protect environmental values. Access easements provide legal right of passage. The landscape architect must identify all existing easements during site inventory because they constrain where structures, planting, and grading can occur.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  ADA and PROWAG establish minimum accessibility requirements for all public outdoor spaces. ✔  CWA Section 404 requires permits for any disturbance to wetlands or waters of the US. ✔  NEPA requires environmental review for projects with a federal nexus (funding, land, or permits). ✔  ESA prohibits harming endangered species or destroying critical habitat. ✔  NHPA Section 106 requires consideration of effects on historic properties for federal actions. ✔  Standard of care = reasonable competence, not perfection; falling below it creates liability. ✔  Duty to warn requires landscape architects to alert clients to known hazardous conditions. ✔  Easements constrain design — identify all during site inventory.
1. A site inventory reveals the presence of jurisdictional wetlands. The project proposes to fill a portion of the wetland for a parking lot. Which permit is required?
A)  NPDES stormwater permit
B)  CWA Section 404 permit from the Army Corps of Engineers
C)  NEPA Environmental Impact Statement
D)  Building permit
Answer: B. Section 404 of the Clean Water Act requires a permit from the Army Corps of Engineers for any discharge of fill material into waters of the United States, including wetlands.
2. A landscape architect discovers contaminated soil during a site visit for a park design project. The contamination is outside the project scope. The landscape architect should:
A)  Ignore it because it is outside the project scope
B)  Notify the client of the hazardous condition
C)  Begin remediation without client authorization
D)  Report it to the EPA directly
Answer: B. The duty to warn requires a landscape architect to notify the client of known hazardous conditions, even if they are outside the current project scope.
A)  All projects to avoid historic properties
B)  Federal agencies to consider effects on historic properties
C)  State governments to protect all buildings over 50 years old
D)  Landscape architects to obtain preservation certification
Answer: B. Section 106 requires federal agencies to take into account the effects of their undertakings on properties listed in or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places.

s2_book.title: Chapter 12: Comprehensive Review and Exam Strategy

content.text: This final chapter brings together the key themes from all four domains and provides exam-day strategies for Section 2.

rows: SITES, sustainability, cultural landscapes, design theory, D/H ratio, Kevin Lynch
Programming, space standards, McHarg, zoning, transect, green infrastructure, bubble diagrams
ADA/PROWAG, circulation, grading, slopes, stormwater BMPs, planting design, xeriscape
Materials, cost estimating, value engineering, life cycle cost, lighting, regulations, liability

content.text: Based on the exam blueprint and practitioner feedback, these topics appear most frequently:
•  ADA requirements — slopes (5/2/8.33%), ramp standards, parking ratios, clear floor space
•  Slope ranges — which slopes are appropriate for which uses
•  Stormwater BMPs — which practices work on which soil types
•  Sustainability rating systems — especially SITES vs. LEED
•  Kevin Lynch's five elements — paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks
•  D/H ratio and spatial enclosure
•  Zoning standards — FAR, setbacks, lot coverage, density calculations
•  Secretary of the Interior's Standards — four treatment approaches
•  Cost estimating accuracy by design phase
•  McHarg's overlay suitability analysis
•  Xeriscape principles
•  Environmental regulations — CWA 404, NEPA, ESA, NHPA 106

1. Read every word of the question. The exam is designed to test careful reading. Words like MOST, LEAST, PRIMARY, FIRST, and EXCEPT change the correct answer entirely. Underlining these words mentally can prevent misreading.

2. Eliminate wrong answers. If you are unsure, start by eliminating options you know are incorrect. Removing even one option significantly improves your odds. Two eliminations give you a 50/50 chance.

3. Watch for absolutes. Answers containing "always," "never," "all," or "none" are often wrong because most landscape architecture decisions depend on context. Answers with "typically," "generally," or "most appropriate" are more likely correct.

4. Multiple-response questions require ALL correct answers. Read every option carefully. Selecting an extra wrong answer or missing a correct answer gives zero credit. If unsure about one option, consider whether it is clearly wrong or possibly right.

5. Manage your time. You have 85 questions in 180 minutes — about 2 minutes per question. Flag difficult questions and return to them. Do not spend 5 minutes on one question that you could spend answering three others.
6. Use the CLARB demo exam. The free demo exam on the CLARB website familiarizes you with the testing interface, question formats, and the flag-and-review system. Practice with it before exam day.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Master Planning (33%) is the largest domain — prioritize programming, zoning, and site analysis study. ✔  Memorize ADA numbers: 5% running slope, 2% cross slope, 8.33% ramp, 30' max run, 5' × 5' landings. ✔  Know slope ranges for every common land use. ✔  Understand which BMPs work on which soils (HSG A-D). ✔  Know the difference between SITES (landscapes) and LEED (buildings). ✔  Read question qualifiers carefully: MOST, LEAST, PRIMARY, FIRST, EXCEPT. ✔  Use the 2-minute-per-question pace and flag difficult questions for review.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is conducting a site inventory for a 50-acre park project. Which of the following should be the FIRST step in the inventory process?

choices.text: Conducting a detailed soil analysis across the entire site
Reviewing existing data including surveys, aerial photographs, GIS data, and public records
Interviewing all adjacent property owners
Preparing a preliminary grading plan

s2_exam.explanation: Reviewing existing data is the most efficient first step before conducting field work.

s2_exam.question: A topographic survey of a project site shows contour lines that are closely spaced on the western portion and widely spaced on the eastern portion. This indicates:

choices.text: The western portion has gentle slopes and the eastern portion has steep slopes
The western portion has steep slopes and the eastern portion has gentle slopes
Both portions have the same slope
The elevation is higher on the western portion

s2_exam.explanation: Closely spaced contours indicate steep slopes; widely spaced contours indicate gentle slopes.

s2_exam.question: When evaluating an existing site, a landscape architect identifies a stand of mature trees. Which of the following data is MOST important to collect for each tree?

choices.text: The date each tree was planted
The lumber value of each tree
The aesthetic preference of the client for each tree
Species, size (DBH), condition, and canopy spread

s2_exam.explanation: Species, DBH, condition, and canopy spread are essential for evaluating tree preservation and design.

s2_exam.question: A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) is conducted to:

choices.text: Determine the exact location and extent of soil contamination
Remediate any existing contamination on the site
Establish the market value of the property
Identify potential environmental contamination liabilities through records review, site reconnaissance, and interviews

s2_exam.explanation: A Phase I ESA identifies potential contamination through records review, site reconnaissance, and interviews without intrusive testing.

s2_exam.question: Which of the following soil characteristics is MOST critical for determining the suitability of a site for stormwater infiltration?

choices.text: Soil color
Soil temperature
Soil texture and permeability (infiltration rate)
Soil pH

s2_exam.explanation: Soil texture and permeability directly determine infiltration rates and stormwater management feasibility.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is analyzing a site in the Northern Hemisphere for solar exposure. Which slope orientation receives the MOST direct sunlight throughout the year?

choices.text: North-facing slope
East-facing slope
West-facing slope
South-facing slope

s2_exam.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes receive the most direct sunlight throughout the year.

s2_exam.question: A site analysis reveals that prevailing winter winds come from the northwest. Which design strategy would BEST mitigate wind exposure for an outdoor seating area?

choices.text: Locate the seating area on the northwest side of the site
Orient the seating area to face northwest for maximum ventilation
Plant a dense evergreen windbreak to the northwest of the seating area
Install deciduous trees to the northwest of the seating area

s2_exam.explanation: A dense evergreen windbreak to the northwest provides year-round protection from prevailing winter winds.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is assessing viewsheds from a proposed hilltop overlook. A viewshed analysis would BEST be conducted using:

choices.text: A soil boring test
A traffic impact study
A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment
GIS-based terrain modeling and line-of-sight analysis

s2_exam.explanation: GIS-based terrain modeling with line-of-sight analysis is the standard method for viewshed assessment.

s2_exam.question: When analyzing a site's hydrology, the landscape architect identifies a 100-year floodplain boundary. This boundary indicates:

choices.text: An area that has a 1% chance of flooding in any given year
An area that floods every 100 years
An area where construction is always prohibited
An area that will never flood if properly graded

s2_exam.explanation: The 100-year floodplain has a 1% annual chance of flooding, not a literal 100-year cycle.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is analyzing a site with a high water table. Which of the following design considerations is MOST directly affected?

choices.text: Selection of exterior lighting fixtures
The color palette for hardscape materials
The style of site furnishings
Foundation design, plant selection, and subsurface drainage

s2_exam.explanation: A high water table directly affects foundations, plant selection, and subsurface drainage design.

s2_exam.question: A soil percolation test is PRIMARILY used to determine:

choices.text: The structural bearing capacity of the soil
The nutrient content of the soil
The depth to bedrock
The rate at which water moves through the soil

s2_exam.explanation: Percolation tests measure the rate water moves through soil, important for septic and infiltration design.

s2_exam.question: Which USDA soil texture has the HIGHEST infiltration rate?

choices.text: Clay
Clay loam
Silt
Sand

s2_exam.explanation: Sandy soils have the largest particle size and highest infiltration rate among the options.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect reviews a USDA Web Soil Survey report for a project site. The report classifies the soil as "hydric." This classification indicates:

choices.text: The soil is well-drained and suitable for construction
The soil has high structural bearing capacity
The soil formed under conditions of saturation and may indicate the presence of wetlands
The soil is contaminated with heavy metals

s2_exam.explanation: Hydric soils formed under saturated conditions and are one of three indicators of wetlands.

s2_exam.question: A site has expansive clay soils. Which of the following is the PRIMARY concern for site development?

choices.text: The soil will not support plant growth
The soil has excessive permeability
The soil will shrink and swell with changes in moisture content, potentially damaging structures
The soil is too acidic for most plants

s2_exam.explanation: Expansive clays shrink and swell with moisture changes, causing structural damage.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect identifies a plant community dominated by cattails, sedges, and rushes during a site inventory. This plant community MOST likely indicates:

choices.text: A dry, upland environment
A recently disturbed construction site
A mature deciduous forest
A wetland or hydric soil conditions

s2_exam.explanation: Cattails, sedges, and rushes are hydrophytic plants that indicate wetland or hydric conditions.

s2_exam.question: The concept of ecological succession refers to:

choices.text: The sudden destruction of a plant community by fire
The spread of invasive species across a region
The predictable, sequential change in plant community composition over time
The seasonal changes in leaf color

s2_exam.explanation: Ecological succession is the predictable, sequential change in plant community composition over time.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a project in a region with endemic species. Which of the following is the MOST important consideration?

choices.text: Preserving habitat for endemic species and incorporating native plant communities
Replacing endemic species with non-native ornamental varieties
Introducing species from other regions to increase biodiversity
Removing all existing vegetation and starting with a new plant palette

s2_exam.explanation: Preserving habitat for endemic species is critical to maintaining regional biodiversity and ecosystem function.

s2_exam.question: A riparian buffer zone serves which PRIMARY ecological function?

choices.text: Filtering pollutants, stabilizing stream banks, and providing wildlife habitat
Providing parking for site visitors
Increasing the amount of impervious surface near waterways
Creating space for recreational sports fields

s2_exam.explanation: Riparian buffers filter pollutants, stabilize banks, and provide habitat along waterways.

s2_exam.question: The urban heat island effect is PRIMARILY caused by:

choices.text: Increased tree canopy coverage in cities
Higher elevations found in urban areas
Large areas of impervious surfaces and reduced vegetation that absorb and re-radiate heat
Increased rainfall in urban areas compared to surrounding areas

s2_exam.explanation: Impervious surfaces absorb and re-radiate heat, and reduced vegetation decreases cooling, creating heat islands.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing an outdoor plaza in a hot, arid climate. Which strategy would MOST effectively reduce the microclimate temperature?

choices.text: Installing dark-colored asphalt pavement
Incorporating shade trees, light-colored paving, and water features
Removing all vegetation to reduce maintenance
Enclosing the space with tall walls to block all air movement

s2_exam.explanation: Shade trees, light-colored paving, and water features work together to reduce microclimate temperatures.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is developing a program for a community park. The MOST effective method for identifying community needs and priorities is:

choices.text: Conducting stakeholder engagement, including public meetings, surveys, and interviews
Relying solely on the landscape architect's professional judgment
Copying the program from a similar park in another community
Asking the city council to decide all programming elements

s2_exam.explanation: Stakeholder engagement through multiple methods is the most effective way to identify community needs.

s2_exam.question: A program for a new public space identifies a need for both active recreation and passive contemplation. Which programming strategy BEST addresses both needs?

choices.text: Choosing one use and eliminating the other
Designing the entire site for active recreation only
Creating distinct zones within the site that accommodate both active and passive uses with appropriate transitions
Recommending two separate projects on different sites

s2_exam.explanation: Zoning the site for different use types with transitions is the best strategy for accommodating multiple needs.

s2_exam.question: During programming, a landscape architect discovers that the client's desired program exceeds the capacity of the site. The MOST appropriate response is to:

choices.text: Present the client with an analysis showing site capacity and recommend prioritization of program elements
Design the project with all desired elements regardless of site constraints
Eliminate program elements without consulting the client
Recommend the client purchase additional adjacent property

s2_exam.explanation: Present a site capacity analysis and help the client prioritize program elements within the site's constraints.

s2_exam.question: A site is located within a designated historic district. Before proceeding with design, the landscape architect should:

choices.text: Ignore the historic designation since it only applies to buildings
Design the project without any historical references
Research applicable preservation guidelines and coordinate with the appropriate historic preservation authority
Demolish all existing site features to start fresh

s2_exam.explanation: Historic district designation affects site design; coordination with preservation authorities is required.

s2_exam.question: A project site contains jurisdictional wetlands. Under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, which federal agency is responsible for issuing permits for discharging dredged or fill material into wetlands?

choices.text: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)

s2_exam.explanation: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers issues Section 404 permits for activities in jurisdictional wetlands.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a project on a coastal site subject to the Coastal Zone Management Act. Which of the following is MOST important to consider?

choices.text: The site's proximity to an airport
Coastal erosion, storm surge, sea level rise, and consistency with the state's coastal management program
The availability of parking
The color of proposed building materials

s2_exam.explanation: Coastal projects must address erosion, storm surge, sea level rise, and state coastal management programs.

s2_exam.question: When conducting a site analysis, a landscape architect discovers potential archaeological resources on the site. The landscape architect should:

choices.text: Notify the client and recommend consultation with appropriate authorities before design proceeds
Proceed with construction and document any findings
Remove the artifacts and donate them to a local museum
Ignore the finding since it is not the landscape architect's responsibility

s2_exam.explanation: Archaeological resources require notification and consultation with appropriate authorities before proceeding.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a memorial space. Which of the following is the MOST critical aspect of the programming process?

choices.text: Selecting the most expensive materials available
Engaging stakeholders to understand the significance, narrative, and emotional qualities desired for the space
Copying the design of an existing successful memorial
Maximizing the number of features in the space

s2_exam.explanation: Memorial spaces require deep stakeholder engagement to understand significance and desired emotional qualities.

s2_exam.question: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are MOST useful for:

choices.text: Layering, analyzing, and visualizing spatial data to support site analysis and planning decisions
Creating detailed construction documents
Calculating structural loads for retaining walls
Preparing contract specifications

s2_exam.explanation: GIS excels at layering and analyzing spatial data for planning and site analysis decisions.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect uses a SWOT analysis during the planning process. SWOT stands for:

choices.text: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
Soil, Water, Orientation, Topography
Site, Width, Overlay, Terrain
Slope, Wetlands, Open space, Transportation

s2_exam.explanation: SWOT stands for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats.

s2_exam.question: The carrying capacity of a site refers to:

choices.text: The maximum weight the soil can support
The maximum level of use or development a site can sustain without unacceptable degradation
The maximum number of parking spaces that can fit on the site
The maximum height of buildings allowed by zoning

s2_exam.explanation: Carrying capacity is the maximum use level a site can sustain without unacceptable degradation.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect analyzes a site's existing drainage patterns and identifies a natural swale that collects runoff from a 10-acre area. The BEST approach for site development is to:

choices.text: Fill the swale and redirect drainage through pipes
Pave over the swale to create a parking area
Ignore the drainage pattern in the design
Preserve and integrate the natural drainage feature into the site design

s2_exam.explanation: Preserving natural drainage features is both ecologically and functionally preferable.

s2_exam.question: A watershed analysis for a development project should consider which of the following?

choices.text: The entire upstream contributing drainage area and downstream receiving waters
Only the area within the project boundaries
Only the nearest stream or river
Only areas within the same political jurisdiction

s2_exam.explanation: Watershed analysis must consider the entire upstream contributing area and downstream receiving waters.

s2_exam.question: Kevin Lynch's "The Image of the City" identifies five elements of urban form. Which of the following is NOT one of Lynch's five elements?

choices.text: Paths
Edges
Nodes
Textures

s2_exam.explanation: Lynch's five elements are Paths, Edges, Districts, Nodes, and Landmarks. Textures is not one of them.

s2_exam.question: A figure-ground analysis of an urban site is PRIMARILY used to:

choices.text: Analyze the relationship between built form (figure) and open space (ground)
Determine soil composition
Calculate stormwater runoff volumes
Establish property boundaries

s2_exam.explanation: Figure-ground analysis examines the relationship between built form and open space in an urban context.

s2_exam.question: A landscape architect is analyzing vehicular and pedestrian circulation patterns on a site. The PRIMARY goal of this analysis is to:

choices.text: Maximize the number of vehicular travel lanes
Identify conflicts, opportunities, and appropriate separation between modes of circulation
Eliminate all pedestrian access to reduce liability
Ensure vehicles have priority over pedestrians in all areas

s2_exam.explanation: Circulation analysis identifies conflicts and opportunities for appropriate separation between modes.

s2_exam.question: A traffic calming strategy for a residential neighborhood might include which of the following?

choices.text: Widening all roads to accommodate higher speeds
Removing all sidewalks
Installing speed tables, chicanes, and narrowing travel lanes
Increasing the posted speed limit

s2_exam.explanation: Speed tables, chicanes, and lane narrowing are established traffic calming measures.

s2_exam.question: During site inventory, the landscape architect identifies existing underground utilities. Why is the accurate location of utilities CRITICAL to the design process?

choices.text: To determine the aesthetic quality of the site
To avoid conflicts with proposed site features and ensure safe construction, as well as to plan for required easements and setbacks
To calculate the site's property tax assessment
To determine the site's zoning classification

s2_exam.explanation: Accurate utility locations prevent conflicts, ensure safety during construction, and inform easement planning.

s2_exam.question: The Rational Method (Q = CiA) is used to:

choices.text: Calculate the structural load on a retaining wall
Determine the soil's bearing capacity
Estimate peak stormwater runoff from a drainage area
Calculate the volume of cut and fill for a grading plan

s2_exam.explanation: The Rational Method estimates peak stormwater runoff rate from a drainage area.

s2_exam.question: In the Rational Method, the "C" coefficient represents:

choices.text: The cost of construction
The runoff coefficient, reflecting the proportion of rainfall that becomes surface runoff
The contour interval of the topographic map
The circumference of the drainage pipe

s2_exam.explanation: The "C" coefficient represents the runoff coefficient -- the proportion of rainfall that becomes surface runoff.

content.text: Aligned to the CLARB Exam Blueprint (Effective December 2023)
90 Scored Items  |  Computer-Based  |  MC + Select All + Drag & Drop + Hotspot  |  3 Hours

LARE Section 3 tests your ability to prepare construction documents, write specifications, manage the bidding process, and administer construction contracts. It is the most technically detailed section of the LARE, requiring knowledge of materials, construction methods, detailing standards, and professional practice procedures.

The exam uses four question types: multiple choice, select all that apply, drag and drop, and hotspot (clicking on a location in an image). Hotspot questions may ask you to identify elements on a construction detail, place notes on a plan, or locate features on a site layout.

Half the exam focuses on your ability to read, interpret, and prepare construction drawings and details. This domain covers layout plans, grading plans, planting plans, irrigation plans, lighting plans, and construction details.
•  Title sheet — project information, location map, sheet index, general notes, legend
•  Demolition plan — existing features to be removed, protected, or relocated
•  Layout/dimensioning plan — horizontal locations of all improvements referenced to control points
•  Grading plan — existing and proposed contours, spot elevations, slopes, drainage arrows
•  Utility plan — storm sewer, sanitary sewer, water, electric, gas, telecom
•  Planting plan — plant locations, species, sizes, quantities, planting details
•  Irrigation plan — system layout, head locations, pipe sizes, controller zones
•  Lighting plan — fixture locations, types, circuits, photometric data
•  Details — construction details for walls, paving, steps, ramps, fences, site furnishings
•  Specifications — written requirements for materials, products, and execution (separate document)
•  Existing contours shown dashed; proposed contours shown solid
•  Spot elevations at: building corners, top/bottom of walls, top/bottom of steps, inlet/outlet of structures, high/low points
•  Slope annotations: percentage (%) for surface slopes, ratio (H:V) for embankments
•  Drainage arrows showing direction of surface flow
•  Finished Floor Elevation (FFE) at all building entrances
•  Top of Wall (TW) and Bottom of Wall (BW) elevations on all retaining walls
•  Flow line (FL) and rim/grate elevations at all drainage structures
•  Dimensions referenced to property lines, building faces, or established control points
•  Coordinate system: State Plane or project grid with northing/easting
•  Horizontal curves: radius, arc length, chord length, delta angle
•  Offset dimensions — perpendicular distance from a baseline to a feature
•  Tolerances — acceptable deviation from plan dimensions (typically ±1/4" for layout)
•  Retaining walls — types, materials, drainage, reinforcement
–  Gravity walls: rely on mass (stone, concrete); typically < 4' height
–  Cantilever walls: reinforced concrete; engineered for height > 4'
–  Segmental retaining walls (SRW): modular block; geogrid reinforcement for > 4'
–  All walls require drainage: perforated pipe, gravel backfill, filter fabric, weep holes
•  Pavements — base preparation, material layers, joint types
–  Concrete: subgrade, compacted base (4-6" aggregate), 4-6" concrete, control joints
–  Asphalt: subgrade, compacted base (6-8" aggregate), binder course, wearing course
–  Unit pavers: subgrade, compacted base, setting bed (1" sand), pavers, edge restraint
•  Steps and ramps — ADA compliance, materials, drainage
–  Steps: 2R + T = 26" (typical); risers 4-7", treads 11-14"; 1% slope on treads for drainage
–  Ramps: 1:12 max slope, 30' max run, 5'×5' landings, handrails both sides, edge protection
•  Fences and walls — post spacing, footing depth, material connections
–  Post spacing: typically 6-8' on center
–  Post footings: below frost line, typically 1/3 of total post length below grade
•  Site furnishings — benches, bollards, trash receptacles, bike racks; anchorage details
•  Plant schedule: botanical name, common name, size at installation, quantity, spacing, condition
•  Planting details: tree pit, shrub bed, groundcover, container planting
–  Tree planting: hole 2-3× root ball width, depth = root ball height, root flare at or above grade
–  Backfill: native soil (amended only if necessary), no soil on top of root ball
–  Mulch: 3-4" organic mulch, pulled 3-6" away from trunk (no "mulch volcanoes")
–  Staking: stakes outside root ball, flexible ties, remove after 1-2 growing seasons
•  Soil volume requirements for trees: minimum 600-1,000 CF per tree in urban conditions
•  Structural soil and suspended pavement systems for trees in paved areas
•  System components: controller, mainline, lateral lines, valves, heads/emitters, backflow preventer
•  Head types: spray (small areas, high precipitation rate), rotors (large areas, lower rate), drip (beds, trees)
•  Matched precipitation rates — all heads in a zone should apply water at the same rate
•  Backflow prevention required by code — RPZ or double-check valve assembly
•  Smart controllers: ET-based, weather-based, or soil moisture sensor-based scheduling
•  Pressure regulation — maintain optimal operating pressure at each head
•  Pipe sizing — based on flow rate (GPM) and maximum velocity (typically 5 fps)
Specifications are the written companion to construction drawings. While drawings show where and how much, specifications describe quality, materials, products, and execution methods.
•  Construction Specifications Institute (CSI) MasterFormat organizes specifications into divisions
•  Key divisions for landscape architecture:
–  Division 01 — General Requirements (general conditions, submittals, quality assurance)
–  Division 03 — Concrete (footings, walls, flatwork)
–  Division 04 — Masonry (unit masonry walls, stone veneer)
–  Division 05 — Metals (railings, fences, structural steel)
–  Division 26 — Electrical (site lighting)
–  Division 31 — Earthwork (grading, excavation, fill, erosion control)
–  Division 32 — Exterior Improvements (paving, curbs, walls, fences, irrigation, planting)
–  Division 33 — Utilities (storm drainage, water, sanitary sewer)
•  Prescriptive (proprietary): specifies exact products by manufacturer and model number
–  Advantage: precise control over quality and appearance
–  Disadvantage: limits competition, may increase cost
•  Performance: specifies required performance criteria without naming products
–  Advantage: encourages innovation and competition
–  Disadvantage: harder to enforce, requires clear performance standards
•  Reference standard: references published standards (ASTM, ANSI, ACI)
–  Example: "Concrete shall conform to ASTM C94 with minimum 28-day compressive strength of 4,000 psi"
•  "Or equal" specifications: name a product but allow substitutions of equal quality
–  Substitution requests require submittal review and approval
•  Part 1 — General: scope, references, submittals, quality assurance, delivery/storage, warranties
•  Part 2 — Products: manufacturers, materials, fabrication, finishes, mixes
•  Part 3 — Execution: preparation, installation, field quality control, cleaning, protection
•  Invitation to Bid (ITB) / Advertisement — public notice of bidding opportunity
•  Pre-bid conference — walk-through and Q&A with prospective bidders
•  Addenda — written changes or clarifications issued during the bidding period
•  Bid opening — public opening (public projects) or private review (private projects)
•  Bid evaluation — responsiveness, responsibility, price, qualifications
•  Notice of Award — formal notification to the selected contractor
•  Notice to Proceed (NTP) — authorizes the contractor to begin work, starts the contract time
•  Agreement — contract between owner and contractor (price, schedule, scope)
•  General conditions — rights, responsibilities, procedures (AIA A201 is the standard)
•  Supplementary conditions — project-specific modifications to general conditions
•  Drawings — graphic representation of the work
•  Specifications — written description of materials and execution
•  Addenda — modifications issued during bidding
•  Change orders — modifications after contract execution (require owner approval)

Construction administration (CA) is the landscape architect's role during construction. It involves observing the work, reviewing submittals, responding to questions, processing changes, and ensuring the project is built according to the contract documents.
•  Pre-construction conference — introductions, procedures, schedule, communication protocols
•  Review of contractor's schedule (CPM or bar chart)
•  Review of erosion and sediment control plan — install BMPs before grading begins
•  Tree protection — install fencing at drip line before any site work
•  Contractor submittals — shop drawings, product data, samples for LA review
•  Shop drawings — contractor-prepared detailed drawings showing fabrication and installation
•  Product data — manufacturer's literature, specifications, and test reports
•  Samples — physical samples of materials (pavers, stone, mulch, paint colors)
•  Review actions: Approved, Approved as Noted, Revise and Resubmit, Rejected
•  LA review is for conformance with design intent — NOT for means and methods of construction
•  Contractor remains responsible for accuracy of dimensions and construction methods
•  Site observations (NOT inspections) — LA visits site to observe work in progress
–  "Observation" = general conformance with design intent
–  "Inspection" = implies guarantee of compliance (creates liability); avoid this term
•  Observation reports — document conditions observed, work in progress, weather, personnel on site
•  Photo documentation — date-stamped photos of work in progress and completed work
•  Critical observation points:
–  Subgrade preparation before paving
–  Footing excavations before concrete placement
–  Drainage pipe installation before backfill
–  Retaining wall drainage installation before backfill
–  Plant material at delivery (verify species, size, condition, root ball)
–  Finish grade before planting
•  Request for Information (RFI) — contractor's written request for clarification of documents
–  LA must respond promptly and in writing
–  RFI responses may not change the scope, cost, or contract time
•  Change orders — formal modification to the contract
–  Initiated by owner, LA, or contractor
–  Requires written description of change, cost impact, and time impact
–  Must be approved by owner before work proceeds
•  Construction Change Directive (CCD) — owner-directed change when agreement on cost/time has not yet been reached; contractor must proceed with work
•  Substantial completion — project is sufficiently complete for the owner to use it for its intended purpose
–  Certificate of Substantial Completion issued by the LA
–  Punch list — list of items to be completed or corrected
–  Warranty period begins at substantial completion
•  Final completion — all punch list items resolved, all closeout documents submitted
•  Closeout documents:
–  As-built drawings (record drawings) — contractor's marked-up drawings showing actual construction
–  Operation and maintenance manuals
–  Warranties and guarantees
–  Lien releases — contractor and subcontractors certify all payments received
–  Final payment application
•  Retainage — typically 5-10% of each payment withheld until final completion

rows: Versatile, moldable, durable; requires control joints
Structural applications, thin sections, high-load areas
Moderate weathering; not for ground contact
Lightweight, corrosion-resistant; lower strength than steel
Ground contact rated; CCA replaced by ACQ/CA-B
Low maintenance; no rot; higher initial cost than wood
12" beyond top and bottom of ramp
Required on both sides: curb, rail, or wall
2 risers difficult to see; requires visual contrast

s3_guide.title: CSI MasterFormat Divisions for Landscape Architecture

rows: Submittals, quality assurance, temporary facilities, cleaning
Unit masonry, stone, manufactured stone veneer
Structural steel, railings, fences, gratings, metal fabrications
Rough carpentry, finish carpentry, decking, pergolas
Grading, excavation, fill, soil stabilization, erosion control
Paving, curbs, walls, fences, irrigation, planting, furnishings
Storm drainage, water distribution, sanitary sewer

content.text: •  Construction Plans and Details is 50% of the exam — spend the most time studying details, materials, and plan reading.
•  Practice reading construction details and identifying components. The exam uses hotspot questions that ask you to locate features on detail drawings.
•  Memorize the step formula (2R + T = 26") and ADA ramp standards (1:12, 30' max run, 5'×5' landings).
•  Know CSI MasterFormat division numbers, especially 31 (Earthwork), 32 (Exterior Improvements), and 33 (Utilities).
•  Understand the 3-part specification format (General, Products, Execution) and specification types (prescriptive, performance, reference standard).
•  Know the difference between observation and inspection — the LA observes, never inspects.
•  Understand the bidding sequence: advertisement → pre-bid → addenda → bid opening → evaluation → award → NTP.
•  Know the difference between substantial completion and final completion, and what triggers the warranty period.
•  Study submittal review actions: Approved, Approved as Noted, Revise and Resubmit, Rejected.
•  Understand retainage, change orders, RFIs, and the roles of owner, LA, and contractor during construction.

s3_book.title: Preface: How to Use This Book

content.text: This study book is designed to give you everything you need to pass LARE Section 3: Construction Documentation and Administration. Section 3 is the most technically detailed section of the LARE exam. It tests whether you can translate a design into buildable documents, write specifications that communicate quality and performance requirements, navigate the bidding process, and administer a construction contract from pre-construction through project closeout.
The content is organized around the three domains of the CLARB exam blueprint:

Half the exam tests your ability to read, interpret, and prepare construction documents — drawings and details. Spend the majority of your study time on Chapters 1 through 6. The remaining half splits between specifications/bidding and construction administration, both of which are process-heavy and can be studied efficiently through understanding the sequence and vocabulary.

EXAM FORMAT:  Section 3 uses four question types: standard multiple choice, select all that apply (multiple correct answers), drag and drop (place items in the correct order or location), and hotspot (click on a specific location in an image). Hotspot questions may ask you to identify components in a construction detail or locate features on a plan. Practice reading details carefully before the exam.

Construction drawings are the primary means by which a landscape architect communicates design intent to the contractor. They are legal documents that, together with specifications, define exactly what is to be built. Every line, dimension, note, and symbol on a construction drawing carries contractual weight. Understanding how to read and prepare these documents is the foundation of Section 3.
A complete set of landscape construction drawings follows a standardized sequence. Each sheet type serves a specific purpose, and the set is organized from general to specific:

rows: Project name, location, owner, design team, sheet index, location map, general notes, abbreviations, legend
Features to remove, protect, or relocate; limits of clearing and grubbing; tree protection fencing
Horizontal dimensions and locations of all improvements; control points; construction setbacks
Existing and proposed contours, spot elevations, slopes, drainage arrows, FFE, TW/BW
Storm sewer, water, sanitary, electric, gas, telecom; pipe sizes, inverts, manholes
Plant locations, species, sizes, spacing; plant schedule; planting notes
Pipe layout, heads, valves, controller, backflow preventer; irrigation schedule
Fixture locations, types, circuits, photometric data, panel schedule
Construction details for all site elements — walls, paving, steps, ramps, fences, furnishings

content.text: The prefix system varies by firm, but the logic is consistent: demolition comes first (what is removed before anything is built), then layout (where things go), then grading (how the land is shaped), then utilities (what goes underground), then planting and irrigation (what grows), then lighting (what illuminates), and finally details (how things are constructed).
Construction drawings use standardized graphic conventions so that contractors can read them without ambiguity:

Line weights: Heavier lines indicate elements that are cut or in the foreground. Lighter lines indicate elements beyond the cut plane or in the background. Property lines are typically the heaviest lines on a plan. Existing features to remain are shown medium weight. New construction is shown in the heaviest line weight within the drawing area.

Line types: Solid lines represent visible edges. Dashed lines represent hidden or underground features (footings below grade, underground pipes). Dot-dash lines represent centerlines. Long-dash-short-dash lines represent property boundaries. Chain-dotted lines represent easements or setbacks.

Existing vs. proposed: On grading plans, existing contours are shown as dashed lines and proposed contours as solid lines. On demolition plans, features to be removed are marked with an X or shown in a distinctive pattern. Features to be protected are circled or highlighted with a protection boundary.

Scales: Plans are typically drawn at 1"=10', 1"=20', 1"=30', or 1"=40' depending on site size and level of detail needed. Details are drawn at larger scales: 1/2"=1', 3/4"=1', 1"=1', 1-1/2"=1', or 3"=1'. Sections through walls, steps, and pavements use these larger scales to show material layers and dimensions clearly.

EXAM TIP:  The exam may show a construction drawing and ask you to interpret line types. Remember: solid = visible, dashed = hidden/underground/existing contours, dot-dash = centerline. If a plan shows a dashed circle around a tree, it represents the drip line (canopy edge) used for tree protection.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Construction drawings are legal documents that define exactly what is to be built. ✔  Sheet sequence: title → demolition → layout → grading → utility → planting → irrigation → lighting → details. ✔  Line weights: heavier = foreground/cut; lighter = background/beyond. ✔  Line types: solid = visible, dashed = hidden/underground, dot-dash = centerline. ✔  Existing contours = dashed; proposed contours = solid. ✔  Plan scales: 1"=10' to 1"=40'; detail scales: 1/2"=1' to 3"=1'.

subsections.title: 1. On a grading plan, existing contour lines are typically shown as:

content.text: A)  Solid lines
B)  Dashed lines
C)  Dot-dash lines
D)  Double lines
Answer: B. Existing contours are shown dashed to distinguish them from proposed contours, which are shown solid.

subsections.title: 2. A dot-dash line on a construction drawing typically represents a:

content.text: A)  Property line
B)  Centerline
C)  Underground utility
D)  Easement
Answer: B. Dot-dash lines are the standard convention for centerlines on construction drawings.

subsections.title: 3. In a construction drawing set, the demolition plan appears BEFORE the layout plan because:

content.text: A)  It is alphabetically first
B)  Existing features must be removed or protected before new construction begins
C)  It requires less detail
D)  The contractor prefers this sequence
Answer: B. Demolition comes first because clearing, grubbing, and protection of existing features must occur before any new construction can begin.

Pavements are the most common construction element in landscape architecture. Whether it is a plaza, a parking lot, a walkway, or a patio, the landscape architect must understand the structural layers, joint types, material options, and construction details that ensure long-term performance. The exam tests your knowledge of pavement systems in detail.
All pavements share a common structural logic: loads applied at the surface are distributed through successively thicker layers down to the subgrade. Each layer serves a specific function:

Subgrade: The native soil that supports the pavement structure. Subgrade quality (bearing capacity, drainage, frost susceptibility) determines how thick the layers above it must be. Poor subgrades (clay, organic soils) require thicker base layers or soil stabilization. The subgrade must be compacted to 95% of maximum dry density (Modified Proctor, ASTM D1557) before base placement.

Subbase: An optional layer of granular material (bank-run gravel) placed on weak subgrades to improve load distribution and drainage. Typically 4-6 inches of compacted material. Not always required if the subgrade has adequate bearing capacity.

Base course: The primary structural layer. Typically 4-8 inches of compacted crushed aggregate (often specified as ASTM D2940 or state DOT equivalent). The base distributes wheel loads and provides drainage below the surface. It must be compacted to 95% Modified Proctor density.
Surface course: The wearing surface — concrete, asphalt, unit pavers, or stone. This is what users see and walk or drive on. Surface thickness depends on the material and the expected traffic loads.

MEMORY AID:  Pavement layers from bottom to top: Subgrade → Subbase (optional) → Base → Surface. Think of it as a sandwich: the bread (surface) gets all the wear, but the filling (base and subbase) provides the structural support.

Concrete is the most versatile pavement material. It can be formed into any shape, finished in many textures, and colored to match any design palette. But concrete's rigidity means it must accommodate two types of movement:

Shrinkage cracking: As concrete cures, it shrinks. Without control joints, shrinkage creates random, unsightly cracks. Control joints are tooled or saw-cut grooves (typically 1/4 to 1/3 of slab depth) that create planes of weakness where the slab will crack in a controlled, straight line. Control joints should be spaced at a maximum of 10-12 feet in each direction, and panels should be roughly square (aspect ratio no greater than 1.5:1).
