Expansion/contraction: Temperature changes cause concrete to expand and contract. Expansion joints (also called isolation joints) are full-depth separations filled with compressible material. They are placed wherever concrete abuts a fixed structure — buildings, walls, utility structures, curbs — to allow the slab to move without pushing against (and cracking) the adjacent element.
Construction joints: Joints placed where concrete placement stops for the day ("cold joints"). They include a keyway or dowels to transfer loads across the joint and maintain alignment.

Standard concrete for landscape applications is specified at 4,000 psi minimum 28-day compressive strength with 4-6% air entrainment in freeze-thaw climates. Air entrainment introduces microscopic air bubbles that accommodate ice crystal expansion within the concrete, preventing surface scaling and spalling.

EXAM TIP:  Control joint spacing is one of the most tested construction topics. The rule: maximum 10-12 feet in each direction, keep panels roughly square. If an exam question shows a 5-foot-wide sidewalk, control joints should be spaced every 5-10 feet to keep panels square.

Interlocking concrete pavers (ICP) and clay brick pavers are set on a compacted aggregate base with a 1-inch sand setting bed. The system is flexible — individual pavers can shift slightly to accommodate minor settlement without cracking, and damaged pavers can be replaced without disturbing adjacent units.
A typical unit paver section from bottom to top:
•  Compacted subgrade (95% Modified Proctor)
•  6-8 inches compacted aggregate base (vehicular) or 4-6 inches (pedestrian)
•  1 inch sand setting bed (ASTM C33 concrete sand; screeded level, NOT compacted before pavers)
•  Pavers (typically 2-3/8" to 3-1/8" thick for pedestrian, 3-1/8" for vehicular)
•  Joint sand swept into paver joints (polymeric sand for weed/insect resistance)
•  Edge restraints — concrete, aluminum, or steel L-angles — are ESSENTIAL to prevent spreading

Permeable interlocking concrete pavers (PICP): Identical to standard pavers except the joints are wider and filled with small aggregate (not sand) to allow water infiltration. The aggregate base below is open-graded (no fines) to create a reservoir for stormwater storage and infiltration. PICPs can manage their own runoff footprint plus additional runoff from adjacent impervious areas.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A landscape architect specifies PICP for a parking lot on a site with Hydrologic Soil Group B soils. The pavers are 3-1/8" thick with No. 8 aggregate in the joints and No. 57 stone in the base reservoir. The open-graded base is 12 inches deep, providing approximately 4 inches of water storage (40% void ratio × 12" = 4.8" storage). An overflow connection to the storm sewer handles extreme events. The system eliminates the need for a separate detention basin, saving the client $80,000 in infrastructure costs.

Asphalt (hot-mix asphalt, HMA) is a flexible pavement that tolerates minor subgrade movement without cracking. It is lower cost than concrete, can be placed quickly, and is easily repaired by patching. However, it requires periodic maintenance (sealcoating every 3-5 years, crack sealing) and has a shorter life span than concrete (15-20 years vs. 25-40 years for well-maintained concrete).
A typical asphalt section:
•  Compacted subgrade
•  6-8 inches compacted aggregate base
•  2-3 inches asphalt binder course (coarser aggregate, provides structural support)
•  1-2 inches asphalt wearing course (finer aggregate, smooth driving/walking surface)

Porous asphalt: An open-graded asphalt mix placed over a stone reservoir base (identical concept to PICP). Water passes through the porous surface into the stone reservoir for infiltration. Porous asphalt requires protection from sediment and is not suitable for high-traffic roads, but works well for parking lots and low-speed access drives.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Pavement structure: subgrade → subbase (optional) → base → surface. ✔  Subgrade and base must be compacted to 95% Modified Proctor density. ✔  Concrete control joints: max 10-12' spacing, square panels, 1/4 to 1/3 slab depth. ✔  Expansion joints separate concrete from fixed structures (buildings, walls). ✔  Air entrainment (4-6%) is required in freeze-thaw climates to prevent scaling. ✔  Unit pavers require: compacted base, 1" sand setting bed, pavers, joint sand, edge restraints. ✔  Permeable systems (PICP, porous asphalt, porous concrete) use open-graded aggregate base as stormwater reservoir.

subsections.title: 1. Control joints in a 4-inch concrete sidewalk should be spaced at a maximum of:

content.text: A)  4 feet
B)  6 feet
C)  10-12 feet
D)  20 feet
Answer: C. Control joints should be spaced at 10-12 feet maximum (2-3× slab thickness in feet). For a 4" slab, this is 8-12 feet, with 10' being the standard maximum.

subsections.title: 2. The purpose of an expansion joint in concrete paving is to:

content.text: A)  Direct shrinkage cracking to a controlled location
B)  Allow the slab to expand and contract without pushing against adjacent structures
C)  Create decorative patterns in the surface
D)  Increase the compressive strength of the concrete
Answer: B. Expansion (isolation) joints are full-depth separations that allow thermal movement without transferring forces to adjacent structures.

subsections.title: 3. Unit pavers require edge restraints because:

content.text: A)  They improve the aesthetic appearance
B)  Without restraint, the pavers will spread apart and the system will fail
C)  Building codes require them for ADA compliance
D)  They provide drainage channels
Answer: B. Edge restraints are structurally essential — without them, horizontal forces from traffic and thermal expansion cause pavers to spread, opening joints and destabilizing the system.

subsections.title: 4. Air entrainment in concrete is important in cold climates because:

content.text: A)  It increases compressive strength
B)  Microscopic air bubbles accommodate ice crystal expansion, preventing surface scaling
C)  It makes the concrete lighter and easier to place
D)  It improves the color of the finished surface
Answer: B. Air entrainment creates tiny voids that absorb the pressure from ice formation within the concrete, preventing the surface scaling and spalling caused by freeze-thaw cycles.

s3_book.title: Chapter 3: Retaining Walls and Site Structures

content.text: Retaining walls hold back earth where grade changes are necessary — at building pads, along drives, at terraces, and where slopes are too steep to be stabilized by vegetation alone. The landscape architect must understand wall types, structural principles, drainage requirements, and when to involve a structural engineer.

A retaining wall is required when the desired grade change cannot be achieved within an acceptable slope. If the available horizontal distance is insufficient for a stable slope (typically 2:1 or 3:1), a wall provides a vertical grade change within a minimal footprint. Walls are also used for aesthetic purposes — creating defined terraces, seat walls, raised planters, and architectural edges.

EXAM TIP:  In most jurisdictions, retaining walls over 4 feet in exposed height (measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall) require structural engineering. The landscape architect designs walls up to 4 feet; taller walls require a structural engineer's stamp. Know this threshold.

rows: Relies on mass and self-weight to resist earth pressure
Stone, precast concrete, mass concrete, gabions
Reinforced concrete stem and footing act as lever; soil weight on heel stabilizes
Up to 6' unreinforced; higher with geogrid
Interlocking modular blocks with setback (batter); geogrid reinforces soil behind wall
Vertical ribs (counterforts behind, buttresses in front) brace the stem at intervals
Reinforcing strips or grids extend into compacted fill behind decorative facing panels
Concrete panels or blocks with steel/geosynthetic reinforcement
Steel beams or interlocking sheets driven into ground; lagging spans between piles
Steel H-piles, timber lagging, steel sheet piles

content.text: Drainage is the single most important factor in retaining wall performance. Water behind a retaining wall creates hydrostatic pressure — a force that acts horizontally against the wall, in addition to the lateral earth pressure the wall is already resisting. Saturated soil is also heavier than dry soil, increasing the loads on the wall. A wall designed to resist dry soil pressure can fail catastrophically if drainage is inadequate and water builds up behind it.
Every retaining wall must include:
•  Free-draining granular backfill — 12 inches minimum of clean gravel or crushed stone directly behind the wall
•  Perforated drainage pipe (typically 4" diameter) at the base of the wall, behind the footing, sloped to a positive outlet
•  Geotextile filter fabric between the granular backfill and the native soil to prevent fine soil particles from clogging the drainage layer
•  Weep holes (in masonry and concrete walls) — openings through the wall face that allow water to drain out, typically 4" diameter at 6-8' spacing along the base

MEMORY AID:  Wall drainage checklist: GPFW — Gravel backfill, Perforated pipe, Filter fabric, Weep holes. Every retaining wall needs all four. If one is missing, water will build up and the wall will eventually fail.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A segmental retaining wall fails three years after construction. The landscape architect investigates and finds that the contractor used native clay soil as backfill instead of the specified free-draining aggregate. Water could not drain, hydrostatic pressure built up during rain events, and the wall tilted and eventually collapsed. This failure was preventable with proper backfill material and a site observation at the critical moment — before backfill placement.
Outdoor steps must be designed for comfort, safety, and accessibility. The fundamental design relationship is:

2R + T = 26" (where R = riser height and T = tread depth). This formula produces a comfortable walking stride. Within this formula, risers should be 4" to 7" (6" is the most comfortable outdoor riser) and treads should be 11" minimum (14" is comfortable for outdoor steps where a more relaxed pace is appropriate). Each tread should slope 1% toward the front (nosing) for drainage.

rows: 34-38" height above nosing; 12" extension top and bottom
< 3 risers = tripping hazard; provide a ramp instead
At direction changes and every 12' of vertical rise

content.text: MEMORY AID:  Step formula: 2R + T = 26. A 6" riser: 2(6) + T = 26, so T = 14". A 7" riser: 2(7) + T = 26, so T = 12". These are the two most common outdoor combinations.

EXAM TIP:  Fewer than 3 risers is a tripping hazard — people do not notice a single step or two-step change. If the elevation change requires only 1-2 risers, consider a ramp instead, or add a visual contrast strip to make the steps obvious.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Retaining walls over 4' exposed height typically require structural engineering. ✔  Wall types: gravity (mass), cantilever (reinforced concrete), segmental (modular blocks), MSE (reinforced fill). ✔  All retaining walls need drainage: gravel backfill, perforated pipe, filter fabric, weep holes (GPFW). ✔  Hydrostatic pressure from water behind a wall is the #1 cause of wall failure. ✔  Step formula: 2R + T = 26". Risers 4-7", treads 11" minimum. ✔  Fewer than 3 risers is a tripping hazard — use a ramp or add visual contrast. ✔  Handrails required both sides if drop exceeds 30"; height 34-38" above nosing.
1. A landscape architect designs outdoor steps with 6-inch risers. Using the step formula 2R + T = 26, the tread depth should be:
A)  11 inches
B)  12 inches
C)  14 inches
D)  16 inches
Answer: C. 2(6) + T = 26, so T = 14 inches.

subsections.title: 2. The PRIMARY cause of retaining wall failure is:

content.text: A)  Inadequate footing depth
B)  Excessive wall height
C)  Poor drainage behind the wall
D)  Use of the wrong block type

Answer: C. Hydrostatic pressure from water accumulating behind the wall is the leading cause of retaining wall failure. Proper drainage (gravel, perforated pipe, filter fabric, weep holes) is essential.
3. In most jurisdictions, a retaining wall requires structural engineering review when its exposed height exceeds:
A)  2 feet
B)  4 feet
C)  6 feet
D)  8 feet
Answer: B. Most building codes require structural engineering for retaining walls exceeding 4 feet of exposed height.

Planting plans and details translate the design intent — which plants go where and why — into instructions the contractor can follow to install them correctly. Incorrect planting installation is one of the most common causes of plant failure. Trees planted too deep, mulch piled against trunks, root balls left in burlap too long, and inadequate soil volume in urban settings all lead to premature decline and death. The landscape architect's details and specifications must prevent these failures.
The tree planting detail is one of the most important details in any landscape construction document set. A properly detailed tree pit gives a tree the conditions it needs to establish and thrive:
Hole width: 2 to 3 times the diameter of the root ball. A wider hole encourages lateral root growth into loosened soil, which is critical for stability and water uptake.

Hole depth: Equal to the height of the root ball — no deeper. The root flare (the point where the trunk widens at the base) must be at or slightly above the surrounding grade. Planting too deep is the single most common planting error and causes slow decline and death by suffocating the root flare.

Backfill: Use the native excavated soil. Research has shown that amending backfill with organic matter creates a "bathtub effect" — roots stay in the amended zone and never grow into the surrounding native soil. The exception is when native soil is completely unsuitable (heavy clay, contaminated, rubble-filled), in which case engineered planting soil is specified.

Root flare exposure: Remove all soil, burlap, and wire basket material from the top of the root ball to expose the root flare. Cut and fold down burlap and wire from the top third of the ball after the tree is set in the hole. Remove all synthetic burlap entirely (it does not decompose).

Mulch: Apply 3 to 4 inches of organic mulch (shredded hardwood bark, pine straw) in a ring extending to the edge of the planting hole. Pull mulch 3 to 6 inches away from the trunk — never pile mulch against the trunk ("mulch volcano"), which traps moisture against the bark, promotes decay, and encourages girdling roots.

Staking: Stake only if the tree cannot stand upright on its own (windy sites, bare-root stock, top-heavy canopy). Use 2-3 stakes outside the root ball, attached with flexible ties (not wire through hose, which can girdle). Remove stakes after 1-2 growing seasons — extended staking prevents the trunk from developing taper and strength.

MEMORY AID:  Tree planting critical rules: Wide hole (2-3× root ball), shallow depth (flare at grade), native backfill, NO mulch volcano, stakes removed after 1-2 years. Remember: "Wide, Shallow, Native, No Volcano, Temporary Stakes."

Trees in urban environments — street trees, parking lot trees, plaza trees — face unique challenges: limited soil volume, compacted soil beneath pavement, restricted rooting space, reflected heat, salt exposure, and mechanical damage. The landscape architect must specify systems that give urban trees adequate rooting conditions:

Soil volume: A shade tree needs 600 to 1,000 cubic feet of quality soil to reach maturity. A typical 4'×4' tree pit in a sidewalk provides only about 50 CF — far too little. Without adequate soil volume, urban trees decline within 7-15 years.

Structural soil: A gap-graded mix of stone aggregate and soil that can be compacted to support pavement loads while maintaining enough pore space for root growth. CU-Structural Soil (developed at Cornell University) uses 80% angular stone and 20% clay loam with hydrogel. Roots grow through the voids between stones.

Suspended pavement: Structural cells (Silva Cells, Stratavault) or concrete structures support the pavement on pillars or decks above uncompacted, high-quality planting soil. This provides the best growing conditions because the soil is never compacted, but it is the most expensive option.

Continuous planting trenches: Connecting individual tree pits into continuous trenches under sidewalks greatly increases shared soil volume. A trench 5' wide and 3' deep running the length of a block can provide 1,000+ CF per tree.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A streetscape project specifies a suspended pavement system for a row of Red Oaks. The system uses structural cells to create a continuous 5-foot-deep planting trench beneath the sidewalk, filled with high-quality loam. Each tree has access to approximately 1,200 CF of uncompacted soil. After 15 years, the trees have canopies spanning 40 feet — comparable to trees in parks — while the sidewalk above remains level and undamaged.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Tree pit: 2-3× root ball width, depth = root ball height, root flare at or above grade. ✔  Backfill with native soil to avoid the bathtub effect; do not amend unless soil is truly unsuitable. ✔  Mulch: 3-4" depth, pulled 3-6" from trunk — never create a mulch volcano. ✔  Remove stakes after 1-2 growing seasons; extended staking weakens trunks. ✔  Urban trees need 600-1,000 CF of soil to reach maturity. ✔  Solutions for urban planting: structural soil, suspended pavement, continuous trenches.

subsections.title: 1. The most common cause of tree failure after planting is:

content.text: A)  Insufficient watering
B)  Planting too deep (root flare buried)
C)  Using the wrong soil amendment
D)  Staking too tightly
Answer: B. Planting too deep buries the root flare, suffocating it and leading to slow decline. The root flare must be at or slightly above grade.

subsections.title: 2. A shade tree in an urban setting needs approximately how much soil volume to reach maturity?

content.text: A)  50-100 cubic feet
B)  200-400 cubic feet
C)  600-1,000 cubic feet
D)  2,000-3,000 cubic feet
Answer: C. Research indicates shade trees need 600-1,000 CF of quality soil. Standard tree pits provide far less, leading to premature decline.

subsections.title: 3. Mulch should be pulled 3-6 inches away from a tree trunk to prevent:

content.text: A)  Root competition with shrubs
B)  Moisture retention against bark that causes decay and girdling roots
C)  Nutrient depletion at the trunk
D)  Insect attraction to the mulch
Answer: B. Mulch piled against the trunk (mulch volcano) traps moisture, promotes bark decay, and encourages girdling roots that can strangle the tree.

Irrigation systems deliver water to landscapes efficiently and reliably. The landscape architect designs the system layout, specifies equipment, and ensures the system meets the project's water management goals. The exam tests your understanding of system components, design principles, and water conservation strategies.

rows: Municipal supply, well, pond, reclaimed water; pressure and flow capacity must be verified
Prevents contaminated irrigation water from flowing back into the potable supply
Required by all plumbing codes; RPZ (reduced pressure zone) or DCVA (double check valve assembly)
Smart controllers use ET data, weather stations, or soil moisture sensors to adjust schedules automatically
Carries water from source to zone valves
Pressurized at all times; PVC Schedule 40 or polyethylene
Controls water flow to each zone
Electric solenoid valves; one per zone; sized for zone flow rate
Carries water from zone valve to heads/emitters
Pressurized only when zone is active; PVC Class 200 or polyethylene
Apply water to small areas in fixed pattern
High precipitation rate (1.5-2.0 in/hr); spacing based on radius; head-to-head coverage
Apply water to large areas in rotating stream
Low precipitation rate (0.5-1.0 in/hr); spacing 40-60' radius
Apply water slowly and directly to root zone
Very low rate; eliminates overspray and runoff; ideal for beds, trees, slopes
Prevents misting (too high) and poor coverage (too low)

content.text: Matched precipitation rates: All heads within a single zone must apply water at the same rate. Mixing spray heads (high rate) and rotors (low rate) in the same zone means sprays will overwater while rotors underwater. Never mix head types in a zone.
Head-to-head coverage: Each sprinkler head's throw should reach the adjacent head. This ensures uniform coverage with no dry spots between heads. Spacing equals the head's effective radius.

Hydrozoning: Group plants with similar water needs on the same irrigation zone. Turf (high water) on one zone, shrub beds (medium) on another, native/drought-tolerant (low or no irrigation) on a separate zone or no zone at all.

Pipe sizing: Pipe diameter must accommodate the flow rate (GPM) of the zone without exceeding maximum velocity — typically 5 feet per second. Exceeding this velocity causes water hammer (pressure surges when valves close) and excessive friction loss.

EXAM TIP:  Never mix spray heads and rotors in the same zone — this is one of the most common exam questions about irrigation design. The reason is matched precipitation rates: spray heads apply 1.5-2.0 in/hr while rotors apply 0.5-1.0 in/hr. Mixing them in one zone makes uniform watering impossible.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Every irrigation system needs a backflow preventer to protect the potable water supply. ✔  Smart controllers adjust irrigation schedules based on weather, ET, or soil moisture data. ✔  Never mix spray heads and rotors in the same zone — their precipitation rates are incompatible. ✔  Head-to-head coverage: each head's throw reaches the adjacent head for uniform distribution. ✔  Hydrozoning groups plants by water need on separate irrigation zones. ✔  Maximum pipe velocity: 5 fps to prevent water hammer and excessive friction loss.

subsections.title: 1. Mixing spray heads and rotors in the same irrigation zone will cause:

content.text: A)  Excessive water pressure
B)  Uneven water distribution due to different precipitation rates
C)  Backflow contamination
D)  Controller malfunction
Answer: B. Spray heads apply water at 1.5-2.0 in/hr while rotors apply at 0.5-1.0 in/hr. Mixing them means areas served by sprays get 2-3× more water than areas served by rotors.

subsections.title: 2. The purpose of a backflow preventer in an irrigation system is to:

content.text: A)  Reduce water pressure to operating levels
B)  Prevent contaminated irrigation water from entering the potable supply
C)  Filter debris from the water supply
D)  Regulate flow to each zone

Answer: B. Backflow preventers are required by plumbing codes to prevent potentially contaminated irrigation water (fertilizer, pesticides, soil bacteria) from siphoning back into the drinking water supply.
A)  Every sprinkler head is the same brand
B)  Each head's throw reaches the next adjacent head
C)  Heads are placed at the same height
D)  All heads operate simultaneously
Answer: B. Head-to-head coverage spaces heads so that each sprinkler's throw reaches the adjacent head, eliminating dry spots and ensuring uniform water distribution.

Site lighting serves safety, security, wayfinding, and aesthetic purposes. The landscape architect specifies fixture types, mounting heights, lamp sources, and distribution patterns to create an effective, energy-efficient, and dark-sky-compliant lighting design.

rows: Total light output from a source
Brightness perceived by the human eye
How accurately colors appear under the light
Light output per watt of electricity

content.text: Different areas of a site require different fixture types and light levels:

Pedestrian-scale fixtures (10-14' mounting height): Illuminate walkways, plazas, and seating areas. Create a comfortable, human-scaled atmosphere. Typically 1-2 foot-candles on walkways, 2-5 fc in plazas. Use warm color temperatures (2700-3000K) for inviting atmosphere.

Area/roadway fixtures (20-30' mounting height): Illuminate parking lots, drives, and large open areas. Higher output, wider distribution. Typically 1-5 fc for parking, 0.5-1 fc for roadways. Neutral to cool color temperatures acceptable.

Bollard lights (30-42" height): Mark path edges, define boundaries, and provide low-level ambient light. NOT intended as primary pathway illumination — they light the ground immediately adjacent, not a wide path. Often supplemented with pole-mounted fixtures.
Accent/landscape lights: Uplights for trees and architecture, in-grade lights for columns and walls, underwater lights for fountains. Used for drama and visual interest, not safety or security.
The International Dark-Sky Association (IDA) promotes responsible outdoor lighting to reduce light pollution, conserve energy, and protect nocturnal ecosystems. Dark-sky-compliant fixtures are:
•  Full cutoff — no light emitted above the horizontal plane (0° uplight)
•  Shielded — lamp is recessed within the fixture housing so it is not directly visible
•  Warm color temperature — 3000K or less (reduces blue-light sky glow)
•  Properly aimed — directed only where light is needed, minimizing spill onto adjacent properties

EXAM TIP:  Dark sky compliance = full cutoff fixtures (no uplight) + warm color temperature (≤3000K) + minimized light trespass. If the exam asks how to reduce light pollution, these are the key strategies.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Illuminance (foot-candles) measures light arriving at a surface; luminance measures perceived brightness. ✔  Pedestrian lighting: 10-14' height, 1-2 fc, warm (2700-3000K). Parking: 20-30' height, 1-5 fc. ✔  Bollard lights mark edges but are not primary path illumination. ✔  Dark sky compliance: full cutoff fixtures, no uplight, ≤3000K color temperature, minimize light trespass. ✔  CRI of 80+ ensures accurate color rendering; 90+ is excellent.

subsections.title: 1. A full cutoff fixture is important for dark sky compliance because:

content.text: A)  It increases light output efficiency
B)  It emits no light above the horizontal plane, reducing sky glow
C)  It is required by the building code in all jurisdictions
D)  It produces warmer color temperatures
Answer: B. Full cutoff fixtures direct all light downward (no light above 90°), which is the primary strategy for reducing sky glow and light pollution.

subsections.title: 2. The recommended maximum color temperature for dark-sky-compliant outdoor lighting is:

content.text: Answer: B. IDA recommends 3000K or less for outdoor lighting. Warmer temperatures produce less blue light, which contributes disproportionately to sky glow and disrupts nocturnal wildlife.

Specifications are the written companion to construction drawings. While drawings show where things go and how they are dimensioned, specifications describe the quality of materials, the standards they must meet, the methods of installation, and the procedures for testing and acceptance. Together, drawings and specifications form the technical core of the contract documents.

A drawing can show a retaining wall as 4 feet tall with specific dimensions, but it cannot convey the compressive strength of the concrete, the grade of reinforcing steel, the cure time, the acceptable finish quality, the backfill compaction requirement, or the warranty period. Specifications fill this gap. Without specifications, the contractor can use the cheapest materials and methods that technically satisfy the drawing — which may not meet the designer's intent for quality and durability.

The Construction Specifications Institute (CSI) MasterFormat is the standard organizing framework for construction specifications in North America. It divides all construction work into 50 divisions. Landscape architects work most frequently with these divisions:

rows: 31 10 00 Site Clearing, 31 20 00 Earth Moving, 31 25 00 Erosion Control

content.text: MEMORY AID:  Key CSI divisions for landscape architecture: 31-32-33. Division 31 = Earthwork (what you move). Division 32 = Exterior Improvements (what you build and plant on the surface). Division 33 = Utilities (what goes underground). Know these three division numbers.
Each specification section follows a standardized three-part format established by CSI:

Part 1 — General: Defines the scope of the section, references applicable standards, lists required submittals, establishes quality assurance requirements, and describes delivery, storage, and handling requirements. This part answers: "What is covered, what standards apply, and what must the contractor submit before starting work?"

Part 2 — Products: Specifies the materials, products, and equipment to be used. Names manufacturers (in proprietary specs), describes material properties, defines fabrication requirements, and sets finish standards. This part answers: "What materials and products must the contractor use?"

Part 3 — Execution: Describes how the work is to be performed — surface preparation, installation methods, tolerances, field quality control (testing and inspection), cleaning, and protection of completed work. This part answers: "How must the contractor install it?"

rows: Names specific products by manufacturer and model
Precise control over quality, appearance, and performance
Limits competition; may increase cost; potential sole-source issues on public projects
States required performance outcomes without naming products
Encourages innovation and competition; contractor selects means
Harder to enforce; requires measurable performance criteria; more review effort
References published standards (ASTM, ANSI, ACI, AWS)
Requires specifier to understand the referenced standard's requirements
Names a product as the basis, allows substitutions of equal quality
"Equal" is subjective; requires careful review of substitution requests

content.text: EXAM TIP:  Public projects often require open competition and may not allow proprietary (sole-source) specifications. Performance and "or equal" specifications are preferred for public work to allow multiple manufacturers to bid, keeping costs competitive.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Specifications describe quality, materials, and methods; drawings show geometry and dimensions. ✔  CSI MasterFormat divisions 31 (Earthwork), 32 (Exterior Improvements), and 33 (Utilities) are most relevant to landscape architecture. ✔  Three-part format: Part 1 (General — scope, submittals), Part 2 (Products — materials), Part 3 (Execution — installation methods). ✔  Prescriptive specs name specific products; performance specs set outcomes; reference standards cite published standards. ✔  Public projects typically require open competition — avoid sole-source proprietary specifications.
1. A specification that states "Concrete shall conform to ASTM C94 with minimum 28-day compressive strength of 4,000 psi" is an example of a:
A)  Prescriptive specification
B)  Performance specification
C)  Reference standard specification
D)  Proprietary specification
Answer: C. This specification references a published ASTM standard and sets measurable criteria based on that standard — making it a reference standard specification.

subsections.title: 2. In the CSI three-part specification format, Part 2 addresses:

content.text: A)  Scope, submittals, and quality assurance
B)  Materials, manufacturers, and products
C)  Installation methods and field quality control
D)  Contract terms and conditions
Answer: B. Part 2 (Products) specifies the materials, manufacturers, products, fabrication, and finish standards.

subsections.title: 3. Landscape planting specifications are organized under CSI MasterFormat Division:

content.text: Answer: C. Division 32 (Exterior Improvements) includes Section 32 90 00 Planting, along with paving, irrigation, and other site improvements.

Bidding is the process by which a contractor is selected to build the project. The landscape architect plays a critical role in the bidding process — preparing bid documents, answering bidder questions, issuing addenda, evaluating bids, and recommending award. Understanding the bidding sequence and the documents involved is essential for both professional practice and the exam.
The bidding process follows a defined sequence:

1. Advertisement / Invitation to Bid (ITB): Public projects must be publicly advertised (newspaper, online portals). Private projects may use an invited list of pre-qualified contractors. The advertisement states the project scope, bid due date, and where to obtain documents.

2. Pre-bid conference: An optional (sometimes mandatory) meeting where prospective bidders visit the site, ask questions, and clarify the scope. The LA records questions and distributes answers to all bidders via an addendum.

3. Bidder questions and addenda: During the bidding period, contractors submit written questions (Requests for Information). The LA responds by issuing addenda — written documents that modify, clarify, or supplement the bid documents. Addenda are sent to all plan holders to ensure a level playing field. All bidders must acknowledge receipt of all addenda in their bids.

4. Bid submission and opening: Bids are submitted sealed by the deadline. Public project bids are opened publicly and read aloud. Private project bids may be opened privately. Late bids are typically rejected.

5. Bid evaluation: The LA reviews bids for responsiveness (did the bidder include everything required?) and the owner evaluates responsibility (is the bidder qualified and capable?). The lowest responsive, responsible bidder typically wins public projects. Private owners may consider factors beyond price.
6. Notice of Award: Formal notification to the selected contractor that they have been awarded the contract.
7. Contract execution: The owner and contractor sign the agreement. The contractor provides bonds (performance and payment) and insurance certificates.

8. Notice to Proceed (NTP): The owner's authorization for the contractor to begin work. The NTP establishes the official start date and begins the contract time (calendar days or working days to substantial completion).

MEMORY AID:  Bidding sequence: A-P-A-B-E-N-C-N. Advertise → Pre-bid conference → Addenda → Bid opening → Evaluation → Notice of Award → Contract execution → Notice to Proceed. The contract time starts at NTP, not at award.

The bid documents include everything needed for contractors to prepare a bid: drawings, specifications, invitation to bid, bid form, instructions to bidders, and any addenda. After the contract is awarded, the bid documents become part of the contract documents, which also include:
•  Owner-contractor agreement (AIA A101 or equivalent)
•  General conditions (AIA A201 — the standard industry document defining rights and responsibilities)
•  Supplementary conditions (project-specific modifications)
•  Performance bond — guarantees the contractor will complete the work
•  Payment bond — guarantees the contractor will pay subcontractors and suppliers
•  Insurance certificates — liability, workers' compensation, vehicle coverage

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Public projects require public advertisement; private projects may use invited bidders. ✔  Addenda modify bid documents during bidding — they are distributed to ALL plan holders. ✔  All bidders must acknowledge all addenda in their bid. ✔  Lowest responsive, responsible bidder typically wins public projects. ✔  Notice to Proceed (NTP) starts the contract time — not the notice of award. ✔  Performance bond guarantees completion; payment bond guarantees payment to subs and suppliers.
1. During bidding, the landscape architect discovers an error on the drawings. The correction should be communicated through:
A)  A verbal notification at the pre-bid conference
B)  An addendum issued to all plan holders
C)  An email to the lowest bidder only
D)  A change order
Answer: B. Errors or changes during bidding must be communicated through written addenda distributed to all plan holders to maintain a fair bidding process.

subsections.title: 2. The contract time (days to substantial completion) begins at:

content.text: A)  The date of the bid opening
B)  The date of the notice of award
C)  The date of the notice to proceed
D)  The date of the first site observation
Answer: C. The Notice to Proceed (NTP) is the owner's formal authorization to begin work and establishes the start of the contract time.
A)  The owner against contractor default
B)  Subcontractors and suppliers against non-payment by the contractor
C)  The landscape architect against professional liability
D)  The contractor against owner non-payment
Answer: B. A payment bond guarantees that the contractor will pay subcontractors and material suppliers, protecting them from financial loss.

Construction administration (CA) is the landscape architect's role during the construction phase. CA is not construction management — the LA does not direct the contractor's work, control the schedule, or supervise workers. Instead, the LA acts as the owner's representative to ensure the project is built in general conformance with the contract documents. Understanding the boundaries of this role is critical for both practice and the exam.

rows: Observe work for general conformance with design intent
Review submittals for conformance with design intent
Approve means, methods, or safety procedures
Process pay applications and recommend payment
Issue certificates of substantial and final completion
Reject work that does not conform to contract documents

content.text: EXAM TIP:  The distinction between "observation" and "inspection" is critical. The LA OBSERVES work for general conformance with design intent. "Inspection" implies a guarantee that the work meets every requirement — a liability trap. If the exam uses "inspection," it is often the wrong answer.

Submittals are documents the contractor provides to the LA for review before materials are fabricated or delivered. They verify that the contractor intends to use materials and products that conform to the specifications. Types of submittals include:

Shop drawings: Detailed drawings prepared by the contractor or manufacturer showing fabrication and installation details for custom items — metal railings, custom benches, precast elements, stone patterns. The LA reviews shop drawings for conformance with design intent, not for structural adequacy or dimensional accuracy (that is the contractor's responsibility).
Product data: Manufacturer's literature, cut sheets, technical specifications, and test reports for specified products — pavers, fixtures, irrigation equipment, furnishings.
Samples: Physical samples of materials — mortar color, paver finish, stone sample, mulch type, stain color — for the LA to review for color, texture, and quality.
Review actions:
•  Approved — submittal conforms; proceed with fabrication/delivery
•  Approved as Noted — submittal conforms with minor corrections noted; proceed with noted changes
•  Revise and Resubmit — submittal has significant issues; correct and resubmit before proceeding
•  Rejected — submittal does not conform; completely redo and resubmit

Request for Information (RFI): A written question from the contractor seeking clarification of the contract documents. RFIs should not change scope, cost, or time — they clarify what is already in the documents. The LA must respond in writing, promptly, and the response becomes part of the project record. If answering an RFI reveals a need for design changes, a change order is required.

Change Order: A formal modification to the contract that changes the scope, cost, or time. Change orders require written description, cost justification, schedule impact analysis, and owner approval. The LA reviews the contractor's pricing and makes a recommendation, but the owner makes the final decision on approval.

Construction Change Directive (CCD): When the owner needs work to proceed before a change order is negotiated, a CCD directs the contractor to proceed with the change. The cost and time impacts are negotiated afterward. CCDs are used when delay would be more costly than proceeding without agreed pricing.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  During excavation, the contractor discovers an unmarked utility that conflicts with the proposed retaining wall footing. The contractor submits an RFI asking how to proceed. The LA evaluates the conflict and determines the wall must be shifted 3 feet, changing the grading and adjacent paving layout. Because this changes the scope, the LA prepares a change order describing the revised work, the contractor prices the change ($12,000 additional), and the owner approves the change order. The LA documents everything in writing.
The contractor submits periodic pay applications (typically monthly) requesting payment for work completed. The process:
•  Contractor submits Application for Payment (AIA G702/G703) listing completed quantities for each bid item
•  LA reviews the application against observed progress and recommends payment
•  Owner withholds retainage — typically 5-10% of each payment — as security against defects and incomplete work
•  Retainage is released at final completion after all punch list items, warranties, and lien releases are received

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  The LA OBSERVES (not inspects) work for general conformance with design intent. ✔  The LA does not direct workers, control schedules, approve means/methods, or guarantee compliance. ✔  Submittal review actions: Approved, Approved as Noted, Revise and Resubmit, Rejected. ✔  The LA reviews submittals for design intent — NOT for structural adequacy or dimensional accuracy. ✔  RFIs clarify the documents; change orders modify scope/cost/time; CCDs direct work before negotiation. ✔  Retainage (5-10%) is withheld from each payment and released at final completion.

subsections.title: 1. During construction, the landscape architect's primary role is to:

content.text: A)  Manage the contractor's schedule and supervise workers
B)  Observe work for general conformance with the contract documents
C)  Inspect every aspect of construction and certify compliance
D)  Direct the contractor's means and methods of construction
Answer: B. The LA observes work for general conformance with design intent. The LA does not manage schedules, supervise workers, or inspect (which implies a guarantee of compliance).

subsections.title: 2. A contractor submits a shop drawing for a custom metal railing. The LA's review should verify:

content.text: A)  Structural calculations and load capacity
B)  Conformance with the design intent shown in the contract documents
C)  The contractor's welding procedures and safety protocols
D)  The manufacturer's pricing and delivery schedule
Answer: B. The LA reviews shop drawings for conformance with design intent. Structural adequacy is the contractor/engineer's responsibility; means and methods are the contractor's responsibility.
A)  Substantial completion
B)  Final completion
C)  60 days after the last payment application
D)  The end of the warranty period
Answer: B. Retainage is released at final completion — after all punch list items are resolved, closeout documents submitted, and lien releases received.

Project closeout is the final phase of construction administration. It encompasses the transition from active construction to a completed, usable project. Understanding the distinction between substantial completion and final completion — and the procedures and documents associated with each — is heavily tested on the exam.

Substantial completion is the point at which the project is sufficiently complete that the owner can use it for its intended purpose, even though minor items remain to be finished or corrected. It is a critical contractual milestone because:
•  The owner takes possession and begins using the project
•  The warranty period begins (typically 1 year for construction, 1-2 years for plant material)
•  Risk of loss transfers from contractor to owner
•  Liquidated damages (if applicable) stop accruing
•  The LA issues a Certificate of Substantial Completion

Punch list: At the substantial completion walkthrough, the LA and owner identify remaining items that need to be completed or corrected. The punch list is a written document listing every item, its location, and the required action. The contractor must complete all punch list items within the time specified (typically 30-60 days). The LA re-inspects to verify completion.

Final completion occurs when all punch list items are resolved, all closeout documents have been submitted and accepted, and the contractor has fulfilled every obligation under the contract. At final completion:
•  Retainage is released (final payment to contractor)
•  Owner executes final acceptance
•  All closeout documents have been received and accepted

rows: Show actual construction — dimensions, elevations, locations as built, including all field changes
Contractor (marked-up set); LA may prepare final clean drawings
Instructions for operating and maintaining systems (irrigation, lighting, equipment)
Written commitments on material and workmanship quality for specified periods
Certification that all subcontractors and suppliers have been paid in full
Attic stock of pavers, replacement parts, spare filters, etc.
On-site training for owner's maintenance staff on irrigation systems, lighting controls, etc.

content.text: MEMORY AID:  Closeout documents: AOWLS + T. As-builts, O&M manuals, Warranties, Lien releases, Spare parts, Training. The contractor owes you AOWLS and Training before getting final payment.
The warranty period begins at substantial completion — NOT at final completion. Standard warranty periods:
•  General construction: 1 year from substantial completion
•  Plant material: 1-2 years from substantial completion (varies by specification)
•  Plant replacement guarantee typically requires one full growing season
•  Extended warranties for specific items (roofing, waterproofing, certain equipment) may exceed 1 year

EXAM TIP:  The warranty period starts at substantial completion, not final completion. This is a frequently tested distinction. If the exam asks when the warranty clock starts, the answer is substantial completion.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Substantial completion: project usable for intended purpose; warranty begins; risk transfers to owner. ✔  Punch list identifies items to complete/correct; created at the substantial completion walkthrough. ✔  Final completion: all punch list items resolved, all closeout documents submitted, retainage released. ✔  Closeout documents: as-builts, O&M manuals, warranties, lien releases, spare parts, training. ✔  Warranty period starts at SUBSTANTIAL completion, not final completion. ✔  Standard construction warranty: 1 year; plant material: 1-2 years.

subsections.title: 1. The warranty period for construction work typically begins at:

content.text: A)  Notice to proceed
B)  50% completion
C)  Substantial completion
D)  Final completion
Answer: C. Warranties begin at substantial completion — the point when the owner can use the project for its intended purpose.

subsections.title: 2. Retainage is released to the contractor at:

content.text: A)  Substantial completion
B)  Final completion
C)  The end of the warranty period
D)  Each monthly payment application
Answer: B. Retainage is withheld throughout construction and released at final completion after all punch list items and closeout documents are resolved.
A)  The original design intent
B)  Actual field conditions as constructed, including all changes
C)  The contractor's proposed construction method
D)  The landscape architect's design alternatives
Answer: B. As-built (record) drawings document what was actually constructed, including field changes, dimensional variations, and RFI/change order modifications.

s3_book.title: Chapter 11: Comprehensive Review and Exam Strategy

rows: Grading plans, pavement details, walls, steps, planting details, irrigation, lighting
CSI MasterFormat, 3-part format, spec types, bidding sequence, contract documents
Submittals, observation vs. inspection, RFIs, change orders, closeout, warranty

content.text: •  Concrete control joint spacing (10-12' max, square panels)
•  Step formula: 2R + T = 26"
•  Retaining wall drainage (gravel, perforated pipe, filter fabric, weep holes)
•  Tree planting: root flare at grade, no mulch volcano, native backfill
•  Observation vs. inspection — the LA observes, never inspects
•  Submittal review actions (Approved, Approved as Noted, Revise and Resubmit, Rejected)
•  CSI MasterFormat divisions 31, 32, 33
•  Three-part specification format (General, Products, Execution)
•  Bidding sequence (advertise → pre-bid → addenda → bid opening → evaluate → award → NTP)
•  Substantial completion vs. final completion; warranty starts at substantial
•  Retainage released at final completion
•  Change orders vs. RFIs vs. Construction Change Directives
•  ADA ramp requirements (1:12, 30' max, 5'×5' landings)
•  Backflow prevention in irrigation systems
•  Dark sky compliance (full cutoff, ≤3000K)
•  You have 90 questions in 3 hours — 2 minutes per question.
•  Hotspot questions: read the prompt carefully to understand what you are clicking on.
•  Drag-and-drop questions: arrange items in the correct sequence (e.g., bidding steps, pavement layers).
•  Select-all questions: every option must be evaluated independently; one wrong selection = zero credit.
•  Flag uncertain questions and return to them — do not spend 4 minutes on one question.
•  For construction detail questions, trace the layers from bottom to top systematically.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a formal garden. Which of the following design principles is MOST characteristic of formal design?

choices.text: Asymmetrical balance with irregular planting patterns
Symmetrical balance with strong axial organization
Random placement of materials and plantings
Exclusive use of native meadow plantings

s3_exam.explanation: Formal gardens are characterized by symmetry, axial organization, and geometric forms.

s3_exam.question: The principle of "unity" in landscape design is BEST achieved by:

choices.text: Using as many different materials and plant species as possible
Making each area of the site completely different from the others
Using only one plant species throughout the entire site
Repeating design elements such as materials, forms, colors, and textures to create visual coherence

s3_exam.explanation: Unity is achieved through repetition and consistency of design elements throughout the site.

s3_exam.question: In design, the concept of "scale" refers to:

choices.text: The perceived size of elements in relation to the human body and surrounding context
The weight of construction materials
The cost of the project
The number of elements in a design

s3_exam.explanation: Scale refers to the perceived size of elements relative to the human body and surrounding context.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect uses a sequence of spaces that transition from large and open to small and enclosed. This design technique creates:

choices.text: Spatial monotony
Confusion for the user
Uniformity across the site
A sense of spatial compression and release that enhances the experience of movement through the landscape

s3_exam.explanation: Alternating spatial compression and release creates a dynamic experience of movement through landscape.

s3_exam.question: The "genius loci" of a site refers to:

choices.text: The site's zoning classification
The construction budget for the project
The unique spirit, character, or sense of place inherent to a specific location
The IQ of the designer

s3_exam.explanation: Genius loci refers to the unique spirit or character of a place.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a pedestrian plaza. Which of the following dimensions would provide the MOST comfortable width for a primary pedestrian walkway?

choices.text: 3 feet
2 feet
5 feet
10 feet or wider

s3_exam.explanation: Primary pedestrian walkways in plazas should be 10 feet or wider to accommodate multiple users and ADA requirements.

s3_exam.question: When designing a vehicular drop-off area at a public building entrance, the landscape architect should ensure:

choices.text: Vehicles must back up to exit the drop-off
The drop-off allows one-way circulation with adequate queuing and a clear connection to the building entrance
The drop-off is located as far from the building entrance as possible
The drop-off eliminates all pedestrian crossings

s3_exam.explanation: Drop-offs should allow one-way flow with queuing space and a clear pedestrian connection to the entrance.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing an amphitheater. The seating area should be oriented so that:

choices.text: The audience faces directly into the afternoon sun
The stage is at the highest point and the audience sits below
Sound is directed away from the audience
The audience faces north or northeast to minimize sun glare during evening performances

s3_exam.explanation: Orienting the audience north or northeast minimizes sun glare during afternoon and evening events.

s3_exam.question: When designing a children's play area within a public park, which of the following is the MOST important consideration?

choices.text: Providing clear sight lines for caregiver supervision, age-appropriate equipment zones, and appropriate safety surfacing
Locating the play area adjacent to a major road for visibility
Using the tallest available equipment to maximize play value
Eliminating all shade to ensure maximum sun exposure

s3_exam.explanation: Clear sight lines for supervision, age-appropriate zones, and safety surfacing are the most critical safety considerations.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a parking lot for 200 vehicles. Which of the following strategies BEST reduces the environmental impact of the parking area?

choices.text: Using conventional asphalt with no landscaping
Maximizing the asphalt area to eliminate all landscaping maintenance
Painting the asphalt a lighter color
Incorporating bioswales, shade trees, permeable paving, and landscape islands to reduce heat island effect and manage stormwater

s3_exam.explanation: Bioswales, shade trees, permeable paving, and landscape islands reduce environmental impact through stormwater management and heat island mitigation.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is selecting trees for a streetscape design. Which of the following characteristics is MOST important for street tree selection?

choices.text: The tree should produce large fruit for foraging
The tree should be the fastest-growing species available
The tree should have a form and root structure compatible with the urban environment, including tolerance for compacted soils, limited root space, and urban heat
The tree should require frequent pruning to maintain shape

s3_exam.explanation: Street trees must tolerate urban conditions including compacted soils, limited root space, heat, and pollution.

s3_exam.question: In a planting design, "layering" refers to:

choices.text: Applying multiple coats of mulch
Planting all species at the same height
Stacking soil amendments in the planting bed
Arranging plants in vertical layers (canopy, understory, shrub, groundcover) to create spatial complexity and ecological function

s3_exam.explanation: Layering creates vertical plant structure from canopy to groundcover for spatial and ecological complexity.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a rain garden. Which of the following plant characteristics is MOST important for plant selection?

choices.text: Plants that require consistently dry conditions
Plants with deep tap roots that cannot spread
Plants that tolerate both periodic inundation and dry periods
Plants that require daily irrigation

s3_exam.explanation: Rain garden plants must tolerate alternating wet and dry conditions.

s3_exam.question: When designing a foundation planting for a building, the landscape architect should consider:

choices.text: Using the tallest available trees directly against the building wall
Mature plant size, building scale, maintenance access, window locations, and structural clearances
Only the appearance of plants at the time of installation
Placing all shrubs at uniform spacing regardless of species

s3_exam.explanation: Foundation plantings must account for mature size, building scale, maintenance access, and clearances.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect specifies a mix of deciduous and evergreen plants in a design. Which of the following is the PRIMARY design benefit of this approach?

choices.text: It reduces the total number of plants needed
It provides year-round visual interest, with seasonal variety from deciduous plants and winter structure from evergreens
It eliminates the need for maintenance
It ensures all plants flower at the same time

s3_exam.explanation: Mixing deciduous and evergreen plants provides seasonal variety and year-round structure.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a lawn area for passive recreation. Which slope range is MOST appropriate for comfortable use?

choices.text: Greater than 33%

s3_exam.explanation: Slopes of 0.5% to 3% provide adequate drainage while remaining comfortable for passive recreation.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect designs a berm to screen a parking lot from an adjacent residential area. The berm should be designed with:

choices.text: Slopes no steeper than 3:1 (horizontal to vertical) for mowable turf and adequate height to screen views
Vertical sides for maximum screening efficiency
A flat top at least 50 feet wide
Slopes steeper than 1:1 to minimize the footprint

s3_exam.explanation: Berms with mowable turf should have slopes no steeper than 3:1 for maintenance and stability.

s3_exam.question: When designing a terrace on a hillside site, the landscape architect should consider:

choices.text: Placing all retaining walls at maximum allowable height to minimize the number of walls
Using a series of walls with appropriate heights, incorporating proper drainage behind walls, and creating usable spaces between terraces
Eliminating all retaining walls and allowing the slope to remain natural
Using only gravity walls regardless of the height requirement

s3_exam.explanation: Terracing should use appropriately sized walls with drainage and create usable spaces between terraces.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is selecting paving materials for a public plaza in a climate with freeze-thaw cycles. Which of the following is the MOST important material property to consider?

choices.text: Color
Cost per square foot
Absorption rate and freeze-thaw resistance
Country of origin

s3_exam.explanation: In freeze-thaw climates, low absorption and freeze-thaw resistance prevent material deterioration.

s3_exam.question: Which of the following wall types is MOST appropriate for a retaining wall with a height of 6 feet or more?

choices.text: Dry-stacked stone wall
Engineered reinforced concrete or mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) wall
Timber landscape wall
Stacked railroad ties

s3_exam.explanation: Walls 6 feet or taller require engineered solutions like reinforced concrete or MSE for structural safety.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect specifies unit pavers for a pedestrian area. The PRIMARY advantage of unit pavers over poured-in-place concrete is:

choices.text: Unit pavers allow for easier repair of individual sections, accommodate minor ground movement, and can be permeable
Unit pavers are always less expensive
Unit pavers never require maintenance
Unit pavers are structurally stronger than concrete

s3_exam.explanation: Unit pavers allow individual repair, accommodate ground movement, and can be installed as permeable systems.

s3_exam.question: When selecting wood for an outdoor bench, the landscape architect should specify:

choices.text: Untreated pine for its low cost
Interior-grade plywood
Naturally durable or sustainably sourced species (e.g., black locust, FSC-certified ipe) appropriate for exterior exposure
Any wood species regardless of durability

s3_exam.explanation: Naturally durable or sustainably sourced exterior-grade wood is appropriate for outdoor furniture.

s3_exam.question: According to ADA guidelines, an accessible ramp with a rise greater than 6 inches requires:

choices.text: Handrails on both sides
Handrails on one side only
No handrails if the ramp is less than 30 feet long
Handrails only at the top landing

s3_exam.explanation: ADA requires handrails on both sides of ramps with a rise greater than 6 inches.

s3_exam.question: Universal design differs from ADA compliance in that:

choices.text: Universal design aims to create environments usable by all people to the greatest extent possible, going beyond minimum code requirements
Universal design only applies to public buildings
Universal design has lower standards than ADA
Universal design applies only to interior spaces

s3_exam.explanation: Universal design creates environments usable by all people, going beyond minimum ADA compliance.

s3_exam.question: An accessible route must have a minimum clear width of:

choices.text: 24 inches
48 inches
60 inches
36 inches

s3_exam.explanation: ADA requires a minimum clear width of 36 inches for accessible routes.

s3_exam.question: At an accessible parking space, an access aisle must be provided. The access aisle must be:

choices.text: At least 60 inches wide and marked to discourage parking
The same width as the parking space
Located on the driver's side only
Eliminated if the parking space is wider than standard

s3_exam.explanation: Access aisles must be at least 60 inches wide and marked to prevent parking.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a reflecting pool for a civic plaza. The MOST important design consideration for public safety is:

choices.text: Making the pool as deep as possible for visual impact
Allowing unrestricted public access to the deepest areas
Limiting water depth, providing visible edges, and ensuring proper water treatment to prevent health hazards
Using untreated water for ecological purposes

s3_exam.explanation: Public water features must limit depth, define edges, and maintain water quality for safety.

s3_exam.question: When designing an irrigation system for a public landscape, the landscape architect should specify:

choices.text: A single zone for the entire site to simplify installation
Overhead spray irrigation for all planting areas including groundcovers
Manual watering only to reduce costs
Separate zones based on plant water requirements, sun exposure, and soil conditions (hydrozoning)

s3_exam.explanation: Hydrozoning groups plants with similar water needs into separate irrigation zones for efficiency.

s3_exam.question: When designing exterior lighting for a pedestrian pathway, the landscape architect should consider:

choices.text: Using the brightest fixtures available at the closest spacing
Eliminating all lighting to reduce energy consumption
Providing adequate and uniform illumination levels for safety while minimizing light pollution and glare
Directing all light fixtures upward for decorative effect

s3_exam.explanation: Pathway lighting should provide adequate, uniform illumination while minimizing pollution and glare.

s3_exam.question: Bollard lighting is MOST appropriate for:

choices.text: Providing low-level pathway lighting and defining edges
Illuminating large parking areas
Floodlighting building facades
Lighting athletic fields

s3_exam.explanation: Bollard lights provide low-level illumination appropriate for pathways and edge definition.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a green roof for a commercial building. Which of the following is a PRIMARY benefit of a green roof?

choices.text: It eliminates the need for structural reinforcement of the roof
It is always less expensive than a conventional roof
It requires no maintenance
It reduces stormwater runoff, mitigates heat island effect, and provides habitat

s3_exam.explanation: Green roofs reduce stormwater runoff, mitigate heat island effect, and provide habitat value.

s3_exam.question: Low Impact Development (LID) strategies include which of the following?

choices.text: Maximizing impervious surfaces and piping all stormwater to the nearest stream
Using only conventional curb and gutter stormwater systems
Bioretention cells, permeable paving, green roofs, and rainwater harvesting
Eliminating all vegetation from the site

s3_exam.explanation: LID strategies include bioretention, permeable paving, green roofs, and rainwater harvesting.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is selecting plants for a xeriscape design. Which of the following is the MOST important criterion?

choices.text: Selecting plants that require supplemental irrigation throughout their lifespan
Selecting only cacti and succulents regardless of the climate
Selecting drought-tolerant plants adapted to the local climate that minimize water use once established
Selecting tropical species for their visual appeal

s3_exam.explanation: Xeriscape designs prioritize drought-tolerant, climate-adapted plants that minimize water use once established.

s3_exam.question: A bioswale is designed to:

choices.text: Store large volumes of water permanently
Increase the velocity of stormwater runoff
Replace all underground stormwater piping on a site
Convey and filter stormwater runoff through vegetation and engineered soil media

s3_exam.explanation: Bioswales convey and filter stormwater through vegetation and engineered soil media.

s3_exam.question: When designing a detention basin for a development, the landscape architect should ensure:

choices.text: The basin has appropriate side slopes for safety and maintenance, an outlet structure to control discharge, and an emergency overflow
The basin has vertical concrete walls for maximum capacity
The basin is designed to hold water permanently
The basin is fenced off with no public access

s3_exam.explanation: Detention basins need safe side slopes, outlet structures, and emergency overflows.

s3_exam.question: A concept plan is typically presented during which phase of the design process?

choices.text: Construction documentation
Schematic design
Bidding and negotiation
Construction administration

s3_exam.explanation: Concept plans are typically presented during schematic design.

s3_exam.question: A section drawing is MOST useful for communicating:

choices.text: Vertical relationships, elevation changes, spatial proportions, and the relationship between ground plane and vertical elements
The plan-view layout of the site
Legal property boundaries
Underground utility locations only

s3_exam.explanation: Section drawings communicate vertical relationships, elevation changes, and spatial proportions.

s3_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a pergola for a garden. The PRIMARY function of a pergola is to:

choices.text: Provide a fully waterproof shelter
Define space, provide filtered shade, and support climbing plants
Serve as a permanent storage structure
Block all views from the garden

s3_exam.explanation: Pergolas define space, provide filtered shade, and support climbing plants without full weather protection.

s3_exam.question: When designing a freestanding seat wall, the MOST comfortable seat height for adults is approximately:

choices.text: 12 inches
18 inches
30 inches
42 inches

s3_exam.explanation: Approximately 18 inches is the most comfortable seat wall height for adults.

s3_exam.question: During design development, the landscape architect refines the approved schematic design. Which of the following is typically accomplished during this phase?

choices.text: The landscape architect conducts the initial site inventory and analysis
The landscape architect refines spatial relationships, selects specific materials and furnishings, and develops detailed design solutions
The landscape architect develops the final construction documents ready for bidding
The landscape architect administers the construction contract

s3_exam.explanation: Design development refines spatial relationships, selects specific materials, and develops detailed solutions.

content.text: Aligned to the CLARB Exam Blueprint (Effective December 2023)
70 Scored Items  |  Computer-Based  |  MC + Select All + Drag & Drop + Hotspot  |  3 Hours

LARE Section 4 is the most quantitative section of the exam. It tests your ability to read and manipulate contour lines, calculate slopes, design grading plans, size drainage structures, and apply stormwater management principles. Many questions require mathematical calculations — slope percentages, cut/fill volumes, runoff calculations, and pipe sizing.

The exam uses all four question types: multiple choice, select all that apply, drag and drop, and hotspot. Hotspot questions may ask you to place contour lines, locate drainage structures, or identify high/low points on a grading plan.
The largest domain. You must be fluent in reading and drawing contours, calculating slopes, grading surfaces and structures, and understanding earthwork calculations.
•  Contour lines connect points of equal elevation above a datum (typically MSL)
•  Contour interval = vertical distance between adjacent contour lines (1', 2', 5', 10')
•  Index contours: every 5th contour, drawn heavier and labeled with elevation
•  Contour rules:
–  Contours never cross (except overhanging cliffs, not on exam)
–  Contours never split or branch
–  Contours always close on themselves (may close beyond map edge)
–  Closely spaced contours = steep slope; widely spaced = gentle slope
–  Contours crossing a stream form V's pointing UPSTREAM (uphill)
–  Contours crossing a ridge form V's pointing DOWNHILL
•  Slope (%) = (Rise / Run) × 100
•  Slope (ratio) = Run : Rise (e.g., 3:1 means 3 horizontal to 1 vertical = 33.3%)
•  Given contour map: Rise = number of contours crossed × contour interval; Run = horizontal distance measured on map
•  Converting between formats:

rows: Crown or consistent slope; tight tolerance
Max for vegetated slope without wall

content.text: •  Plane surfaces — uniform slope in one direction; contours are parallel, equally spaced
•  Warped planes — surface slopes in two directions simultaneously; contours converge or diverge
•  Crowns — high point along center, slopes both sides (roads, athletic fields)
•  Valleys / swales — low point along center, slopes inward from both sides
•  Berms — raised earthen mounds for screening, drainage diversion, or aesthetics
•  Grading at buildings — FFE set first; grade slopes away min 2% for 10'
•  Grading at walls — spot elevations at TW and BW; drainage behind wall essential
•  Contour grading for paths — contours deflect along path alignment; path cross-slope ≤ 2%
•  Cut = removing earth (lowering grade); Fill = adding earth (raising grade)
•  Average End Area Method: Volume = [(A₁ + A₂) / 2] × L (where A = cross-section area, L = distance between sections)
•  Grid Method: divide site into grid; calculate cut/fill depth at each grid point; multiply by grid cell area
•  Balanced earthwork: cut volume ≈ fill volume (minimize hauling)
•  Shrink/swell factors: excavated soil expands 15-25% (bank to loose); compacted fill shrinks 10-15% (bank to compacted)
–  1.0 CY bank soil → ~1.2 CY loose soil → ~0.9 CY compacted fill
•  Topsoil stripping, stockpiling, and replacement: strip before grading, stockpile on-site, replace after rough grading

The second-largest domain tests your understanding of hydrology, runoff calculations, and stormwater best management practices. You must be able to calculate runoff using the Rational Method, understand time of concentration, and select appropriate BMPs.
•  Watershed — land area that drains to a common outlet point
•  Drainage divide — ridge line separating adjacent watersheds
•  Time of concentration (Tc) — time for water to travel from the most hydraulically distant point to the outlet
–  Longer Tc = lower peak flow rate (runoff spreads out over time)
–  Shorter Tc = higher peak flow rate (runoff arrives at once)
•  Impervious vs. pervious surfaces:
–  Impervious (roofs, pavement): high runoff, low infiltration
–  Pervious (turf, forest, gravel): lower runoff, higher infiltration
•  Development increases impervious area → increases runoff volume and peak rate → requires management
•  Q = peak runoff rate (cubic feet per second, cfs)
•  C = runoff coefficient (dimensionless, 0 to 1)
–  Roofs/pavement: C = 0.90-0.95
–  Gravel surfaces: C = 0.40-0.60
–  Lawns (flat): C = 0.10-0.25
–  Lawns (steep): C = 0.25-0.35
–  Forest/woodland: C = 0.05-0.25
•  i = rainfall intensity (inches/hour) for the design storm and Tc
•  A = drainage area (acres)
•  Composite C for mixed surfaces: Cw = Σ(Cn × An) / ΣAn
•  Rational Method valid for watersheds < 200 acres; for larger areas use SCS/NRCS methods
•  Used for larger watersheds and storage-based design (detention, retention)
•  CN (Curve Number) = function of soil type (HSG) and land cover
–  CN 100 = total runoff (impervious); CN 30 = very low runoff (forest on HSG A)
•  Higher CN = more runoff; Lower CN = more infiltration
•  HSG A soils: lowest CN values; HSG D soils: highest CN values
•  Composite CN for mixed land covers: weighted by area
•  Storms described by recurrence interval (return period): 2-yr, 10-yr, 25-yr, 100-yr
•  2-year storm: minor system design (inlets, storm sewer, swales)
•  10-year storm: typical minor system design standard in many jurisdictions
•  25-year storm: major drainage system, culverts, channel design
•  100-year storm: flood hazard delineation (FEMA FIRM maps), emergency overflow
•  IDF curves (Intensity-Duration-Frequency): charts relating rainfall intensity to duration and frequency

rows: Allow runoff to soak into ground
Rain gardens, infiltration trenches, permeable pavement, dry wells
Temporarily store and slowly release runoff
Detention basins (dry ponds), underground detention, extended detention
Sand filters, bioretention, tree box filters, media filters
Green roofs, cisterns, disconnection, soil amendments

content.text: •  Detention (dry pond): stores water temporarily; drains completely between storms; controls peak flow rate
–  Outlet structure controls release rate (orifice, weir, riser pipe)
–  Typically designed to release post-development peak at ≤ pre-development rate
•  Retention (wet pond): maintains permanent pool; provides water quality treatment
–  Permanent pool allows settling of suspended solids and biological uptake of nutrients
–  Often combined with extended detention above the permanent pool for peak flow control
•  Erosion = detachment of soil particles; Sediment = transport and deposition of eroded soil
•  Erosion control prevents soil from detaching (source control)
–  Temporary: erosion control blankets, hydromulch, temporary seeding, rolled erosion control products
–  Permanent: established vegetation, riprap, turf reinforcement mats
•  Sediment control captures eroded soil before it leaves the site (trap and detain)
–  Silt fence, sediment basins, inlet protection, construction entrance (stabilized pad)
•  ESC measures installed BEFORE grading begins; maintained throughout construction
•  NPDES Construction General Permit required for sites ≥ 1 acre of disturbance
–  Requires Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP)
This domain tests your knowledge of the physical infrastructure that collects and conveys stormwater: inlets, pipes, manholes, culverts, channels, and outlets.
•  Sheet flow — thin, unchannelized flow across a surface (first 150-300' max)
•  Concentrated flow — runoff converges into defined channels (swales, ditches, gutters)
•  Swales — shallow, vegetated channels that convey runoff slowly; side slopes ≤ 3:1; longitudinal slope 1-5%
•  Gutters — paved channels along roads that collect and convey runoff to inlets
•  Level spreaders — devices that convert concentrated flow back to sheet flow for treatment/infiltration
•  Inlets (catch basins) — structures that collect surface runoff and deliver it to underground pipes
–  Types: grate inlet, curb inlet, combination (grate + curb opening)
–  Grate inlets in pedestrian areas: bicycle-safe grate (slots perpendicular to travel, <1/2" openings)
–  Locate at low points, intersections, building entries, upstream of crosswalks
•  Storm sewer pipe — underground pipe that conveys collected runoff
–  Materials: reinforced concrete pipe (RCP), corrugated metal (CMP), HDPE, PVC
–  Minimum pipe size: typically 12" or 15" diameter
–  Minimum velocity: 2.5-3.0 fps (self-cleaning to prevent sediment buildup)
–  Maximum velocity: 10-15 fps (prevent pipe erosion)
•  Manholes — access points for maintenance and inspection; required at changes in pipe direction, size, or slope
–  Typical spacing: maximum 300-400' between manholes
•  Outfall — point where storm sewer discharges to a receiving water body or detention facility
–  Energy dissipation required at outfall (riprap apron, stilling basin) to prevent erosion
•  Manning's Equation: V = (1.49/n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2)
–  V = velocity (fps); n = Manning's roughness coefficient; R = hydraulic radius (ft); S = slope (ft/ft)
–  For full pipe flow: Q = V × A (flow rate = velocity × cross-sectional area)
•  Manning's n values:
–  Concrete pipe (smooth): n = 0.012-0.013
–  Corrugated metal: n = 0.022-0.025
–  HDPE (smooth interior): n = 0.012
–  Natural channel: n = 0.030-0.050
–  Grass-lined swale: n = 0.030-0.040
•  Pipe sizing: determine Q (from Rational Method), select pipe slope, apply Manning's to find minimum diameter
•  Culverts convey water under roads, paths, or embankments
•  Headwater depth should not exceed 1.2× culvert diameter (inlet control)
•  End treatments: headwalls, wingwalls, flared end sections — prevent erosion and improve hydraulic entry
•  Trash racks at culvert inlets in areas with debris
•  French drains — gravel-filled trenches with perforated pipe to intercept and redirect groundwater
•  Underdrains — perforated pipe below bioretention, permeable pavement, or athletic fields to drain excess water
•  Foundation drains — perforated pipe at building footings to prevent hydrostatic pressure on foundations
•  Filter fabric wraps perforated pipe and separates gravel from native soil to prevent clogging

rows: Peak runoff rate (cfs); C = coefficient, i = intensity, A = area (acres)
Weighted runoff coefficient for mixed surfaces
Flow velocity in pipes and channels
Moderate slope; limit for some mowing
Max vegetated slope without retaining wall

content.text: •  This is the MOST mathematical section. Practice slope calculations until they are automatic.
•  Memorize the Rational Method (Q = CiA) and common C values for different surfaces.
•  Practice reading contour maps — identify ridges, valleys, drainage divides, steep vs. gentle slopes.
•  Know slope standards for every site use (athletic fields, parking, walks, lawns, buildings).
•  Understand detention vs. retention — what each does, when each is used.
•  Know erosion control (prevents detachment) vs. sediment control (captures eroded soil).
•  Understand Manning's equation conceptually — higher n = rougher = slower; steeper S = faster.
•  Know minimum pipe velocity (2.5-3 fps for self-cleaning) and maximum (10-15 fps to prevent erosion).
•  Memorize key conversions: 1 acre = 43,560 SF, 1 CY = 27 CF.
•  Practice the CLARB demo exam for hotspot questions — you may need to place contour lines or drainage structures.
•  Review Hydrologic Soil Groups (A-D) and how they affect runoff and BMP selection.
