•  Understand cut/fill volume estimation using average end area and grid methods.
Aligned to the CLARB Exam Blueprint (Effective December 2023)
70 Scored Items  |  MC + Select All + Drag & Drop + Hotspot  |  3 Hours

s4_book.title: Preface: How to Use This Book

content.text: This study book is designed to give you everything you need to pass LARE Section 4: Grading, Drainage, and Stormwater Management. This is the most quantitative section of the LARE exam. Where Sections 1-3 test your knowledge of concepts, principles, and processes, Section 4 tests your ability to do the math — to calculate slopes, determine runoff rates, size pipes, estimate earthwork volumes, and apply these calculations to real grading and drainage problems.

If math makes you nervous, this book will help. Every formula is explained in plain language, every calculation is demonstrated step by step, and every concept is connected to practical applications you will encounter in professional practice and on the exam.
The content is organized around the three domains of the CLARB exam blueprint:

EXAM FORMAT:  Section 4 uses all four question types: standard multiple choice, select all that apply, drag and drop (arranging items in sequence), and hotspot (clicking on a location in a plan or detail). Hotspot questions may ask you to place contour lines on a grading plan, locate the correct position for a drainage inlet, or identify the high point in a drainage area. Practice interpreting topographic plans before the exam.

Topography — the shape of the land surface — is represented on maps and plans using contour lines. Contour lines are the fundamental graphic language of grading and drainage. Before you can grade a site, calculate slopes, or design a drainage system, you must be able to read contour lines as fluently as you read text. This chapter teaches you how.

A contour line connects all points at the same elevation above a reference datum, typically mean sea level (MSL). If you could walk along a contour line, you would be walking perfectly level — never going up or down. Every point on the 100-foot contour line is exactly 100 feet above sea level.

The contour interval is the vertical distance between consecutive contour lines. A 2-foot contour interval means each successive line represents a 2-foot change in elevation. Every fifth contour (the index contour) is drawn with a heavier line weight and is labeled with its elevation for easy reading.
Contour lines follow strict rules that never vary. Understanding these rules allows you to interpret any topographic map:

1. Contour lines never cross. Each line represents a unique elevation. Two different elevations cannot exist at the same point on the ground surface. (The rare exception — an overhanging cliff — will not appear on the exam.)
2. Contour lines never split or branch. A contour line is continuous and does not fork into two paths.

3. Contour lines always close on themselves. They form complete loops, although the loop may extend beyond the edge of the map. A closed contour on a map indicates either a hilltop (if inner contours are higher) or a depression (if inner contours are lower, marked with tick marks called hachures).

4. Spacing indicates steepness. Closely spaced contours indicate steep slopes — the elevation changes rapidly over a short horizontal distance. Widely spaced contours indicate gentle slopes — the elevation changes gradually. Evenly spaced contours indicate a uniform (constant) slope.

5. Contours crossing streams form V's pointing upstream. Water flows downhill, so the stream bed is at the lowest point in the valley. Contour lines bend upstream (toward higher elevations) where they cross the stream. This creates a V-pattern pointing uphill. This is one of the most important rules for reading drainage patterns.

6. Contours crossing ridges form V's pointing downhill. A ridge is the opposite of a valley — it is the high point between two drainage courses. Contour lines bend toward lower elevations as they cross a ridge, creating V's pointing downhill.

MEMORY AID:  Streams and ridges: V's point UP for streams (water flows down, contours point up). V's point DOWN for ridges (land rises, contours point down). Remember: "V's point opposite to what the feature does."

EXAM TIP:  Hotspot questions may ask you to identify the location of a stream, ridge, or drainage divide on a contour map. Look for the V-pattern in the contour lines. V's pointing uphill = stream. V's pointing downhill = ridge/drainage divide.

rows: Concentric closed loops, highest in center
Inner contours have highest elevations; no hachures
Concentric closed loops with hachure marks
Tick marks on inner side indicate ground slopes inward/down
Elongated high area; V's point downhill
Contours bend toward lower elevations along spine
Elongated low area; V's point uphill
Contours bend toward higher elevations along drainage
Low point on a ridge between two summits
Consistent elevation change over consistent distance
Contours get farther apart going downhill
Slope flattens toward bottom; you cannot see the base from the top
Contours get closer together going downhill
Slope steepens toward bottom; you can see the base from the top
Very closely spaced or touching contours
Near-vertical slope; sometimes shown with a cliff symbol

content.text: CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Contour lines connect points of equal elevation; the contour interval is the vertical distance between successive lines. ✔  Contour lines never cross, split, or end — they always close on themselves. ✔  Closely spaced contours = steep slope; widely spaced = gentle slope. ✔  V's pointing upstream (uphill) indicate streams; V's pointing downhill indicate ridges. ✔  Concentric circles = hilltop (no hachures) or depression (with hachures). ✔  Convex slopes flatten downhill (contours spread); concave slopes steepen downhill (contours compress).
1. On a contour map with a 2-foot interval, five contour lines cross a 100-foot horizontal distance. The slope of this area is:
Answer: D. Five contour lines at 2' interval = 10' of rise (5 × 2 = 10). Slope = (10/100) × 100 = 10%.

subsections.title: 2. Contour lines that form V-shapes pointing toward HIGHER elevations indicate:

content.text: A)  A ridge
B)  A hilltop
C)  A stream valley
D)  A depression
Answer: C. Contour V's point upstream (toward higher elevations) where they cross a stream valley. The V opens downhill in the direction of water flow.

subsections.title: 3. Contour lines that become progressively farther apart as you move downhill indicate:

content.text: A)  A concave slope
B)  A convex slope
C)  A uniform slope
D)  A cliff
Answer: B. A convex slope flattens toward the bottom — contours spread apart going downhill. On a convex slope, you cannot see the base from the top.

Slope calculation is the single most fundamental skill tested on Section 4. You will be asked to calculate slopes from contour maps, between spot elevations, and for design features like ramps, parking lots, swales, and building pads. This chapter teaches you to calculate slope in any format and convert between formats confidently.
Slope is the ratio of vertical change (rise) to horizontal distance (run). It can be expressed in three formats:
Percentage (%): Slope = (Rise ÷ Run) × 100. A 5% slope rises 5 feet for every 100 feet of horizontal distance. This is the most common format for grading plans.

Ratio (H:V): Expressed as horizontal distance to vertical distance. A 3:1 slope means 3 feet horizontal for every 1 foot vertical. This format is common for embankments and steep slopes. To convert: 3:1 = 1/3 = 33.3%.
Decimal / fraction: Slope = Rise ÷ Run (without multiplying by 100). A decimal slope of 0.05 = 5%. This format is used in engineering formulas like Manning's equation (where S = slope in ft/ft).
To calculate slope between two points on a contour map:

Step 1: Determine the rise — count the number of contour lines crossed between the two points and multiply by the contour interval. If Point A is on the 98-foot contour and Point B is on the 106-foot contour, the rise is 106 - 98 = 8 feet.
Step 2: Measure the horizontal run — the straight-line distance between the two points on the map, measured using the map scale. If the distance is 200 feet, the run is 200 feet.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  An exam question shows a contour map with 5-foot contour intervals. You measure the distance between the 350' and 375' contour lines along a proposed path alignment and find it spans 500 feet horizontally. The rise is 375 - 350 = 25 feet. The slope is (25 ÷ 500) × 100 = 5%. This path is at the maximum slope for an accessible route — any steeper and it would require ramp construction.
The exam may ask you to find the elevation of a point that falls between two contour lines. This requires interpolation:
Interpolation formula: Elevation = Lower contour + (distance from lower contour ÷ total distance between contours) × contour interval.
For example: a point is located 60% of the way from the 100-foot contour to the 102-foot contour (2-foot interval). Its elevation is 100 + (0.60 × 2) = 101.2 feet.

EXAM TIP:  When the exam shows a contour map and asks for the elevation at a specific point, use linear interpolation between the two nearest contour lines. Measure the point's proportional distance between the contours, then multiply by the contour interval and add to the lower contour elevation.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Slope (%) = (Rise ÷ Run) × 100. ✔  Three formats: percentage (5%), ratio (20:1), decimal (0.05). ✔  To convert ratio to percentage: divide 1 by the H value. Example: 3:1 = 1÷3 = 0.333 = 33.3%. ✔  From contour maps: count contours crossed × interval = rise; measure horizontal distance = run. ✔  Interpolation finds elevation between contours: proportional distance × contour interval + lower contour.

subsections.title: 1. A 3:1 slope expressed as a percentage is:

content.text: Answer: C. 3:1 means 3 feet horizontal for every 1 foot vertical. As a percentage: (1÷3) × 100 = 33.3%.

subsections.title: 2. A proposed path runs 400 feet from elevation 250.0 to elevation 262.0. The slope is:

content.text: Answer: B. Rise = 262.0 - 250.0 = 12 feet. Run = 400 feet. Slope = (12÷400) × 100 = 3%.
3. A point is located halfway between the 96-foot and 100-foot contour lines (4-foot interval). Its interpolated elevation is:
A)  96 feet
B)  97 feet
C)  98 feet
D)  99 feet
Answer: C. Halfway = 50%. Elevation = 96 + (0.50 × 4) = 98 feet.

Grading design is the art and science of reshaping the land to serve design intent — directing water, creating accessible routes, building level pads, and sculpting landforms. This chapter teaches you how to grade common site features by manipulating contour lines on a plan.

Positive drainage: Every surface must slope to direct water away from buildings and toward collection points. The minimum slope adjacent to buildings is 2% for at least 10 feet. There are no exceptions — water against a foundation causes structural damage, mold, and liability.

Balance cut and fill: Ideally, the volume of earth removed (cut) equals the volume of earth added (fill) within the site. This minimizes the cost and environmental impact of importing or exporting soil. The grading plan should be designed to achieve this balance whenever possible.

Match existing grades at boundaries: Proposed grades must meet existing grades at property lines. You cannot direct additional runoff onto a neighbor's property or create grade differences that cause instability at the boundary.

Preserve existing features: Minimize grading within the drip line of trees to be preserved. Protect root zones from fill (which suffocates roots) and cut (which severs roots). A common exam scenario: a tree to be preserved sits in an area where fill is proposed — the correct response is to install a retaining wall or tree well to keep the existing grade at the tree's root zone.

Design for constructability: Grading must be achievable with standard construction equipment. Avoid unnecessarily complex contour configurations. Slopes must be within constructable ranges, and transitions between grades must be smooth.

A flat surface (parking lot, plaza, athletic field) appears flat but actually must have a consistent slope for drainage. On a grading plan, this appears as parallel, equally spaced contour lines crossing the surface.

To calculate contour spacing for a desired slope: Spacing = Contour Interval ÷ Slope (as decimal). For a 2% slope with 1-foot contour interval: Spacing = 1.0 ÷ 0.02 = 50 feet between contour lines. For a 5% slope: Spacing = 1.0 ÷ 0.05 = 20 feet.

MEMORY AID:  Contour spacing = Interval ÷ Slope. Bigger slope = closer contours. A 2% slope with 1' interval has contours every 50 feet. A 5% slope has contours every 20 feet. Double the slope = half the spacing.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A landscape architect is grading a parking lot at 2% slope. The lot is 200 feet long. With a 1-foot contour interval, contours are spaced 50 feet apart (1.0 ÷ 0.02 = 50). Four contour lines cross the lot, creating 4 feet of elevation change across the 200-foot length. The low end receives a catch basin to collect runoff.

Grading around buildings is one of the most critical — and most tested — grading scenarios. The landscape architect must ensure positive drainage away from all sides of the building while meeting the finished floor elevation (FFE) at entries with accessible routes.
•  Set the FFE first — it controls all surrounding grades
•  Minimum 2% slope away from the building for at least 10 feet on all sides
•  At entries: match the FFE with an accessible route at ≤ 5% running slope and ≤ 2% cross slope
•  Contour lines bend AWAY from the building (showing water flowing away from the foundation)
•  Spot elevations at all building corners, door thresholds, and area drain locations

EXAM TIP:  If a hotspot question asks you to draw contours around a building, remember: contours BEND AWAY from the building on all sides. This is the graphic representation of positive drainage. The highest point is at the building; the lowest point is away from it.

A swale is a shallow, vegetated channel designed to convey surface runoff. On a grading plan, a swale appears as contour lines bending uphill along the low point of the channel — the same V-pattern you see at natural streams, but designed and constructed.
•  Longitudinal slope (along the swale): 1% minimum (to prevent ponding), 5% maximum (to prevent erosion)
•  Side slopes: 3:1 maximum for mowable turf swales; 4:1 preferred for accessible areas
•  Bottom width: typically 2-4 feet for a grass swale
•  Depth: typically 12-18 inches
•  Velocity: design for low velocity (< 4 fps) to prevent erosion in vegetated swales
Paths must balance drainage needs (cross slope to shed water) with accessibility requirements (maximum slopes for wheelchairs):
•  Cross slope: 2% maximum for accessible paths
•  Longitudinal slope: 5% maximum for accessible routes (over 5% = ramp)
•  On a contour map, contours deflect (bend) along the path alignment in the direction of the downhill slope
•  The amount of contour deflection shows the path's longitudinal slope — more deflection = steeper path

Ramps: Maximum slope 8.33% (1:12). Maximum rise per run: 30 inches (so at 1:12 slope, maximum run = 30 feet between landings). Landings: 5' × 5' minimum at top, bottom, and every 30 feet. Contours crossing a ramp are more closely spaced than on adjacent terrain if the ramp is steeper than the natural grade.

Steps integrated with grading: Where the natural slope exceeds ramp feasibility, steps may be required alongside the ramp. The grading must accommodate both — the ramp at 8.33% and the steps at the appropriate riser/tread configuration. Both must tie into the surrounding grade at top and bottom landings.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Positive drainage: 2% minimum away from buildings for at least 10 feet. ✔  Balance cut and fill to minimize import/export costs. ✔  Match existing grades at property lines — never redirect runoff onto neighbors. ✔  Contour spacing = Interval ÷ Slope. Double the slope = half the spacing. ✔  Contours bend AWAY from buildings (positive drainage) and UPHILL along swales (like streams). ✔  Swale slopes: 1-5% longitudinal, 3:1 max side slopes for mowable turf. ✔  Path cross slope: 2% max. Over 5% longitudinal = ramp. Ramps: 8.33% max, 30' max run.
1. A parking lot is being graded at 2% slope using 1-foot contour intervals. The contour lines should be spaced:
A)  10 feet apart
B)  20 feet apart
C)  50 feet apart
D)  100 feet apart
Answer: C. Contour spacing = Interval ÷ Slope = 1.0 ÷ 0.02 = 50 feet apart.

subsections.title: 2. When drawing proposed contours around a building, the contours should:

content.text: A)  Run parallel to the building walls
B)  Bend toward the building (concave toward building)
C)  Bend away from the building (convex toward building)
D)  Cross through the building footprint
Answer: C. Contours bend away from the building on all sides, showing that the ground slopes away from the foundation — the graphic representation of positive drainage.

subsections.title: 3. A grassed swale has a longitudinal slope of 0.5%. This slope is problematic because:

content.text: A)  It is too steep and will cause erosion
B)  It is below the 1% minimum and will cause ponding
C)  It exceeds ADA requirements
D)  It will cause the swale to overflow
Answer: B. The minimum longitudinal slope for a swale is 1%. Below 1%, water will pond in the swale rather than flowing to the outlet.

Earthwork is the process of moving soil — cutting high areas down and filling low areas up to achieve the proposed grades. Estimating earthwork volumes is essential for cost estimation, construction scheduling, and determining whether soil must be imported or exported. The exam tests your understanding of cut/fill concepts and basic volume estimation methods.

Cut is the removal of earth to lower the existing grade to the proposed grade. Fill is the addition of earth to raise the existing grade to the proposed grade. On a grading plan, cut and fill areas are identified by comparing existing contours to proposed contours:
•  Where proposed contours are LOWER than existing contours at the same location → CUT
•  Where proposed contours are HIGHER than existing contours at the same location → FILL
•  Where proposed and existing contours coincide → no grade change (daylight line / zero cut-fill line)

Daylight line: The line where cut or fill slopes meet the existing grade. Beyond the daylight line, no grading occurs. The daylight line defines the limits of disturbance and determines how far grading impacts extend from the proposed feature.
The most common method for calculating earthwork along a linear feature (road, channel, path). The site is divided into cross-sections at regular intervals:
Volume = [(A₁ + A₂) / 2] × L where A₁ and A₂ are the cut (or fill) areas of adjacent cross-sections, and L is the distance between them.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A road cut has cross-section areas of 120 SF at Station 0+00 and 180 SF at Station 1+00 (100 feet apart). Volume = [(120 + 180) / 2] × 100 = 15,000 CF ÷ 27 = 556 cubic yards of cut.

Used for large, irregular areas. The site is divided into a grid of square cells (typically 25' × 25' or 50' × 50'). At each grid intersection, the cut or fill depth is calculated by subtracting the existing elevation from the proposed elevation. The volume of each cell is:

subsections.title: Cell volume = Average cut/fill depth at corners × Cell area

content.text: The total volume is the sum of all cell volumes.
Soil changes volume when it is excavated and when it is compacted:

rows: Soil as it exists in the ground before excavation
Soil after excavation — air fills spaces between particles
Soil after placement and compaction as fill

content.text: This means that 100 cubic yards of cut (bank measure) produces only about 85-95 cubic yards of compacted fill. To achieve a balanced site, you actually need slightly more cut than fill.

MEMORY AID:  Soil swell/shrink: Bank soil EXPANDS when you dig it up (loose) and SHRINKS when you compact it (compacted fill). To balance a site, you need about 10-15% more bank-measure cut volume than the fill volume you need to place.

EXAM TIP:  If the exam asks for earthwork volume, pay attention to whether the answer should be in bank, loose, or compacted cubic yards. The same volume of earth has different measurements depending on its state. Always use bank cubic yards for cut/fill comparisons unless told otherwise.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Cut lowers grade (proposed < existing); fill raises grade (proposed > existing). ✔  The daylight line is where cut/fill slopes meet the existing grade — it defines the limits of disturbance. ✔  Average End Area: Volume = [(A₁ + A₂) / 2] × L — used for linear features. ✔  Grid Method: calculate cut/fill depth at grid intersections, average × cell area — used for large areas. ✔  Bank soil expands 15-25% when excavated (loose) and shrinks 5-15% when compacted. ✔  1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. Always convert to CY for cost estimation.
1. Two cross-sections 50 feet apart show cut areas of 80 SF and 120 SF. The cut volume between them is:
A)  100 cubic yards
B)  185 cubic yards
C)  5,000 cubic feet
D)  Both A and C are correct expressions
Answer: D. Volume = [(80+120)/2] × 50 = 5,000 CF. Converting: 5,000 ÷ 27 = 185 CY. Wait — let me recalculate. 5,000 ÷ 27 = 185.2 CY ≈ 185 CY. The answer is 5,000 CF or approximately 185 CY.
2. 100 bank cubic yards of clay soil is excavated. Approximately how many loose cubic yards will the excavated soil occupy?
A)  85 cubic yards
B)  100 cubic yards
C)  115-125 cubic yards
D)  150 cubic yards
Answer: C. Excavated (loose) soil expands 15-25% from bank volume. 100 bank CY × 1.15 to 1.25 = 115 to 125 loose CY.

This chapter applies the grading principles from previous chapters to specific site features you will encounter on the exam: roads, parking lots, athletic fields, berms, retention/detention basins, and transitions between grades.

Road crowns: Roads are typically crowned — the centerline is the highest point, and the pavement slopes 2% toward both edges where curb and gutter collect runoff. On a contour map, a crowned road shows contour lines bending in the direction of the crown's high point along the centerline, with a symmetrical V-pattern at each contour crossing.

Parking lots: Large parking lots are typically divided into drainage sub-areas. Each sub-area slopes toward a catch basin or landscape island with a bioretention area. Slopes range from 1% minimum (to prevent ponding) to 5% maximum. ADA accessible routes through the parking lot must not exceed 2% cross slope. Accessible parking stalls must be on the flattest portion of the lot.
Athletic fields require the tightest grading tolerances on any site. They must be flat enough for fair play but sloped enough for drainage:
•  Slope: 1% minimum to 2% maximum
•  Options: crown (high center, slopes both sides) or consistent slope (one direction)
•  Tolerance: ±0.04 feet (approximately ½ inch) — extremely tight
•  Subsurface drainage (perforated pipe in gravel blanket) often required for rapid drainage
•  Amended sand-based rootzone mix (USGA spec for high-use fields) improves drainage

Berms are raised earthen mounds used for visual screening, noise attenuation, drainage diversion, and topographic interest. Grading a berm requires creating closed contour loops that satisfy slope requirements on all sides:
•  Side slopes: 3:1 maximum for mowable turf; 4:1 or gentler for natural appearance
•  Top: crown or flat top, minimum 3 feet wide for planting
•  Common error: berms too steep (unmaintainable) or too narrow (look artificial)
•  A natural-looking berm has gentle, asymmetric slopes — not a symmetric half-cylinder

Detention basin (dry pond): Graded as a shallow depression with an inlet, an outlet structure (riser pipe, orifice, or weir), and an emergency overflow/spillway. Interior side slopes: 3:1 minimum (4:1 preferred for mowable turf and safety). Bottom slope: 1-2% toward the outlet to drain completely between storms. An access path (10-12' wide) must reach the bottom for maintenance equipment.

Retention basin (wet pond): Similar grading but with a permanent pool. The normal water level is maintained by a riser pipe or weir. Above the normal pool, storage volume accommodates storm events. A safety bench (shallow, gently sloped area around the perimeter) is required — typically 15-25 feet wide at 6:1 slope or flatter. An aquatic bench supports emergent vegetation for water quality treatment.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A detention basin is designed to manage the 10-year storm for a 5-acre commercial development. The basin has 3:1 side slopes, a flat bottom sloped at 1.5% toward a 12" riser pipe outlet, and a 100-year emergency spillway at 1 foot above the 10-year high water level. The landscape architect grades a 10-foot-wide maintenance access ramp at 10% slope into the basin. Contour lines on the grading plan show concentric closed loops getting progressively lower toward the basin bottom.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Roads are crowned with 2% slope to each side; contours form V's at the crown. ✔  Parking lots: 1-5% slope; ADA routes ≤ 2% cross slope; catch basins at low points. ✔  Athletic fields: 1-2% slope, ±0.04' tolerance, often require subsurface drainage. ✔  Berms: 3:1 max mowable slopes, minimum 3' wide top, asymmetric for natural look. ✔  Detention basins: 3:1 interior slopes, 1-2% bottom slope to outlet, maintenance access required. ✔  Retention basins: permanent pool + safety bench (15-25' wide, 6:1 slope) + aquatic bench.
1. A detention basin has interior side slopes of 3:1. The basin is 6 feet deep. How far horizontally do the slopes extend from the top edge to the basin floor?
A)  6 feet
B)  12 feet
C)  18 feet
D)  24 feet
Answer: C. A 3:1 slope means 3 feet horizontal for every 1 foot vertical. At 6 feet deep: 3 × 6 = 18 feet horizontal.

subsections.title: 2. The maximum slope for a mowed turf athletic field is:

content.text: Answer: B. Athletic fields must slope between 1% and 2% — flat enough for fair play, steep enough for drainage.

s4_book.title: Chapter 6: Hydrology and the Water Cycle

content.text: Hydrology is the study of water movement through the environment. Understanding how rainfall becomes runoff — and how development alters this process — is the foundation of stormwater management. The exam tests your understanding of the hydrologic cycle, watersheds, and how development increases runoff.
Rainfall follows multiple pathways when it reaches the ground:
Interception: Rainfall caught by vegetation canopy before reaching the ground. A mature tree canopy can intercept 15-40% of rainfall. This water evaporates directly from leaf surfaces.

Infiltration: Water soaking into the soil surface. Infiltration rate depends on soil type (HSG A soils infiltrate fastest, HSG D slowest), soil moisture, slope, and vegetative cover. Infiltrated water becomes either soil moisture (used by plants) or groundwater recharge.

Surface runoff: Water that does not infiltrate and flows across the surface toward streams, ponds, or drainage systems. Runoff increases dramatically when pervious surfaces (soil, vegetation) are replaced by impervious surfaces (roofs, pavement).

Evapotranspiration (ET): Water returned to the atmosphere through evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants. ET is the largest component of the water cycle in most climates — 40-60% of rainfall is returned to the atmosphere through ET.
Development converts pervious surfaces (forest, meadow, agricultural land) to impervious surfaces (roofs, roads, parking lots). This has profound effects on the water cycle:

rows: Clean — filtered by soil and vegetation
Polluted — carries oils, metals, sediment, nutrients

content.text: This is why stormwater management is required for all development projects. The goal is to mimic pre-development hydrology as closely as possible by managing runoff rate, volume, and quality.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Rainfall partitions into interception, infiltration, surface runoff, and evapotranspiration. ✔  Development increases impervious cover, which increases runoff volume, peak rate, and pollutant loading. ✔  Development decreases infiltration, evapotranspiration, and groundwater recharge. ✔  Stormwater management aims to replicate pre-development hydrology: rate, volume, and quality. ✔  Time of concentration decreases with development (faster runoff = higher peak flows).

subsections.title: 1. Development of a forested site into a suburban neighborhood will MOST likely result in:

content.text: A)  Decreased surface runoff and increased infiltration
B)  Increased surface runoff and decreased infiltration
C)  No change in runoff patterns
D)  Increased evapotranspiration
Answer: B. Replacing pervious forest with impervious roofs and pavement dramatically increases surface runoff and decreases infiltration.

subsections.title: 2. Time of concentration decreases after development because:

content.text: A)  Runoff travels faster over smooth impervious surfaces than through vegetation
B)  The drainage area becomes smaller
C)  Rainfall intensity decreases in urban areas
D)  Groundwater levels rise in developed areas
Answer: A. Smooth impervious surfaces accelerate runoff flow compared to the rough, vegetated surfaces that slow water in undeveloped conditions. Shorter Tc = higher peak flow rate.

The Rational Method is the most widely used formula for calculating peak stormwater runoff rate from small drainage areas (less than 200 acres). It is the formula most likely to appear on the exam. If you learn one formula for Section 4, learn this one.
Q = C × i × A
Q = peak runoff rate in cubic feet per second (cfs). This is the maximum instantaneous flow rate at the outlet of the drainage area during the design storm.

C = runoff coefficient (dimensionless, between 0 and 1). Represents the fraction of rainfall that becomes surface runoff. A C of 0.90 means 90% of rainfall runs off (impervious surface). A C of 0.15 means only 15% runs off (lawn on flat ground). The remaining rainfall is intercepted, infiltrated, or evaporated.

i = rainfall intensity in inches per hour (in/hr). Obtained from IDF (Intensity-Duration-Frequency) curves for the project location. The duration used equals the time of concentration (Tc) of the drainage area. The frequency (return period) is specified by the local stormwater ordinance — typically 10-year for minor systems, 100-year for major systems.
A = drainage area in acres. The total area contributing runoff to the point of interest. One acre = 43,560 square feet.
Most drainage areas contain a mix of surface types — some pavement, some lawn, some roof. The composite (weighted) runoff coefficient accounts for this mix:
Where Cn is the C value for each surface type and An is the area of each surface type.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:  A 2-acre site contains 0.5 acres of roof (C = 0.95), 0.7 acres of parking (C = 0.90), and 0.8 acres of lawn on clay soil (C = 0.20). The composite C = [(0.95 × 0.5) + (0.90 × 0.7) + (0.20 × 0.8)] / (0.5 + 0.7 + 0.8) = [0.475 + 0.630 + 0.160] / 2.0 = 1.265 / 2.0 = 0.63. Using i = 4.2 in/hr (10-year, Tc = 15 minutes), Q = 0.63 × 4.2 × 2.0 = 5.29 cfs.

MEMORY AID:  Rational Method: Q = CIA. Think "CIA agents handle the flow" — C is the character of the surface, I is the intensity of the storm, A is the area of the watershed. Multiply all three to get the flow rate Q.

EXAM TIP:  When calculating composite C, make sure all areas sum to the total drainage area. It is easy to forget a surface type or double-count an area. Double-check: Σ An = total area. Also verify your units — A must be in acres, i in inches/hour.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Q = CiA: Q in cfs, C dimensionless (0-1), i in in/hr, A in acres. ✔  Rational Method is valid for drainage areas < 200 acres. ✔  Higher C = more runoff (impervious surfaces); lower C = less runoff (pervious, flat, sandy). ✔  Composite C = weighted average based on each surface type's area and C value. ✔  Rainfall intensity (i) comes from IDF curves using the time of concentration as the duration. ✔  The design storm frequency (2-yr, 10-yr, 100-yr) is set by local stormwater regulations.
1. A 3-acre parking lot (C = 0.90) experiences a 10-year storm with intensity of 5.0 in/hr. The peak runoff rate is:
A)  4.5 cfs
B)  13.5 cfs
C)  15.0 cfs
D)  45.0 cfs
2. Increasing the impervious area of a drainage basin will cause the composite runoff coefficient (C) to:
A)  Decrease
B)  Stay the same
C)  Increase
D)  Become negative
Answer: C. Impervious surfaces have high C values (0.85-0.95). Adding impervious area raises the weighted average C, meaning more rainfall becomes runoff.

subsections.title: 3. The Rational Method uses rainfall intensity based on a duration equal to the:

content.text: A)  Total storm duration
B)  Time of concentration of the drainage area
C)  24-hour rainfall total
D)  Average annual rainfall
Answer: B. The Rational Method assumes that peak runoff occurs when the storm duration equals the time of concentration — the time for runoff from the most distant point to reach the outlet.

BMPs are the physical strategies used to manage stormwater runoff — controlling its rate, volume, and quality. Selecting the right BMP for a given site requires understanding what each practice does, what site conditions it needs, and what it achieves. The exam frequently tests BMP selection based on site constraints.

rows: Allows runoff to soak into the ground
HSG A or B soils; deep water table; low contamination risk
Rain gardens, infiltration trenches, permeable paving, dry wells
Any soil type; peak rate control required
Detention basins, underground detention, extended detention
Stores runoff permanently; treats through settling and biological uptake
Limited space; water quality focus; any soil
Sand filters, bioretention with underdrain, tree box filters
Green roofs, cisterns, soil amendments, disconnection

content.text: Soil type (Hydrologic Soil Group) is the primary factor in BMP selection:

rows: All infiltration practices, rain gardens, permeable paving, infiltration trenches
Retention ponds (water drains away before pool forms)
Most practices; infiltration with proper sizing
Bioretention with underdrain, detention, filtration, retention ponds
Detention basins, wet ponds, constructed wetlands, green roofs, cisterns, bioretention with underdrain

content.text: EXAM TIP:  This table is one of the most important for Section 4. If the exam describes clay soils (HSG D), eliminate all infiltration-only BMPs. Choose detention, retention, or practices with underdrains. If the exam describes sandy soils (HSG A), infiltration practices are ideal.
Detention basins temporarily store stormwater and release it slowly through an outlet structure. They are designed to limit the post-development peak discharge rate to the pre-development rate:
•  Outlet structure: riser pipe with orifice(s) sized to restrict outflow to the pre-development rate
•  Storage volume: must accommodate the difference between post-development inflow and restricted outflow
•  Emergency spillway: handles storms exceeding the design event (typically 100-year)
•  Interior slopes: 3:1 minimum (4:1 preferred for safety and mowing)
•  Bottom: 1-2% slope toward outlet; must drain completely within 24-72 hours to prevent mosquito breeding
•  Maintenance access: 10-12' wide ramp at ≤ 10% slope for equipment to reach the bottom

Bioretention facilities (rain gardens) are shallow, landscaped depressions that collect runoff, filter it through engineered soil media, and either infiltrate it into the ground or drain it through an underdrain:
•  Sizing: typically 5-10% of the contributing impervious area
•  Ponding depth: 6-12 inches maximum (deeper ponding drowns plants)
•  Soil media: engineered mix — typically 60% sand, 20% compost, 20% topsoil; 18-30 inches deep
•  Mulch: 2-3 inches of shredded hardwood (do not use pine bark — it floats)
•  Underdrain: perforated pipe in gravel layer at bottom — required for HSG C and D soils
•  Plants: native, flood-tolerant species that handle alternating wet/dry conditions
•  Overflow: must have overflow structure (riser pipe or overflow grate) at maximum ponding elevation

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  BMP categories: infiltration, detention, retention, filtration, volume reduction. ✔  HSG A/B soils → infiltration practices work. HSG C/D soils → need underdrains or detention. ✔  Detention basins store and release; outlet structure controls release rate. ✔  Detention basins must drain within 24-72 hours to prevent mosquito breeding. ✔  Bioretention sizing: 5-10% of contributing impervious area. ✔  Bioretention ponding depth: 6-12" max; engineered media 18-30" deep. ✔  All BMPs need overflow structures for storms exceeding design capacity.

subsections.title: 1. A site has HSG D clay soils. Which BMP is MOST appropriate?

content.text: A)  Infiltration trench
B)  Dry well
C)  Detention basin
D)  Permeable pavement without underdrain

Answer: C. HSG D soils have very slow infiltration. Infiltration-only practices will fail. Detention basins work on any soil type because they store and release water through an outlet structure, not through infiltration.
2. A bioretention facility should be sized at approximately what percentage of the contributing impervious area?
Answer: B. Standard bioretention sizing is 5-10% of the contributing impervious area, depending on local regulations and soil conditions.

subsections.title: 3. A detention basin must drain completely within 24-72 hours primarily to:

content.text: A)  Prevent structural damage to the outlet
B)  Prevent mosquito breeding in standing water
C)  Allow grass to survive in the basin bottom
D)  Meet FEMA floodplain requirements
Answer: B. Standing water becomes a mosquito breeding habitat within 48-72 hours. Drainage within this window is a public health requirement.

Erosion and sediment control (ESC) protects water quality and prevents soil loss during and after construction. The exam tests your understanding of the difference between erosion control and sediment control, common ESC practices, and the regulatory framework (NPDES permits).

Erosion control prevents soil particles from being detached from the ground surface in the first place. It is source control — keeping the soil in place. Erosion control is always preferred over sediment control because it is more effective and less costly.
Sediment control captures soil particles that have already been eroded before they leave the site or enter a waterway. It is treatment after the fact — a last line of defense.

rows: Temporary seeding, erosion control blankets (ECBs), hydromulch, rolled erosion control products (RECPs), sod, mulch, phased construction, slope reduction
Silt fence, sediment basins, sediment traps, inlet protection (filter socks, drop inlet sediment traps), check dams in channels, construction entrance (stabilized stone pad)

content.text: MEMORY AID:  Erosion control = keep the soil WHERE IT IS (source control). Sediment control = catch the soil AFTER it moves (treatment). Erosion control is always the first priority because it is more effective and cheaper.
•  Install ESC measures BEFORE any grading or clearing begins
•  Minimize the area of disturbance at any one time (phased clearing)
•  Stabilize disturbed areas as quickly as possible (within 14 days of final grading in most regulations)
•  Protect steep slopes with blankets or matting immediately after grading
•  Divert clean upslope water around the construction site (diversion swales/berms)
•  Place silt fence on the downhill side of disturbed areas — along the contour, not down the slope
•  Protect all storm drain inlets with inlet protection devices
•  Maintain ESC measures throughout construction — inspect after every rainfall event

EXAM TIP:  Silt fence is the most commonly misunderstood ESC practice. It is a SEDIMENT control device (captures eroded soil), NOT an erosion control device (does not prevent erosion). Silt fence must be installed along the contour — never run silt fence downhill, or water will flow around the ends and the fence will fail.
The Clean Water Act requires NPDES (National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System) permits for construction sites that disturb 1 acre or more of land. The permit requires:
•  A Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) — a written plan describing all ESC measures
•  Implementation of ESC measures before construction begins
•  Regular inspections (typically every 7 days and after rainfall events ≥ 0.5 inches)
•  Corrective action when measures are damaged or ineffective
•  Final stabilization before permit is terminated (70% vegetative cover in most regions)

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Erosion control prevents soil detachment (source control) — always the first priority. ✔  Sediment control captures eroded soil (treatment) — the last line of defense. ✔  Install ESC measures BEFORE any grading begins. ✔  Silt fence is placed along the contour on the downhill side — never run it downhill. ✔  NPDES permit required for sites ≥ 1 acre of disturbance. ✔  SWPPP documents all ESC measures; inspections every 7 days and after ≥ 0.5" rainfall. ✔  Final stabilization: 70% vegetative cover before permit termination.

subsections.title: 1. Silt fence is classified as a:

content.text: A)  Erosion control measure
B)  Sediment control measure
C)  Stormwater detention practice
D)  Permanent stabilization measure
Answer: B. Silt fence captures soil particles that have already been eroded — it is sediment control (treatment), not erosion control (prevention).

subsections.title: 2. An NPDES construction stormwater permit is required when the site disturbance area is:

content.text: A)  Any size
B)  0.5 acres or more
C)  1 acre or more
D)  5 acres or more
Answer: C. The NPDES Construction General Permit applies to construction activities that disturb 1 acre or more, or that are part of a larger common plan of development that disturbs 1 acre or more.

Drainage infrastructure collects surface runoff and conveys it to an outlet — a stream, detention basin, or regional stormwater system. This chapter covers the physical components of a storm drainage system: inlets, pipes, manholes, channels, culverts, and subsurface drains.

Inlets (catch basins): The entry points where surface water enters the underground storm sewer system. Inlets are located at low points in the grading (where water naturally collects), upstream of crosswalks (to prevent pedestrians from walking through ponded water), at building entries, and at intervals along curbed streets and parking lots.

rows: Horizontal grate over a box structure
Low points in parking lots and plazas; use bicycle-safe grates in pedestrian/bike areas
Opening in the face of a curb
Along curbed streets; captures gutter flow
Highest capacity; used at critical low points
Collecting sheet flow from small areas (patios, courtyards)
Long, narrow grate over a linear channel
Across doorways, garage entries, plaza transitions; intercepts sheet flow

content.text: Storm sewer pipe: Carries collected runoff underground from inlet to inlet and ultimately to the outfall. The most common materials are reinforced concrete pipe (RCP) for larger diameters (15" and up, strong, durable, long-lived) and HDPE for smaller connections and flexible applications. Pipe is designed to flow at or below full capacity for the design storm.

Manholes: Underground access chambers that allow maintenance crews to enter the system for cleaning and inspection. Required at changes in pipe direction, changes in pipe size, changes in pipe slope, junctions of two or more pipes, and at maximum spacing intervals (typically 300-400 feet).

Outfall: The point where the storm sewer system discharges. Outfalls require energy dissipation (riprap apron, stilling basin, or plunge pool) to prevent erosion of the receiving channel from concentrated high-velocity discharge.
Manning's equation calculates flow velocity in pipes and channels. It is the fundamental formula for storm sewer design:

subsections.title: V = flow velocity in feet per second (fps)
n = Manning's roughness coefficient (dimensionless) — lower n = smoother = faster flow
R = hydraulic radius in feet = cross-sectional flow area ÷ wetted perimeter
S = slope of the pipe or channel in feet per foot (decimal, not percent)

rows: Rougher interior; used for culverts and temporary drainage
Varies with bed material, vegetation, obstructions

content.text: The flow rate Q = V × A (continuity equation), where A is the cross-sectional flow area. For a circular pipe flowing full, A = π × D² / 4.

MEMORY AID:  Manning's equation: V = (1.49/n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2). Think "Velma runs slowly" — Velocity depends on Roughness (n) and Slope (S). Smoother surface (lower n) = faster. Steeper slope (higher S) = faster. The 1.49 is a unit conversion factor for US customary units.
•  Minimum pipe diameter: 12" (some jurisdictions require 15" or 18")
•  Minimum velocity: 2.5-3.0 fps — maintains self-cleaning velocity to prevent sediment buildup
•  Maximum velocity: 10-15 fps — prevents pipe erosion and damaging turbulence
•  Minimum cover: 12-24" of soil above pipe crown (varies by pipe material and traffic loading)
•  Pipe slope: steeper = faster velocity = smaller pipe needed; flatter = slower = larger pipe needed
•  Crown matching at manholes: the tops (crowns) of incoming and outgoing pipes align, not the inverts — this prevents backwater effects

French drains: Gravel-filled trenches (typically 12-24" wide, 18-36" deep) with a perforated pipe at the bottom, wrapped in filter fabric. French drains intercept shallow groundwater or surface water that infiltrates into the soil and redirect it to a positive outlet. They are commonly used behind retaining walls, along foundations, at the base of slopes, and at the edges of athletic fields.

Underdrains: Perforated pipes installed below bioretention facilities, permeable pavements, and athletic fields to drain excess water when infiltration alone is insufficient (HSG C/D soils). The underdrain connects to the storm sewer system, providing a positive outlet.

CHAPTER SUMMARY ✔  Inlets: grate (parking lots), curb (streets), combination (high capacity), area drain (small areas), trench drain (linear). ✔  Manholes required at pipe direction changes, size changes, slope changes, junctions, and every 300-400'. ✔  Outfalls require energy dissipation (riprap) to prevent downstream erosion. ✔  Manning's equation: V = (1.49/n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2). Lower n = smoother = faster. ✔  Pipe velocity: 2.5-3 fps minimum (self-cleaning), 10-15 fps maximum (prevent erosion). ✔  Crown matching at manholes — align pipe crowns, not inverts. ✔  French drains intercept groundwater; underdrains drain excess water from BMPs and fields.

subsections.title: 1. Manholes are required in a storm sewer system at all of the following EXCEPT:

content.text: A)  Changes in pipe direction
B)  Changes in pipe material only (same size and slope)
C)  Junctions of two or more pipes
D)  Changes in pipe size
Answer: B. Manholes are required at changes in direction, size, slope, and at junctions — but a simple material change at the same size, slope, and alignment typically does not require a manhole.

subsections.title: 2. The minimum self-cleaning velocity in a storm sewer pipe is approximately:

content.text: A)  0.5 fps
B)  1.5 fps
D)  10 fps
Answer: C. A velocity of 2.5-3.0 fps is needed to prevent sediment from settling in the pipe. Below this, solids accumulate and reduce capacity.

subsections.title: 3. In Manning's equation, a LOWER roughness coefficient (n) produces:

content.text: A)  Slower velocity
B)  Higher velocity
C)  No change in velocity
D)  Greater friction loss
Answer: B. Lower n means a smoother surface, which produces less friction and allows water to flow faster. Smooth concrete pipe (n = 0.012) carries water faster than corrugated metal (n = 0.024).

s4_book.title: Chapter 11: Comprehensive Review and Exam Strategy

rows: Contour reading, slope calculation, grading design, cut/fill, earthwork volumes
Rational Method (Q=CiA), BMP selection, detention/retention, erosion/sediment control
Inlets, pipe sizing, Manning's equation, manholes, subsurface drainage

content.text: •  Slope (%) = (Rise ÷ Run) × 100
•  Contour spacing = Contour interval ÷ Slope (decimal)
•  Q = CiA (Rational Method) — peak runoff rate
•  Composite C = Σ(Cn × An) / ΣAn
•  V = (1.49/n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2) (Manning's equation)
•  Q = V × A (continuity equation)
•  Volume (avg end area) = [(A₁ + A₂) / 2] × L
•  1 acre = 43,560 SF;  1 CY = 27 CF
•  Slope calculation from contour maps and between spot elevations
•  Slope standards for each site use (fields, parking, walks, ramps, lawns, swales, buildings)
•  Contour patterns: streams (V's point uphill), ridges (V's point downhill), hilltops, depressions
•  Positive drainage: 2% minimum away from buildings for 10'
•  The Rational Method (Q = CiA) and composite C calculation
•  BMP selection by soil type (HSG A-D)
•  Detention vs. retention — function, components, and design criteria
•  Erosion control (source) vs. sediment control (treatment)
•  Silt fence placement: along the contour, downhill side — never run downhill
•  NPDES permit triggers (≥ 1 acre disturbance)
•  Manning's equation — conceptual understanding of n, R, and S
•  Pipe velocity limits: 2.5-3 fps minimum, 10-15 fps maximum
•  Earthwork: cut vs. fill, shrinkage/swell factors
•  You have 70 questions in 3 hours — about 2.5 minutes per question. You have more time per question than other sections.
•  This section rewards calculator confidence. Practice Q=CiA and slope calculations until they are automatic.
•  For hotspot questions on grading plans: trace the contour patterns. V's uphill = stream. Concentric circles = hilltop or depression. Closely spaced = steep.
•  Read units carefully. Slope can be in %, ratio, or decimal. Area in acres or square feet. Mixing units is the most common calculation error.
•  When selecting BMPs, always check the soil type first. HSG D soils eliminate most infiltration practices.
•  For drag-and-drop sequence questions: think about what must happen first physically. Erosion control before grading. Subgrade before base. Base before surface.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect needs to determine the slope between two points. Point A is at elevation 102.0 and Point B is at elevation 98.0. The horizontal distance between them is 80 feet. What is the slope percentage?
Contour lines on a grading plan that form a "V" shape pointing uphill indicate:

choices.text: A ridge
A flat area
A retaining wall
A valley or swale

s4_exam.explanation: Contour lines forming a "V" pointing uphill indicate a valley or swale where water collects.

s4_exam.question: When grading around a building, the finished grade should slope AWAY from the building at a minimum of:

choices.text: 2% for 10 feet (or per code)
0.5% for 10 feet
10% for 5 feet
0% -- flat grades are acceptable against buildings

s4_exam.explanation: A minimum 2% slope away from a building for at least 10 feet (or per local code) ensures positive drainage away from the foundation.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a grading plan and needs to calculate the elevation at a point between two contour lines. This process is called:

choices.text: Extrapolation
Triangulation
Benchmarking
Interpolation

s4_exam.explanation: Interpolation estimates values between two known points (contour lines).

s4_exam.question: The maximum slope for an ADA-compliant ramp is:
s4_exam.explanation: ADA requires a maximum ramp slope of 1:12 (8.33%).

s4_exam.question: A proposed grading plan shows a finished floor elevation (FFE) of 100.0. The landscape architect should ensure the grade at the building perimeter is at LEAST:

choices.text: 100.0 (flush with the FFE)
100.5 (6 inches above the FFE)
98.0 (2 feet below the FFE)
99.5 (6 inches below the FFE)

s4_exam.explanation: The grade at the building perimeter should be at least 6 inches below the FFE to prevent water entry.

s4_exam.question: When grading a parking lot, the MINIMUM slope for adequate surface drainage is typically:
s4_exam.explanation: Parking lots typically require 1% to 2% minimum slope for surface drainage.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a swale to convey stormwater. The minimum longitudinal slope for a grass-lined swale to ensure positive drainage is typically:
s4_exam.explanation: Grass-lined swales typically require a minimum 1% to 2% slope for positive drainage.

s4_exam.question: In earthwork calculations, "cut" refers to:

choices.text: Removing soil to lower the grade
Adding soil to raise the grade
Compacting existing soil in place
Importing topsoil from off-site

s4_exam.explanation: Cut is the removal of soil to lower the existing grade.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect is balancing cut and fill on a project site. The PRIMARY goal of balancing cut and fill is to:

choices.text: Maximize the amount of soil exported from the site
Ensure that all cut material is wasted
Create the steepest possible grades
Minimize the need for importing or exporting soil, reducing cost and environmental impact

s4_exam.explanation: Balancing cut and fill minimizes the need for import or export, reducing cost and environmental impact.

s4_exam.question: When estimating earthwork quantities, the average end area method is used to:

choices.text: Calculate the volume of earth between two cross-sections
Calculate the volume of concrete for a foundation
Determine the structural capacity of a retaining wall
Estimate the cost of landscaping materials

s4_exam.explanation: The average end area method calculates earthwork volume between two cross-sections.

s4_exam.question: Soil that has been excavated and placed as fill typically requires a "swell factor" because:

choices.text: The soil shrinks when excavated
The soil becomes heavier when excavated
The soil changes color when disturbed
The excavated soil occupies more volume in a loose state than it did in its undisturbed state

s4_exam.explanation: Excavated soil is loosened and occupies more volume than in its undisturbed state (swell).

s4_exam.question: A French drain is BEST described as:

choices.text: A decorative surface channel with a grate
An open concrete channel
A surface inlet connected to a storm sewer
A subsurface trench filled with gravel and perforated pipe to collect and redirect groundwater

s4_exam.explanation: A French drain is a subsurface trench with gravel and perforated pipe for groundwater collection.

s4_exam.question: Manning's equation is used in drainage design to calculate:

choices.text: The flow velocity and capacity of open channels and pipes
The volume of water in a detention pond
The structural load on a retaining wall
The compaction rate of soil

s4_exam.explanation: Manning's equation calculates flow velocity and capacity in open channels and pipes.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect is sizing a storm drain pipe. If the contributing drainage area increases, the pipe size should:

choices.text: Increase
Decrease
Stay the same
The drainage area has no effect on pipe size

s4_exam.explanation: Larger drainage areas produce more runoff, requiring larger pipes.

s4_exam.question: An area drain (catch basin) is typically placed at:

choices.text: The highest point of the site
Low points where surface water collects
The top of a retaining wall
Directly against the building foundation

s4_exam.explanation: Area drains are placed at low points where surface water collects.

s4_exam.question: The time of concentration for a watershed is:

choices.text: The time it takes for the most distant point in the watershed to stop raining
The time it takes for runoff to travel from the hydraulically most distant point in the watershed to the outlet
The average rainfall duration for a 100-year storm
The time required to empty a detention basin

s4_exam.explanation: Time of concentration is the time for runoff to travel from the most distant point to the outlet.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect designs a subsurface drainage system behind a retaining wall. The PRIMARY purpose of this drainage is to:

choices.text: Irrigate plants on top of the wall
Increase the weight of the wall for stability
Relieve hydrostatic pressure that could cause wall failure
Provide water for a fountain on the opposite side

s4_exam.explanation: Drainage behind retaining walls relieves hydrostatic pressure that could cause wall failure.

s4_exam.question: Pre-development versus post-development runoff analysis is conducted to:

choices.text: Determine the aesthetic impact of the project
Calculate the cost of construction
Ensure that stormwater runoff rates and volumes after development do not exceed pre-development conditions
Determine the number of parking spaces required

s4_exam.explanation: Pre/post analysis ensures development does not increase runoff rates and volumes beyond pre-development levels.

s4_exam.question: A detention basin is designed to:

choices.text: Permanently store all stormwater runoff
Temporarily store stormwater and release it at a controlled rate to reduce peak discharge
Increase the velocity of stormwater leaving the site
Eliminate the need for any downstream stormwater infrastructure

s4_exam.explanation: Detention basins temporarily store water and release it at controlled rates to reduce peak discharge.

s4_exam.question: The difference between a detention basin and a retention basin is:

choices.text: There is no difference
A detention basin is always larger than a retention basin
A detention basin temporarily stores and slowly releases water; a retention basin permanently holds water
A retention basin releases water faster than a detention basin

s4_exam.explanation: Detention temporarily stores and releases water; retention permanently holds water (like a pond).

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect specifies permeable interlocking concrete pavers (PICP) for a parking area. The PRIMARY stormwater benefit of PICP is:

choices.text: It increases surface runoff
It eliminates the need for any stormwater management
It allows stormwater to infiltrate through the paver joints into an aggregate base, reducing runoff volume
It is impervious like conventional concrete

s4_exam.explanation: PICP allows stormwater to infiltrate through joints into the aggregate base, reducing runoff volume.

s4_exam.question: A typical construction detail for a concrete walkway should include:

choices.text: Cross-section showing subgrade preparation, aggregate base depth, concrete thickness, reinforcement, joints, and finish
Only the plan view dimensions
Only the surface finish specification
Only the color of the concrete

s4_exam.explanation: A complete walkway detail shows subgrade, base, concrete thickness, reinforcement, joints, and finish.

s4_exam.question: Control joints in concrete flatwork are provided to:

choices.text: Increase the strength of the concrete
Control the location of cracking due to shrinkage
Allow water to pass through the concrete
Provide a decorative pattern only

s4_exam.explanation: Control joints create a weakened plane to control where shrinkage cracking occurs.

s4_exam.question: The spacing of control joints in a 4-inch-thick concrete walkway should typically not exceed:

choices.text: 2 feet
20 feet
50 feet
8 to 10 feet (approximately 2 to 3 times the slab thickness in feet)

s4_exam.explanation: Control joint spacing should be approximately 2 to 3 times the slab thickness in feet. For 4-inch slabs, 8-10 feet is typical.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect is detailing a stone veneer wall. The detail should show:

choices.text: The structural backing (CMU or concrete), mortar bed, veneer stone, cap, footing, and drainage provisions
Only the stone veneer without any structural backing
Only the footing dimensions
Only the height of the wall

s4_exam.explanation: A complete stone veneer detail shows the structural backing, mortar, veneer, cap, footing, and drainage.

s4_exam.question: When detailing a timber deck, the landscape architect should specify:

choices.text: Posts supported on concrete footings extending below the frost line, with appropriate fasteners and flashing
Posts placed directly on the ground surface
No connection between the deck and the building
Untreated lumber for all structural members

s4_exam.explanation: Deck posts require concrete footings below the frost line with proper fasteners and flashing.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect details an accessible curb ramp at a street crossing. The detail should include:

choices.text: A ramp slope of 1:6
No detectable warning surfaces
A ramp that terminates 12 inches above the street surface
A ramp slope not exceeding 1:12, detectable warning surfaces, flared sides, and proper alignment with the crosswalk

s4_exam.explanation: Accessible curb ramps need 1:12 max slope, detectable warnings, flared sides, and crosswalk alignment.

s4_exam.question: In the CSI MasterFormat system, Division 32 covers:

choices.text: Exterior Improvements (site work including paving, planting, and site furnishings)
Concrete
Mechanical systems
Electrical systems

s4_exam.explanation: CSI MasterFormat Division 32 covers Exterior Improvements including paving, planting, and site elements.

s4_exam.question: A prescriptive specification defines:

choices.text: Only the desired performance outcome
Only the contractor's means and methods
The specific materials, products, methods, and installation requirements
Only the project schedule

s4_exam.explanation: Prescriptive specifications define specific materials, products, methods, and installation requirements.

s4_exam.question: The THREE parts of a CSI specification section are:

choices.text: Design, Build, Test
Scope, Schedule, Budget
General, Products, Execution
Materials, Labor, Equipment

s4_exam.explanation: CSI specification sections have three parts: General, Products, and Execution.

s4_exam.question: When a specification includes the phrase "or approved equal," it means:

choices.text: Only the named product may be used
The contractor may propose an alternative product that meets the same performance criteria, subject to the landscape architect's approval
Any product may be substituted without approval
The landscape architect must specify at least 10 alternatives

s4_exam.explanation: "Or approved equal" allows the contractor to propose alternatives meeting the same criteria, subject to approval.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect's construction document set typically includes which of the following sheets?

choices.text: Only a planting plan
Title sheet, demolition plan, layout plan, grading plan, drainage plan, planting plan, irrigation plan, and construction details
Only a grading plan and one detail sheet
Only specifications without any drawings

s4_exam.explanation: A complete CD set includes title, demolition, layout, grading, drainage, planting, irrigation, and details.

s4_exam.question: Dimensions on a layout plan should reference:

choices.text: Estimated distances based on the designer's visual judgment
Distances measured from the nearest tree
Established baselines, property lines, building faces, or control points for accurate field layout
Approximate locations with the note "contractor to verify all dimensions"

s4_exam.explanation: Layout dimensions should reference baselines, property lines, building faces, or control points.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect includes a plant schedule on the planting plan. The schedule should include:

choices.text: Botanical name, common name, quantity, size at installation, spacing (if applicable), root condition, and any special notes
Only the plant's common name
Only the total number of plants
Only the price of each plant

s4_exam.explanation: A plant schedule includes botanical name, common name, quantity, size, spacing, root condition, and notes.

s4_exam.question: A gravity retaining wall relies on which principle for stability?

choices.text: Soil reinforcement with geogrid
Its own mass and weight to resist the lateral pressure of the retained soil
Tiebacks anchored into bedrock
A cantilevered footing

s4_exam.explanation: Gravity walls resist lateral soil pressure through their own mass and weight.

s4_exam.question: The area behind a retaining wall where soil is placed is called:

choices.text: The toe
The backfill zone
The weep hole
The footing

s4_exam.explanation: The area behind a retaining wall where soil is placed is the backfill zone.

s4_exam.question: A landscape architect is designing a freestanding garden wall (not retaining soil). The wall requires a footing that extends:

choices.text: Only to the ground surface
Exactly 1 inch below grade
Above the ground surface for visibility
Below the frost line to prevent heaving

s4_exam.explanation: Freestanding wall footings must extend below the frost line to prevent frost heave.

s4_exam.question: During construction, a silt fence is installed to:

choices.text: Permanently filter stormwater runoff
Temporarily trap sediment from disturbed areas and prevent it from leaving the site during construction
Permanently replace vegetated buffers
Increase the velocity of stormwater runoff

s4_exam.explanation: Silt fences temporarily trap sediment during construction to prevent it from leaving the site.

s4_exam.question: A Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) is typically required for:

choices.text: Any project regardless of size
Only projects within 100 feet of a stream
Construction activities that disturb one acre or more of land (per EPA NPDES requirements)
Only projects on government-owned land

s4_exam.explanation: SWPPP is required for construction disturbing one acre or more under EPA NPDES requirements.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect enters into a contract with a client using AIA or ASLA standard form agreements. Which of the following is the landscape architect's PRIMARY obligation under such agreements?
s1_flash.back: A) Provide professional services with reasonable skill and care
s1_flash.detail: Landscape architects are held to a standard of reasonable skill and care, not perfection or guarantees.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect is negotiating fees for a public park project. Which fee structure would BEST protect the landscape architect when the scope of work is not clearly defined?
s1_flash.back: C) Hourly with a not-to-exceed cap
s1_flash.detail: Hourly with a not-to-exceed cap protects the LA when scope is undefined, limiting client exposure while compensating for actual time spent.

s1_flash.front: In a standard owner-landscape architect agreement, "Additional Services" typically includes which of the following?
s1_flash.back: B) Expert witness testimony
s1_flash.detail: Expert witness testimony is typically an additional service; schematic design, CD preparation, and CA are basic services.

s1_flash.front: Which contract delivery method gives the owner a single point of responsibility for both design and construction?
s1_flash.back: D) Design-Build
s1_flash.detail: Design-Build provides a single entity responsible for both design and construction.

s1_flash.front: Under a stipulated sum (lump sum) contract, who bears the greatest financial risk if unforeseen conditions arise?
s1_flash.back: A) The contractor
s1_flash.detail: Under a lump sum contract, the contractor assumes the risk of unforeseen conditions since the price is fixed.

s1_flash.front: During construction administration, a landscape architect observes that the contractor is installing a retaining wall foundation at a depth shallower than shown on the construction documents. The landscape architect should FIRST:
s1_flash.back: D) Notify the contractor of the discrepancy and document the observation
s1_flash.detail: The LA should first notify the contractor of the observed discrepancy and document it. The LA typically does not have stop-work authority.

s1_flash.front: A contractor submits a Request for Information (RFI) asking for clarification on a grading detail. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: B) Provide a written response within a reasonable time as defined in the contract
s1_flash.detail: RFIs should be responded to in writing within the timeframe established in the contract to maintain a proper project record.

s1_flash.front: Which of the following is the PRIMARY purpose of a submittal review during construction?
s1_flash.back: D) To confirm that materials and products are consistent with the design intent
s1_flash.detail: Submittal review confirms materials are consistent with design intent, not a guarantee of quality or review of means and methods.

s1_flash.front: A contractor requests a substitution for a specified tree species, claiming the specified species is unavailable. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: A) Evaluate the proposed substitution for design intent, quality, and suitability before responding
s1_flash.detail: The LA should evaluate the substitution against design intent, quality, and suitability before making a decision.

s1_flash.front: During a punch list walkthrough, the landscape architect identifies several items of incomplete work. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: D) Document the incomplete items and establish a timeline for completion before final payment
s1_flash.detail: Document incomplete items and establish a timeline for completion; retainage is typically held to cover punch list work.

s1_flash.front: A critical path method (CPM) schedule shows that landscape installation has zero float. This means:
s1_flash.back: B) Any delay in landscape installation will delay the overall project completion
s1_flash.detail: Zero float on a CPM schedule means the activity is on the critical path; any delay will delay the project.

s1_flash.front: Which of the following is the BEST method for tracking project budget during the design phase?
s1_flash.back: D) Monitoring hours and expenses against budget at regular intervals
s1_flash.detail: Regular monitoring of hours and expenses against budget allows for timely adjustments.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect discovers that the scope of a project has significantly expanded beyond the original agreement. The MOST appropriate action is to:
s1_flash.back: B) Notify the client, document the scope change, and negotiate an amendment to the contract
s1_flash.detail: Scope changes should be documented and the contract amended through proper negotiation.

s1_flash.front: Which of the following is a PRIMARY benefit of phasing a large construction project?
s1_flash.back: B) It allows portions of the project to be used while other portions are still under construction
s1_flash.detail: Phasing allows partial occupancy or use while other portions are still under construction.

s1_flash.front: A project has a fast-track schedule. Which of the following is a characteristic of fast-tracking?
s1_flash.back: A) Design and construction phases overlap, with construction beginning before design is fully complete
s1_flash.detail: Fast-tracking overlaps design and construction phases, beginning construction before design is fully complete.

s1_flash.front: Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), which of the following is the MAXIMUM allowable running slope for an accessible route?
s1_flash.detail: ADA requires a maximum running slope of 1:20 (5%) for accessible routes. Ramps (which are steeper portions) may be up to 1:12.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect seals and signs a set of construction documents. By doing so, the landscape architect is:
s1_flash.back: A) Certifying that the documents were prepared under their responsible charge
s1_flash.detail: Sealing documents certifies they were prepared under the LA's responsible charge; it does not guarantee outcomes.

s1_flash.front: Which of the following activities would MOST LIKELY require the landscape architect to coordinate with a local zoning authority?
s1_flash.back: B) Designing a parking lot layout that must meet minimum landscaping requirements
s1_flash.detail: Parking lot landscaping requirements are typically regulated through local zoning ordinances.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect learns that a proposed project may impact wetlands regulated under the Clean Water Act. The MOST appropriate action is to:
s1_flash.back: C) Advise the client of the regulatory requirements and coordinate with appropriate agencies early in the process
s1_flash.detail: Early coordination with regulatory agencies regarding wetland impacts is essential and a professional responsibility.

s1_flash.front: In most jurisdictions, a landscape architect's license can be revoked or suspended for which of the following?
s1_flash.back: C) Practicing outside the scope of licensure or professional misconduct
s1_flash.detail: Practicing outside the scope of licensure or professional misconduct are grounds for license revocation or suspension.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect is asked by a developer to certify that a project meets local tree preservation ordinance requirements. Upon review, the landscape architect determines the project does NOT fully comply. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: A) Refuse to certify and inform the client of the specific areas of non-compliance
s1_flash.detail: The LA has an ethical and legal obligation to refuse to certify non-compliant work and inform the client of deficiencies.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect discovers a potential conflict of interest because they own stock in a company that manufactures a product they intend to specify. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: C) Disclose the conflict of interest to the client and allow the client to decide how to proceed
s1_flash.detail: Conflicts of interest must be disclosed to the client, who can then make an informed decision.

s1_flash.front: A former client asks a landscape architect for copies of construction documents from a completed project to give to a new designer. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: D) Provide the documents in accordance with the terms of the original contract regarding document ownership
s1_flash.detail: Document ownership and distribution rights are governed by the original contract terms.

s1_flash.front: During a public bidding process, a landscape architect receives a question from one bidder requesting clarification on the specifications. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: A) Issue an addendum with the clarification to all bidders
s1_flash.detail: In public bidding, all clarifications must be issued as addenda to all bidders to ensure fairness.

s1_flash.front: Which of the following bond types protects the owner in the event the contractor fails to complete the project?
s1_flash.back: C) Performance bond
s1_flash.detail: A performance bond guarantees the contractor will complete the work per the contract.

s1_flash.front: An owner on a private project wants to negotiate directly with a single contractor rather than competitively bid the project. This approach is known as:
s1_flash.back: C) Negotiated contract
s1_flash.detail: Directly negotiating with a single contractor is a negotiated contract approach.

s1_flash.front: "Substantial completion" in a construction project is BEST defined as:
s1_flash.back: B) The stage at which the work is sufficiently complete that the owner can occupy or use the project for its intended purpose
s1_flash.detail: Substantial completion is when the work is sufficiently complete for the owner to use it for its intended purpose.

s1_flash.front: A change order is typically used to:
s1_flash.back: D) Document agreed-upon changes to the contract sum, contract time, or scope of work
s1_flash.detail: Change orders document agreed-upon changes to contract sum, time, or scope.

s1_flash.front: Which of the following types of specifications gives the contractor the MOST flexibility in selecting products?
s1_flash.back: D) Performance specification
s1_flash.detail: Performance specifications define required outcomes, giving the contractor maximum flexibility in product selection.

s1_flash.front: Retainage in a construction contract refers to:
s1_flash.back: C) A percentage of each progress payment withheld by the owner until project completion
s1_flash.detail: Retainage is a percentage of each payment withheld until project completion to ensure the contractor completes all work.

s1_flash.front: Professional liability insurance (errors and omissions insurance) for a landscape architect covers:
s1_flash.back: C) Claims arising from negligent professional services
s1_flash.detail: Professional liability (E&O) insurance covers claims arising from negligent professional services.

s1_flash.front: Which of the following is the MOST effective way for a landscape architect to manage risk on a project?
s1_flash.back: D) Maintain thorough documentation throughout all project phases
s1_flash.detail: Thorough documentation is the most effective risk management strategy for design professionals.

s1_flash.front: During the schematic design phase, which type of cost estimate is MOST appropriate?
s1_flash.back: B) Order-of-magnitude estimate
s1_flash.detail: Order-of-magnitude estimates are appropriate for schematic design when limited detail is available.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect's construction cost estimate exceeds the client's budget. The MOST appropriate course of action is to:
s1_flash.back: C) Discuss value engineering options with the client to reduce costs while maintaining design intent
s1_flash.detail: Value engineering explores cost reductions while maintaining design intent, which is the appropriate professional response.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a project seeking LEED certification. Which of the following site-related credits would the landscape architect MOST likely be responsible for?
s1_flash.back: A) Reducing light pollution through exterior lighting design
s1_flash.detail: Exterior lighting design to reduce light pollution (Sustainable Sites credit) falls within the LA's scope of work.

s1_flash.front: When designing a public playground, which of the following standards should the landscape architect reference for safety compliance?
s1_flash.back: A) ASTM and CPSC playground safety guidelines
s1_flash.detail: ASTM F1487 and CPSC Publication 325 are the primary playground safety standards.

s1_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a stormwater management facility for a public park. The PRIMARY consideration for public safety is:
s1_flash.back: C) Balancing stormwater function with safe public access, including appropriate grading, signage, and barriers where needed
s1_flash.detail: Stormwater facilities in public spaces must balance function with safe public access through appropriate design measures.

s1_flash.front: During a multi-disciplinary project, the landscape architect discovers a conflict between the civil engineer's grading plan and the landscape planting plan. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: B) Coordinate with the civil engineer to resolve the conflict before issuing construction documents
s1_flash.detail: Conflicts between disciplines should be resolved through coordination before issuing documents.

s1_flash.front: Meeting minutes from a client meeting should include which of the following?
s1_flash.back: D) Key decisions, action items, responsible parties, and deadlines
