s1_flash.detail: Effective meeting minutes capture key decisions, action items, responsible parties, and deadlines.

s1_flash.front: A contractor claims additional compensation for work they say was not included in the original contract documents. The landscape architect should:
s1_flash.back: A) Review the original contract documents to determine if the work was included and respond accordingly
s1_flash.detail: The LA should review the original documents to determine if the claimed extra work was already included before responding.

s1_flash.front: EXAM FORMAT:  Section 1 uses both standard multiple-choice questions and graphic Advanced Item Types (AITs).
s1_flash.back: AITs present you with maps, diagrams, or images and ask you to interpret them. Practice reading topographic maps, soil surveys, FIRM maps, and aerial photographs before exam day. The free CLARB demo exam lets you practice the testing interface.

s1_flash.front: Memory Aid
s1_flash.back: CLORPT: Climate, Living organisms, O (relief/topography), Rock (parent material), Time. Think "CLORox Plus Time" — these five factors bleach the rock into soil over time.

s1_flash.front: When the exam describes soil behavior, you should be able to work backward to identify the probable texture.
s1_flash.back: If a question says the soil drains rapidly and does not hold moisture, think sand. If it says the soil cracks when dry and is sticky when wet, think clay. If it says the soil feels smooth and erodes easily when wet, think silt.

s1_flash.front: Memory Aid
s1_flash.back: Think of the HSGs as a grading scale from best to worst infiltration: A is the best (like getting an A grade), D is the worst (failing at infiltration). A = Awesome drainage, D = Dreadful drainage.

s1_flash.front: The exam may present soil survey data and ask you to interpret it.
s1_flash.back: Practice using the Web Soil Survey before the exam. Navigate to a site, generate a soil report, and review the properties tables. Pay special attention to drainage class, HSG, depth to restrictive features, and hydric ratings.

s1_flash.front: If the exam describes a soil as hydric, it is telling you the site may contain jurisdictional wetlands requiring Section 404 permits from the Army Corps of Engineers.
s1_flash.back: Hydric soil = potential regulatory constraint. Always recommend further investigation.

s1_flash.front: Memory Aid
s1_flash.back: Key slope thresholds: 1-2% = minimum drainage; 5% = max ADA accessible route; 8.33% (1:12) = max ADA ramp; 25% = max practical constructed slope; 33% (3:1) = max mowable turf. Write these five numbers on your scratch paper when the exam begins.

s1_flash.front: If a question asks which slope orientation is warmest and driest, the answer is south-facing.
s1_flash.back: If it asks which is coolest and most moist, the answer is north-facing. If it asks which receives the most intense heat, the answer is west-facing (afternoon sun).

s1_flash.front: The exam loves to test the concept that development increases runoff.
s1_flash.back: The key mechanism is simple: replacing pervious surfaces (forest, meadow) with impervious surfaces (roofs, pavement) increases the runoff coefficient C, which directly increases Q. This is the fundamental justification for stormwater management requirements.

s1_flash.front: Memory Aid
s1_flash.back: The "100-year flood" has a 1% chance of occurring in any given year. It does NOT mean it floods once every 100 years. Over a 30-year mortgage, a property in the 100-year floodplain has approximately a 26% chance of experiencing at least one flood — a much higher risk than most people realize. This is a commonly tested misconception.

s1_flash.front: The exam may describe vegetation and ask you to infer site conditions.
s1_flash.back: If a question mentions cattails and sedges, the answer almost certainly involves wetlands, hydric soils, or regulatory constraints. If it mentions oaks and hickories, think well-drained upland.

s1_flash.front: If a question asks about reducing urban temperatures or mitigating the heat island effect, look for answers involving trees, vegetation, high-albedo materials, green roofs, or reduced impervious surfaces.
s1_flash.back: Answers involving more pavement, removing trees, or dark materials are always wrong.

s1_flash.front: Memory Aid
s1_flash.back: Match the data to the source: Topo = USGS. Soils = NRCS. Floods = FEMA. Wetlands = USFWS. Demographics = Census. Climate = NOAA. Contamination = EPA. History = SHPO. Zoning = Local Planning. Property = County Recorder.

s1_flash.front: The exam may present a project scenario and ask which level of participation is most appropriate.
s1_flash.back: Match the level to the public's role: if the decision is made and you are sharing information, that is Inform. If you are seeking feedback, that is Consult. If stakeholders are co-designing, that is Collaborate. A design charrette = Involve or Collaborate level.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is conducting a site inventory for a 50-acre park project. Which of the following should be the FIRST step in the inventory process?
s2_flash.back: B) Reviewing existing data including surveys, aerial photographs, GIS data, and public records
s2_flash.detail: Reviewing existing data is the most efficient first step before conducting field work.

s2_flash.front: A topographic survey of a project site shows contour lines that are closely spaced on the western portion and widely spaced on the eastern portion. This indicates:
s2_flash.back: B) The western portion has steep slopes and the eastern portion has gentle slopes
s2_flash.detail: Closely spaced contours indicate steep slopes; widely spaced contours indicate gentle slopes.

s2_flash.front: When evaluating an existing site, a landscape architect identifies a stand of mature trees. Which of the following data is MOST important to collect for each tree?
s2_flash.back: D) Species, size (DBH), condition, and canopy spread
s2_flash.detail: Species, DBH, condition, and canopy spread are essential for evaluating tree preservation and design.

s2_flash.front: A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) is conducted to:
s2_flash.back: D) Identify potential environmental contamination liabilities through records review, site reconnaissance, and interviews
s2_flash.detail: A Phase I ESA identifies potential contamination through records review, site reconnaissance, and interviews without intrusive testing.

s2_flash.front: Which of the following soil characteristics is MOST critical for determining the suitability of a site for stormwater infiltration?
s2_flash.back: C) Soil texture and permeability (infiltration rate)
s2_flash.detail: Soil texture and permeability directly determine infiltration rates and stormwater management feasibility.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is analyzing a site in the Northern Hemisphere for solar exposure. Which slope orientation receives the MOST direct sunlight throughout the year?
s2_flash.back: D) South-facing slope
s2_flash.detail: In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes receive the most direct sunlight throughout the year.

s2_flash.front: A site analysis reveals that prevailing winter winds come from the northwest. Which design strategy would BEST mitigate wind exposure for an outdoor seating area?
s2_flash.back: C) Plant a dense evergreen windbreak to the northwest of the seating area
s2_flash.detail: A dense evergreen windbreak to the northwest provides year-round protection from prevailing winter winds.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is assessing viewsheds from a proposed hilltop overlook. A viewshed analysis would BEST be conducted using:
s2_flash.back: D) GIS-based terrain modeling and line-of-sight analysis
s2_flash.detail: GIS-based terrain modeling with line-of-sight analysis is the standard method for viewshed assessment.

s2_flash.front: When analyzing a site's hydrology, the landscape architect identifies a 100-year floodplain boundary. This boundary indicates:
s2_flash.back: A) An area that has a 1% chance of flooding in any given year
s2_flash.detail: The 100-year floodplain has a 1% annual chance of flooding, not a literal 100-year cycle.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is analyzing a site with a high water table. Which of the following design considerations is MOST directly affected?
s2_flash.back: D) Foundation design, plant selection, and subsurface drainage
s2_flash.detail: A high water table directly affects foundations, plant selection, and subsurface drainage design.

s2_flash.front: A soil percolation test is PRIMARILY used to determine:
s2_flash.back: D) The rate at which water moves through the soil
s2_flash.detail: Percolation tests measure the rate water moves through soil, important for septic and infiltration design.

s2_flash.front: Which USDA soil texture has the HIGHEST infiltration rate?
s2_flash.back: D) Sand
s2_flash.detail: Sandy soils have the largest particle size and highest infiltration rate among the options.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect reviews a USDA Web Soil Survey report for a project site. The report classifies the soil as "hydric." This classification indicates:
s2_flash.back: C) The soil formed under conditions of saturation and may indicate the presence of wetlands
s2_flash.detail: Hydric soils formed under saturated conditions and are one of three indicators of wetlands.

s2_flash.front: A site has expansive clay soils. Which of the following is the PRIMARY concern for site development?
s2_flash.back: C) The soil will shrink and swell with changes in moisture content, potentially damaging structures
s2_flash.detail: Expansive clays shrink and swell with moisture changes, causing structural damage.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect identifies a plant community dominated by cattails, sedges, and rushes during a site inventory. This plant community MOST likely indicates:
s2_flash.back: D) A wetland or hydric soil conditions
s2_flash.detail: Cattails, sedges, and rushes are hydrophytic plants that indicate wetland or hydric conditions.

s2_flash.front: The concept of ecological succession refers to:
s2_flash.back: C) The predictable, sequential change in plant community composition over time
s2_flash.detail: Ecological succession is the predictable, sequential change in plant community composition over time.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a project in a region with endemic species. Which of the following is the MOST important consideration?
s2_flash.back: A) Preserving habitat for endemic species and incorporating native plant communities
s2_flash.detail: Preserving habitat for endemic species is critical to maintaining regional biodiversity and ecosystem function.

s2_flash.front: A riparian buffer zone serves which PRIMARY ecological function?
s2_flash.back: A) Filtering pollutants, stabilizing stream banks, and providing wildlife habitat
s2_flash.detail: Riparian buffers filter pollutants, stabilize banks, and provide habitat along waterways.

s2_flash.front: The urban heat island effect is PRIMARILY caused by:
s2_flash.back: C) Large areas of impervious surfaces and reduced vegetation that absorb and re-radiate heat
s2_flash.detail: Impervious surfaces absorb and re-radiate heat, and reduced vegetation decreases cooling, creating heat islands.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing an outdoor plaza in a hot, arid climate. Which strategy would MOST effectively reduce the microclimate temperature?
s2_flash.back: B) Incorporating shade trees, light-colored paving, and water features
s2_flash.detail: Shade trees, light-colored paving, and water features work together to reduce microclimate temperatures.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is developing a program for a community park. The MOST effective method for identifying community needs and priorities is:
s2_flash.back: A) Conducting stakeholder engagement, including public meetings, surveys, and interviews
s2_flash.detail: Stakeholder engagement through multiple methods is the most effective way to identify community needs.

s2_flash.front: A program for a new public space identifies a need for both active recreation and passive contemplation. Which programming strategy BEST addresses both needs?
s2_flash.back: C) Creating distinct zones within the site that accommodate both active and passive uses with appropriate transitions
s2_flash.detail: Zoning the site for different use types with transitions is the best strategy for accommodating multiple needs.

s2_flash.front: During programming, a landscape architect discovers that the client's desired program exceeds the capacity of the site. The MOST appropriate response is to:
s2_flash.back: A) Present the client with an analysis showing site capacity and recommend prioritization of program elements
s2_flash.detail: Present a site capacity analysis and help the client prioritize program elements within the site's constraints.

s2_flash.front: A site is located within a designated historic district. Before proceeding with design, the landscape architect should:
s2_flash.back: C) Research applicable preservation guidelines and coordinate with the appropriate historic preservation authority
s2_flash.detail: Historic district designation affects site design; coordination with preservation authorities is required.

s2_flash.front: A project site contains jurisdictional wetlands. Under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, which federal agency is responsible for issuing permits for discharging dredged or fill material into wetlands?
s2_flash.back: B) U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
s2_flash.detail: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers issues Section 404 permits for activities in jurisdictional wetlands.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a project on a coastal site subject to the Coastal Zone Management Act. Which of the following is MOST important to consider?
s2_flash.back: B) Coastal erosion, storm surge, sea level rise, and consistency with the state's coastal management program
s2_flash.detail: Coastal projects must address erosion, storm surge, sea level rise, and state coastal management programs.

s2_flash.front: When conducting a site analysis, a landscape architect discovers potential archaeological resources on the site. The landscape architect should:
s2_flash.back: A) Notify the client and recommend consultation with appropriate authorities before design proceeds
s2_flash.detail: Archaeological resources require notification and consultation with appropriate authorities before proceeding.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a memorial space. Which of the following is the MOST critical aspect of the programming process?
s2_flash.back: B) Engaging stakeholders to understand the significance, narrative, and emotional qualities desired for the space
s2_flash.detail: Memorial spaces require deep stakeholder engagement to understand significance and desired emotional qualities.

s2_flash.front: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are MOST useful for:
s2_flash.back: A) Layering, analyzing, and visualizing spatial data to support site analysis and planning decisions
s2_flash.detail: GIS excels at layering and analyzing spatial data for planning and site analysis decisions.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect uses a SWOT analysis during the planning process. SWOT stands for:
s2_flash.back: A) Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
s2_flash.detail: SWOT stands for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats.

s2_flash.front: The carrying capacity of a site refers to:
s2_flash.back: B) The maximum level of use or development a site can sustain without unacceptable degradation
s2_flash.detail: Carrying capacity is the maximum use level a site can sustain without unacceptable degradation.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect analyzes a site's existing drainage patterns and identifies a natural swale that collects runoff from a 10-acre area. The BEST approach for site development is to:
s2_flash.back: D) Preserve and integrate the natural drainage feature into the site design
s2_flash.detail: Preserving natural drainage features is both ecologically and functionally preferable.

s2_flash.front: A watershed analysis for a development project should consider which of the following?
s2_flash.back: A) The entire upstream contributing drainage area and downstream receiving waters
s2_flash.detail: Watershed analysis must consider the entire upstream contributing area and downstream receiving waters.

s2_flash.front: Kevin Lynch's "The Image of the City" identifies five elements of urban form. Which of the following is NOT one of Lynch's five elements?
s2_flash.back: D) Textures
s2_flash.detail: Lynch's five elements are Paths, Edges, Districts, Nodes, and Landmarks. Textures is not one of them.

s2_flash.front: A figure-ground analysis of an urban site is PRIMARILY used to:
s2_flash.back: A) Analyze the relationship between built form (figure) and open space (ground)
s2_flash.detail: Figure-ground analysis examines the relationship between built form and open space in an urban context.

s2_flash.front: A landscape architect is analyzing vehicular and pedestrian circulation patterns on a site. The PRIMARY goal of this analysis is to:
s2_flash.back: B) Identify conflicts, opportunities, and appropriate separation between modes of circulation
s2_flash.detail: Circulation analysis identifies conflicts and opportunities for appropriate separation between modes.

s2_flash.front: A traffic calming strategy for a residential neighborhood might include which of the following?
s2_flash.back: C) Installing speed tables, chicanes, and narrowing travel lanes
s2_flash.detail: Speed tables, chicanes, and lane narrowing are established traffic calming measures.

s2_flash.front: During site inventory, the landscape architect identifies existing underground utilities. Why is the accurate location of utilities CRITICAL to the design process?
s2_flash.back: B) To avoid conflicts with proposed site features and ensure safe construction, as well as to plan for required easements and setbacks
s2_flash.detail: Accurate utility locations prevent conflicts, ensure safety during construction, and inform easement planning.

s2_flash.front: The Rational Method (Q = CiA) is used to:
s2_flash.back: C) Estimate peak stormwater runoff from a drainage area
s2_flash.detail: The Rational Method estimates peak stormwater runoff rate from a drainage area.

s2_flash.front: In the Rational Method, the "C" coefficient represents:
s2_flash.back: B) The runoff coefficient, reflecting the proportion of rainfall that becomes surface runoff
s2_flash.detail: The "C" coefficient represents the runoff coefficient -- the proportion of rainfall that becomes surface runoff.

s2_flash.front: EXAM FORMAT:  Section 2 uses both standard multiple-choice questions and multiple-response questions.
s2_flash.back: Multiple-response questions ask you to select ALL correct answers from a list. You must select every correct option and no incorrect options to receive full credit. Read each question carefully to determine if it asks for the single best answer or all that apply.

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: Triple Bottom Line = People, Planet, Profit. A truly sustainable project scores well on all three. If any leg of the stool is missing, the project will eventually fail.

s2_flash.front: Know the difference between SITES and LEED.
s2_flash.back: SITES is landscape-focused and can certify projects without buildings. LEED is building-focused but includes site-related credits. On the exam, if a question asks about certifying a park, plaza, or streetscape, SITES is the correct framework — not LEED.

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: LID = Little Individual Devices everywhere, instead of one Big Pipe to somewhere else. Distribute, don't concentrate.

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: D/H ratio: think of it as the room you are standing in. A 1:1 ratio feels like a narrow hallway — the walls are as tall as the room is wide. A 4:1 ratio feels like standing in a field — the edges are too far away to define the space.

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: Lynch's 5 elements: PEDAL — Paths, Edges, Districts, nodes (And), Landmarks. Or think PEDNL: People Enter Districts Near Landmarks.

s2_flash.front: The exam frequently tests Lynch's elements.
s2_flash.back: If a question describes a major intersection where several paths converge, the answer is NODE. If it describes a distinctive tower visible from across a park, the answer is LANDMARK. If it describes a linear boundary between two neighborhoods, the answer is EDGE.

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: Secretary's Standards: P-R-R-R. Preservation (keep it), Rehabilitation (adapt it), Restoration (return it to a specific period), Reconstruction (rebuild what's gone). Rehabilitation is the most commonly used because it allows new uses while respecting historic character.

s2_flash.front: Memorize ADA parking requirements.
s2_flash.back: They appear frequently. Know: 1 accessible space per 25 total, van-accessible spaces need 8' access aisles, and all accessible spaces must be on the shortest accessible route to the building entrance.

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: The transect goes from trees to towers: T1 (Nature) → T2 (Rural) → T3 (Suburban) → T4 (Urban) → T5 (Center) → T6 (Core). Each zone gets progressively denser and more urban.

s2_flash.front: If the exam asks what tool shows spatial relationships and adjacencies between program elements at the earliest design stage, the answer is bubble diagram.
s2_flash.back: If it asks what comes next, the answer is concept diagram or functional diagram.

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: ADA slopes: 5-2-8. Maximum running slope = 5%. Maximum cross slope = 2%. Maximum ramp slope = 8.33% (1:12). These three numbers answer most ADA slope questions on the exam.

s2_flash.front: When the exam mentions a walking surface that exceeds 5% running slope, it is no longer an accessible route — it becomes a ramp.
s2_flash.back: Ramps require handrails, landings, and edge protection. If a surface exceeds 8.33%, it does not comply with ADA at all.

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: Slope limits to memorize: Athletic fields = 1-2%. Parking = 1-5%. Accessible route = max 5%. Ramps = max 8.33%. Mowed turf = max 25% (3:1). Unmowed = max 50% (2:1). Building perimeter = min 2% away for 10 feet.

s2_flash.front: When an exam question asks which BMP is appropriate for a clay soil (HSG D) site, eliminate infiltration-based practices (rain garden without underdrain, infiltration trench, permeable pavement without underdrain).
s2_flash.back: Choose detention-based or evapotranspiration-based practices (constructed wetland, green roof, cistern, or bioretention with underdrain).

s2_flash.front: Memory Aid
s2_flash.back: Xeriscape 7 principles: P-S-T-P-I-M-M. Planning, Soil improvement, Turf limits, Plant selection, Irrigation efficiency, Mulch, Maintenance. Think: "Pretty Smart To Plant In Mulched Meadows."

s2_flash.front: If the exam asks how to reduce energy costs for a building in a cold climate, the answer involves deciduous shade trees on the south and west (summer cooling) plus an evergreen windbreak on the north and northwest (winter wind protection).
s2_flash.back: Deciduous trees allow solar gain in winter when their leaves drop.

s2_flash.front: Know the accuracy ranges for each design phase.
s2_flash.back: If the exam asks about the accuracy of a schematic-level cost estimate, the answer is ±15-25%. These ranges are commonly tested.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a formal garden. Which of the following design principles is MOST characteristic of formal design?
s3_flash.back: B) Symmetrical balance with strong axial organization
s3_flash.detail: Formal gardens are characterized by symmetry, axial organization, and geometric forms.

s3_flash.front: The principle of "unity" in landscape design is BEST achieved by:
s3_flash.back: D) Repeating design elements such as materials, forms, colors, and textures to create visual coherence
s3_flash.detail: Unity is achieved through repetition and consistency of design elements throughout the site.

s3_flash.front: In design, the concept of "scale" refers to:
s3_flash.back: A) The perceived size of elements in relation to the human body and surrounding context
s3_flash.detail: Scale refers to the perceived size of elements relative to the human body and surrounding context.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect uses a sequence of spaces that transition from large and open to small and enclosed. This design technique creates:
s3_flash.back: D) A sense of spatial compression and release that enhances the experience of movement through the landscape
s3_flash.detail: Alternating spatial compression and release creates a dynamic experience of movement through landscape.

s3_flash.front: The "genius loci" of a site refers to:
s3_flash.back: C) The unique spirit, character, or sense of place inherent to a specific location
s3_flash.detail: Genius loci refers to the unique spirit or character of a place.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a pedestrian plaza. Which of the following dimensions would provide the MOST comfortable width for a primary pedestrian walkway?
s3_flash.back: D) 10 feet or wider
s3_flash.detail: Primary pedestrian walkways in plazas should be 10 feet or wider to accommodate multiple users and ADA requirements.

s3_flash.front: When designing a vehicular drop-off area at a public building entrance, the landscape architect should ensure:
s3_flash.back: B) The drop-off allows one-way circulation with adequate queuing and a clear connection to the building entrance
s3_flash.detail: Drop-offs should allow one-way flow with queuing space and a clear pedestrian connection to the entrance.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing an amphitheater. The seating area should be oriented so that:
s3_flash.back: D) The audience faces north or northeast to minimize sun glare during evening performances
s3_flash.detail: Orienting the audience north or northeast minimizes sun glare during afternoon and evening events.

s3_flash.front: When designing a children's play area within a public park, which of the following is the MOST important consideration?
s3_flash.back: A) Providing clear sight lines for caregiver supervision, age-appropriate equipment zones, and appropriate safety surfacing
s3_flash.detail: Clear sight lines for supervision, age-appropriate zones, and safety surfacing are the most critical safety considerations.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a parking lot for 200 vehicles. Which of the following strategies BEST reduces the environmental impact of the parking area?
s3_flash.back: D) Incorporating bioswales, shade trees, permeable paving, and landscape islands to reduce heat island effect and manage stormwater
s3_flash.detail: Bioswales, shade trees, permeable paving, and landscape islands reduce environmental impact through stormwater management and heat island mitigation.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is selecting trees for a streetscape design. Which of the following characteristics is MOST important for street tree selection?
s3_flash.back: C) The tree should have a form and root structure compatible with the urban environment, including tolerance for compacted soils, limited root space, and urban heat
s3_flash.detail: Street trees must tolerate urban conditions including compacted soils, limited root space, heat, and pollution.

s3_flash.front: In a planting design, "layering" refers to:
s3_flash.back: D) Arranging plants in vertical layers (canopy, understory, shrub, groundcover) to create spatial complexity and ecological function
s3_flash.detail: Layering creates vertical plant structure from canopy to groundcover for spatial and ecological complexity.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a rain garden. Which of the following plant characteristics is MOST important for plant selection?
s3_flash.back: C) Plants that tolerate both periodic inundation and dry periods
s3_flash.detail: Rain garden plants must tolerate alternating wet and dry conditions.

s3_flash.front: When designing a foundation planting for a building, the landscape architect should consider:
s3_flash.back: B) Mature plant size, building scale, maintenance access, window locations, and structural clearances
s3_flash.detail: Foundation plantings must account for mature size, building scale, maintenance access, and clearances.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect specifies a mix of deciduous and evergreen plants in a design. Which of the following is the PRIMARY design benefit of this approach?
s3_flash.back: B) It provides year-round visual interest, with seasonal variety from deciduous plants and winter structure from evergreens
s3_flash.detail: Mixing deciduous and evergreen plants provides seasonal variety and year-round structure.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a lawn area for passive recreation. Which slope range is MOST appropriate for comfortable use?
s3_flash.detail: Slopes of 0.5% to 3% provide adequate drainage while remaining comfortable for passive recreation.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect designs a berm to screen a parking lot from an adjacent residential area. The berm should be designed with:
s3_flash.back: A) Slopes no steeper than 3:1 (horizontal to vertical) for mowable turf and adequate height to screen views
s3_flash.detail: Berms with mowable turf should have slopes no steeper than 3:1 for maintenance and stability.

s3_flash.front: When designing a terrace on a hillside site, the landscape architect should consider:
s3_flash.back: B) Using a series of walls with appropriate heights, incorporating proper drainage behind walls, and creating usable spaces between terraces
s3_flash.detail: Terracing should use appropriately sized walls with drainage and create usable spaces between terraces.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is selecting paving materials for a public plaza in a climate with freeze-thaw cycles. Which of the following is the MOST important material property to consider?
s3_flash.back: C) Absorption rate and freeze-thaw resistance
s3_flash.detail: In freeze-thaw climates, low absorption and freeze-thaw resistance prevent material deterioration.

s3_flash.front: Which of the following wall types is MOST appropriate for a retaining wall with a height of 6 feet or more?
s3_flash.back: B) Engineered reinforced concrete or mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) wall
s3_flash.detail: Walls 6 feet or taller require engineered solutions like reinforced concrete or MSE for structural safety.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect specifies unit pavers for a pedestrian area. The PRIMARY advantage of unit pavers over poured-in-place concrete is:
s3_flash.back: A) Unit pavers allow for easier repair of individual sections, accommodate minor ground movement, and can be permeable
s3_flash.detail: Unit pavers allow individual repair, accommodate ground movement, and can be installed as permeable systems.

s3_flash.front: When selecting wood for an outdoor bench, the landscape architect should specify:
s3_flash.back: C) Naturally durable or sustainably sourced species (e.g., black locust, FSC-certified ipe) appropriate for exterior exposure
s3_flash.detail: Naturally durable or sustainably sourced exterior-grade wood is appropriate for outdoor furniture.

s3_flash.front: According to ADA guidelines, an accessible ramp with a rise greater than 6 inches requires:
s3_flash.back: A) Handrails on both sides
s3_flash.detail: ADA requires handrails on both sides of ramps with a rise greater than 6 inches.

s3_flash.front: Universal design differs from ADA compliance in that:
s3_flash.back: A) Universal design aims to create environments usable by all people to the greatest extent possible, going beyond minimum code requirements
s3_flash.detail: Universal design creates environments usable by all people, going beyond minimum ADA compliance.

s3_flash.front: An accessible route must have a minimum clear width of:
s3_flash.back: D) 36 inches
s3_flash.detail: ADA requires a minimum clear width of 36 inches for accessible routes.

s3_flash.front: At an accessible parking space, an access aisle must be provided. The access aisle must be:
s3_flash.back: A) At least 60 inches wide and marked to discourage parking
s3_flash.detail: Access aisles must be at least 60 inches wide and marked to prevent parking.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a reflecting pool for a civic plaza. The MOST important design consideration for public safety is:
s3_flash.back: C) Limiting water depth, providing visible edges, and ensuring proper water treatment to prevent health hazards
s3_flash.detail: Public water features must limit depth, define edges, and maintain water quality for safety.

s3_flash.front: When designing an irrigation system for a public landscape, the landscape architect should specify:
s3_flash.back: D) Separate zones based on plant water requirements, sun exposure, and soil conditions (hydrozoning)
s3_flash.detail: Hydrozoning groups plants with similar water needs into separate irrigation zones for efficiency.

s3_flash.front: When designing exterior lighting for a pedestrian pathway, the landscape architect should consider:
s3_flash.back: C) Providing adequate and uniform illumination levels for safety while minimizing light pollution and glare
s3_flash.detail: Pathway lighting should provide adequate, uniform illumination while minimizing pollution and glare.

s3_flash.front: Bollard lighting is MOST appropriate for:
s3_flash.back: A) Providing low-level pathway lighting and defining edges
s3_flash.detail: Bollard lights provide low-level illumination appropriate for pathways and edge definition.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a green roof for a commercial building. Which of the following is a PRIMARY benefit of a green roof?
s3_flash.back: D) It reduces stormwater runoff, mitigates heat island effect, and provides habitat
s3_flash.detail: Green roofs reduce stormwater runoff, mitigate heat island effect, and provide habitat value.

s3_flash.front: Low Impact Development (LID) strategies include which of the following?
s3_flash.back: C) Bioretention cells, permeable paving, green roofs, and rainwater harvesting
s3_flash.detail: LID strategies include bioretention, permeable paving, green roofs, and rainwater harvesting.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is selecting plants for a xeriscape design. Which of the following is the MOST important criterion?
s3_flash.back: C) Selecting drought-tolerant plants adapted to the local climate that minimize water use once established
s3_flash.detail: Xeriscape designs prioritize drought-tolerant, climate-adapted plants that minimize water use once established.

s3_flash.front: A bioswale is designed to:
s3_flash.back: D) Convey and filter stormwater runoff through vegetation and engineered soil media
s3_flash.detail: Bioswales convey and filter stormwater through vegetation and engineered soil media.

s3_flash.front: When designing a detention basin for a development, the landscape architect should ensure:
s3_flash.back: A) The basin has appropriate side slopes for safety and maintenance, an outlet structure to control discharge, and an emergency overflow
s3_flash.detail: Detention basins need safe side slopes, outlet structures, and emergency overflows.

s3_flash.front: A concept plan is typically presented during which phase of the design process?
s3_flash.back: B) Schematic design
s3_flash.detail: Concept plans are typically presented during schematic design.

s3_flash.front: A section drawing is MOST useful for communicating:
s3_flash.back: A) Vertical relationships, elevation changes, spatial proportions, and the relationship between ground plane and vertical elements
s3_flash.detail: Section drawings communicate vertical relationships, elevation changes, and spatial proportions.

s3_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a pergola for a garden. The PRIMARY function of a pergola is to:
s3_flash.back: B) Define space, provide filtered shade, and support climbing plants
s3_flash.detail: Pergolas define space, provide filtered shade, and support climbing plants without full weather protection.

s3_flash.front: When designing a freestanding seat wall, the MOST comfortable seat height for adults is approximately:
s3_flash.back: B) 18 inches
s3_flash.detail: Approximately 18 inches is the most comfortable seat wall height for adults.

s3_flash.front: During design development, the landscape architect refines the approved schematic design. Which of the following is typically accomplished during this phase?
s3_flash.back: B) The landscape architect refines spatial relationships, selects specific materials and furnishings, and develops detailed design solutions
s3_flash.detail: Design development refines spatial relationships, selects specific materials, and develops detailed solutions.

s3_flash.front: EXAM FORMAT:  Section 3 uses four question types: standard multiple choice, select all that apply (multiple correct answers), drag and drop (place items in the correct order or location), and hotspot (click on a specific location in an image).
s3_flash.back: Hotspot questions may ask you to identify components in a construction detail or locate features on a plan. Practice reading details carefully before the exam.

s3_flash.front: The exam may show a construction drawing and ask you to interpret line types.
s3_flash.back: Remember: solid = visible, dashed = hidden/underground/existing contours, dot-dash = centerline. If a plan shows a dashed circle around a tree, it represents the drip line (canopy edge) used for tree protection.

s3_flash.front: Memory Aid
s3_flash.back: Pavement layers from bottom to top: Subgrade → Subbase (optional) → Base → Surface. Think of it as a sandwich: the bread (surface) gets all the wear, but the filling (base and subbase) provides the structural support.

s3_flash.front: Control joint spacing is one of the most tested construction topics.
s3_flash.back: The rule: maximum 10-12 feet in each direction, keep panels roughly square. If an exam question shows a 5-foot-wide sidewalk, control joints should be spaced every 5-10 feet to keep panels square.

s3_flash.front: In most jurisdictions, retaining walls over 4 feet in exposed height (measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall) require structural engineering.
s3_flash.back: The landscape architect designs walls up to 4 feet; taller walls require a structural engineer's stamp. Know this threshold.

s3_flash.front: Memory Aid
s3_flash.back: Wall drainage checklist: GPFW — Gravel backfill, Perforated pipe, Filter fabric, Weep holes. Every retaining wall needs all four. If one is missing, water will build up and the wall will eventually fail.

s3_flash.front: Memory Aid
s3_flash.back: Step formula: 2R + T = 26. A 6" riser: 2(6) + T = 26, so T = 14". A 7" riser: 2(7) + T = 26, so T = 12". These are the two most common outdoor combinations.

s3_flash.front: Fewer than 3 risers is a tripping hazard — people do not notice a single step or two-step change.
s3_flash.back: If the elevation change requires only 1-2 risers, consider a ramp instead, or add a visual contrast strip to make the steps obvious.

s3_flash.front: Memory Aid
s3_flash.back: Tree planting critical rules: Wide hole (2-3× root ball), shallow depth (flare at grade), native backfill, NO mulch volcano, stakes removed after 1-2 years. Remember: "Wide, Shallow, Native, No Volcano, Temporary Stakes."

s3_flash.front: Never mix spray heads and rotors in the same zone — this is one of the most common exam questions about irrigation design.
s3_flash.back: The reason is matched precipitation rates: spray heads apply 1.5-2.0 in/hr while rotors apply 0.5-1.0 in/hr. Mixing them in one zone makes uniform watering impossible.

s3_flash.front: Dark sky compliance = full cutoff fixtures (no uplight) + warm color temperature (≤3000K) + minimized light trespass.
s3_flash.back: If the exam asks how to reduce light pollution, these are the key strategies.

s3_flash.front: Memory Aid
s3_flash.back: Key CSI divisions for landscape architecture: 31-32-33. Division 31 = Earthwork (what you move). Division 32 = Exterior Improvements (what you build and plant on the surface). Division 33 = Utilities (what goes underground). Know these three division numbers.

s3_flash.front: Public projects often require open competition and may not allow proprietary (sole-source) specifications.
s3_flash.back: Performance and "or equal" specifications are preferred for public work to allow multiple manufacturers to bid, keeping costs competitive.

s3_flash.front: Memory Aid
s3_flash.back: Bidding sequence: A-P-A-B-E-N-C-N. Advertise → Pre-bid conference → Addenda → Bid opening → Evaluation → Notice of Award → Contract execution → Notice to Proceed. The contract time starts at NTP, not at award.

s3_flash.front: The distinction between "observation" and "inspection" is critical.
s3_flash.back: The LA OBSERVES work for general conformance with design intent. "Inspection" implies a guarantee that the work meets every requirement — a liability trap. If the exam uses "inspection," it is often the wrong answer.

s3_flash.front: Memory Aid
s3_flash.back: Closeout documents: AOWLS + T. As-builts, O&M manuals, Warranties, Lien releases, Spare parts, Training. The contractor owes you AOWLS and Training before getting final payment.

s3_flash.front: The warranty period starts at substantial completion, not final completion.
s3_flash.back: This is a frequently tested distinction. If the exam asks when the warranty clock starts, the answer is substantial completion.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect needs to determine the slope between two points. Point A is at elevation 102.0 and Point B is at elevation 98.0. The horizontal distance between them is 80 feet. What is the slope percentage?
Contour lines on a grading plan that form a "V" shape pointing uphill indicate:
s4_flash.back: D) A valley or swale
s4_flash.detail: Contour lines forming a "V" pointing uphill indicate a valley or swale where water collects.

s4_flash.front: When grading around a building, the finished grade should slope AWAY from the building at a minimum of:
s4_flash.back: A) 2% for 10 feet (or per code)
s4_flash.detail: A minimum 2% slope away from a building for at least 10 feet (or per local code) ensures positive drainage away from the foundation.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a grading plan and needs to calculate the elevation at a point between two contour lines. This process is called:
s4_flash.back: D) Interpolation
s4_flash.detail: Interpolation estimates values between two known points (contour lines).

s4_flash.front: The maximum slope for an ADA-compliant ramp is:
s4_flash.detail: ADA requires a maximum ramp slope of 1:12 (8.33%).

s4_flash.front: A proposed grading plan shows a finished floor elevation (FFE) of 100.0. The landscape architect should ensure the grade at the building perimeter is at LEAST:
s4_flash.back: D) 99.5 (6 inches below the FFE)
s4_flash.detail: The grade at the building perimeter should be at least 6 inches below the FFE to prevent water entry.

s4_flash.front: When grading a parking lot, the MINIMUM slope for adequate surface drainage is typically:
s4_flash.detail: Parking lots typically require 1% to 2% minimum slope for surface drainage.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a swale to convey stormwater. The minimum longitudinal slope for a grass-lined swale to ensure positive drainage is typically:
s4_flash.detail: Grass-lined swales typically require a minimum 1% to 2% slope for positive drainage.

s4_flash.front: In earthwork calculations, "cut" refers to:
s4_flash.back: A) Removing soil to lower the grade
s4_flash.detail: Cut is the removal of soil to lower the existing grade.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect is balancing cut and fill on a project site. The PRIMARY goal of balancing cut and fill is to:
s4_flash.back: D) Minimize the need for importing or exporting soil, reducing cost and environmental impact
s4_flash.detail: Balancing cut and fill minimizes the need for import or export, reducing cost and environmental impact.

s4_flash.front: When estimating earthwork quantities, the average end area method is used to:
s4_flash.back: A) Calculate the volume of earth between two cross-sections
s4_flash.detail: The average end area method calculates earthwork volume between two cross-sections.

s4_flash.front: Soil that has been excavated and placed as fill typically requires a "swell factor" because:
s4_flash.back: D) The excavated soil occupies more volume in a loose state than it did in its undisturbed state
s4_flash.detail: Excavated soil is loosened and occupies more volume than in its undisturbed state (swell).

s4_flash.front: A French drain is BEST described as:
s4_flash.back: D) A subsurface trench filled with gravel and perforated pipe to collect and redirect groundwater
s4_flash.detail: A French drain is a subsurface trench with gravel and perforated pipe for groundwater collection.

s4_flash.front: Manning's equation is used in drainage design to calculate:
s4_flash.back: A) The flow velocity and capacity of open channels and pipes
s4_flash.detail: Manning's equation calculates flow velocity and capacity in open channels and pipes.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect is sizing a storm drain pipe. If the contributing drainage area increases, the pipe size should:
s4_flash.back: A) Increase
s4_flash.detail: Larger drainage areas produce more runoff, requiring larger pipes.

s4_flash.front: An area drain (catch basin) is typically placed at:
s4_flash.back: B) Low points where surface water collects
s4_flash.detail: Area drains are placed at low points where surface water collects.

s4_flash.front: The time of concentration for a watershed is:
s4_flash.back: B) The time it takes for runoff to travel from the hydraulically most distant point in the watershed to the outlet
s4_flash.detail: Time of concentration is the time for runoff to travel from the most distant point to the outlet.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect designs a subsurface drainage system behind a retaining wall. The PRIMARY purpose of this drainage is to:
s4_flash.back: C) Relieve hydrostatic pressure that could cause wall failure
s4_flash.detail: Drainage behind retaining walls relieves hydrostatic pressure that could cause wall failure.

s4_flash.front: Pre-development versus post-development runoff analysis is conducted to:
s4_flash.back: C) Ensure that stormwater runoff rates and volumes after development do not exceed pre-development conditions
s4_flash.detail: Pre/post analysis ensures development does not increase runoff rates and volumes beyond pre-development levels.

s4_flash.front: A detention basin is designed to:
s4_flash.back: B) Temporarily store stormwater and release it at a controlled rate to reduce peak discharge
s4_flash.detail: Detention basins temporarily store water and release it at controlled rates to reduce peak discharge.

s4_flash.front: The difference between a detention basin and a retention basin is:
s4_flash.back: C) A detention basin temporarily stores and slowly releases water; a retention basin permanently holds water
s4_flash.detail: Detention temporarily stores and releases water; retention permanently holds water (like a pond).

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect specifies permeable interlocking concrete pavers (PICP) for a parking area. The PRIMARY stormwater benefit of PICP is:
s4_flash.back: C) It allows stormwater to infiltrate through the paver joints into an aggregate base, reducing runoff volume
s4_flash.detail: PICP allows stormwater to infiltrate through joints into the aggregate base, reducing runoff volume.

s4_flash.front: A typical construction detail for a concrete walkway should include:
s4_flash.back: A) Cross-section showing subgrade preparation, aggregate base depth, concrete thickness, reinforcement, joints, and finish
s4_flash.detail: A complete walkway detail shows subgrade, base, concrete thickness, reinforcement, joints, and finish.

s4_flash.front: Control joints in concrete flatwork are provided to:
s4_flash.back: B) Control the location of cracking due to shrinkage
s4_flash.detail: Control joints create a weakened plane to control where shrinkage cracking occurs.

s4_flash.front: The spacing of control joints in a 4-inch-thick concrete walkway should typically not exceed:
s4_flash.back: D) 8 to 10 feet (approximately 2 to 3 times the slab thickness in feet)
s4_flash.detail: Control joint spacing should be approximately 2 to 3 times the slab thickness in feet. For 4-inch slabs, 8-10 feet is typical.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect is detailing a stone veneer wall. The detail should show:
s4_flash.back: A) The structural backing (CMU or concrete), mortar bed, veneer stone, cap, footing, and drainage provisions
s4_flash.detail: A complete stone veneer detail shows the structural backing, mortar, veneer, cap, footing, and drainage.

s4_flash.front: When detailing a timber deck, the landscape architect should specify:
s4_flash.back: A) Posts supported on concrete footings extending below the frost line, with appropriate fasteners and flashing
s4_flash.detail: Deck posts require concrete footings below the frost line with proper fasteners and flashing.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect details an accessible curb ramp at a street crossing. The detail should include:
s4_flash.back: D) A ramp slope not exceeding 1:12, detectable warning surfaces, flared sides, and proper alignment with the crosswalk
s4_flash.detail: Accessible curb ramps need 1:12 max slope, detectable warnings, flared sides, and crosswalk alignment.

s4_flash.front: In the CSI MasterFormat system, Division 32 covers:
s4_flash.back: A) Exterior Improvements (site work including paving, planting, and site furnishings)
s4_flash.detail: CSI MasterFormat Division 32 covers Exterior Improvements including paving, planting, and site elements.

s4_flash.front: A prescriptive specification defines:
s4_flash.back: C) The specific materials, products, methods, and installation requirements
s4_flash.detail: Prescriptive specifications define specific materials, products, methods, and installation requirements.

s4_flash.front: The THREE parts of a CSI specification section are:
s4_flash.back: C) General, Products, Execution
s4_flash.detail: CSI specification sections have three parts: General, Products, and Execution.

s4_flash.front: When a specification includes the phrase "or approved equal," it means:
s4_flash.back: B) The contractor may propose an alternative product that meets the same performance criteria, subject to the landscape architect's approval
s4_flash.detail: "Or approved equal" allows the contractor to propose alternatives meeting the same criteria, subject to approval.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect's construction document set typically includes which of the following sheets?
s4_flash.back: B) Title sheet, demolition plan, layout plan, grading plan, drainage plan, planting plan, irrigation plan, and construction details
s4_flash.detail: A complete CD set includes title, demolition, layout, grading, drainage, planting, irrigation, and details.

s4_flash.front: Dimensions on a layout plan should reference:
s4_flash.back: C) Established baselines, property lines, building faces, or control points for accurate field layout
s4_flash.detail: Layout dimensions should reference baselines, property lines, building faces, or control points.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect includes a plant schedule on the planting plan. The schedule should include:
s4_flash.back: A) Botanical name, common name, quantity, size at installation, spacing (if applicable), root condition, and any special notes
s4_flash.detail: A plant schedule includes botanical name, common name, quantity, size, spacing, root condition, and notes.

s4_flash.front: A gravity retaining wall relies on which principle for stability?
s4_flash.back: B) Its own mass and weight to resist the lateral pressure of the retained soil
s4_flash.detail: Gravity walls resist lateral soil pressure through their own mass and weight.

s4_flash.front: The area behind a retaining wall where soil is placed is called:
s4_flash.back: B) The backfill zone
s4_flash.detail: The area behind a retaining wall where soil is placed is the backfill zone.

s4_flash.front: A landscape architect is designing a freestanding garden wall (not retaining soil). The wall requires a footing that extends:
s4_flash.back: D) Below the frost line to prevent heaving
s4_flash.detail: Freestanding wall footings must extend below the frost line to prevent frost heave.

s4_flash.front: During construction, a silt fence is installed to:
s4_flash.back: B) Temporarily trap sediment from disturbed areas and prevent it from leaving the site during construction
s4_flash.detail: Silt fences temporarily trap sediment during construction to prevent it from leaving the site.

s4_flash.front: A Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) is typically required for:
s4_flash.back: C) Construction activities that disturb one acre or more of land (per EPA NPDES requirements)
s4_flash.detail: SWPPP is required for construction disturbing one acre or more under EPA NPDES requirements.

s4_flash.front: EXAM FORMAT:  Section 4 uses all four question types: standard multiple choice, select all that apply, drag and drop (arranging items in sequence), and hotspot (clicking on a location in a plan or detail).
s4_flash.back: Hotspot questions may ask you to place contour lines on a grading plan, locate the correct position for a drainage inlet, or identify the high point in a drainage area. Practice interpreting topographic plans before the exam.

s4_flash.front: Memory Aid
s4_flash.back: Streams and ridges: V's point UP for streams (water flows down, contours point up). V's point DOWN for ridges (land rises, contours point down). Remember: "V's point opposite to what the feature does."

s4_flash.front: Hotspot questions may ask you to identify the location of a stream, ridge, or drainage divide on a contour map.
s4_flash.back: Look for the V-pattern in the contour lines. V's pointing uphill = stream. V's pointing downhill = ridge/drainage divide.

s4_flash.front: When the exam shows a contour map and asks for the elevation at a specific point, use linear interpolation between the two nearest contour lines.
s4_flash.back: Measure the point's proportional distance between the contours, then multiply by the contour interval and add to the lower contour elevation.

s4_flash.front: Memory Aid
s4_flash.back: Contour spacing = Interval ÷ Slope. Bigger slope = closer contours. A 2% slope with 1' interval has contours every 50 feet. A 5% slope has contours every 20 feet. Double the slope = half the spacing.

s4_flash.front: If a hotspot question asks you to draw contours around a building, remember: contours BEND AWAY from the building on all sides.
s4_flash.back: This is the graphic representation of positive drainage. The highest point is at the building; the lowest point is away from it.

s4_flash.front: Memory Aid
s4_flash.back: Soil swell/shrink: Bank soil EXPANDS when you dig it up (loose) and SHRINKS when you compact it (compacted fill). To balance a site, you need about 10-15% more bank-measure cut volume than the fill volume you need to place.

s4_flash.front: If the exam asks for earthwork volume, pay attention to whether the answer should be in bank, loose, or compacted cubic yards.
s4_flash.back: The same volume of earth has different measurements depending on its state. Always use bank cubic yards for cut/fill comparisons unless told otherwise.

s4_flash.front: Memory Aid
s4_flash.back: Rational Method: Q = CIA. Think "CIA agents handle the flow" — C is the character of the surface, I is the intensity of the storm, A is the area of the watershed. Multiply all three to get the flow rate Q.

s4_flash.front: When calculating composite C, make sure all areas sum to the total drainage area.
s4_flash.back: It is easy to forget a surface type or double-count an area. Double-check: Σ An = total area. Also verify your units — A must be in acres, i in inches/hour.

s4_flash.front: This table is one of the most important for Section 4.
s4_flash.back: If the exam describes clay soils (HSG D), eliminate all infiltration-only BMPs. Choose detention, retention, or practices with underdrains. If the exam describes sandy soils (HSG A), infiltration practices are ideal.

s4_flash.front: Memory Aid
s4_flash.back: Erosion control = keep the soil WHERE IT IS (source control). Sediment control = catch the soil AFTER it moves (treatment). Erosion control is always the first priority because it is more effective and cheaper.

s4_flash.front: Silt fence is the most commonly misunderstood ESC practice.
s4_flash.back: It is a SEDIMENT control device (captures eroded soil), NOT an erosion control device (does not prevent erosion). Silt fence must be installed along the contour — never run silt fence downhill, or water will flow around the ends and the fence will fail.

s4_flash.front: Memory Aid
s4_flash.back: Manning's equation: V = (1.49/n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2). Think "Velma runs slowly" — Velocity depends on Roughness (n) and Slope (S). Smoother surface (lower n) = faster. Steeper slope (higher S) = faster. The 1.49 is a unit conversion factor for US customary units.
